activities are carried out in the various states in respect of their aircraft. in other words, it would not be a question of the european civil aviation agency going to a third country to check how ensure that aircraft landing on our territory meet all the requirements and to control how those requirements are met on those aircraft. we must take a further step forward, in the sense that there other things, thanks to this parliament, let us say it clearly - which includes, in the end, a series of guarantees demanded by the european union - reduction in the number of data, the type of data, limitation as to the purpose for which they are to be used, limitation in the time of their use, in short, all the elements that you are perfectly aware of - which allows us to say that, with this the future enlarged europe. this is the only way to achieve general, clear and stable legal rules which will give a future perspective to the investments of the electricity companies and which will at the same time provide reassurance and information to the public on the conditions under which nuclear energy is used within the european union. as regards the proposal for a directive laying down basic obligations and general principles in the field of safety at nuclear installations, the commission has complied with the european parliament's request that nuclear safety be ensured also during the decommissioning process. this is a sensitive issue involving concerns about nuclear safety and the desire for fair competition in the electricity market. the commission proposal, which is legally based on the euratom treaty, makes it possible to meet parliament's expectations in a balanced way. the analysis of parliament's amendments clearly shows that the opinion to be sent to the council will make it possible, in particular, to avoid any attempt by some states to distort the commission's initial proposals. the commission may be somewhat flexible, but it does not intend to back down from the political objectives it set itself when drawing up the proposals. we therefore believe that it is essential to ensure that sufficient financial resources are available to ensure that dismantling operations are carried out under appropriate safety conditions. as regards the proposal for a directive on the management of spent fuel and radioactive waste, i take note of the proposals to amend the timetable for authorizing the establishment and putting into service of the final storage sites. the first discussions in the council have raised comments in line with this idea. it is clear that the two institutions consider the timetable proposed by the commission to be too ambitious. i still believe that the problem is not the proposed dates but that most of the member states have not made sufficient progress in their decisions and work. i do not mean that this is the case in finland, for example, which is making great strides and has taken concrete decisions, or in sweden, which has also made very important steps forward. the commission can also show a certain flexibility in terms of timetable, provided that we are talking about concrete and reasonable deadlines. this is what parliament is proposing: more time, but with specific dates. in that sense, we believe that this margin of flexibility is acceptable. the permanent storage of high-level and long-lived radioactive waste in deep geological formations enjoys international technical consensus that it is currently the best solution to isolate radioactive waste from people and the environment for the long periods needed. which doesn't mean we're not working on other solutions. the commission does not want to close any doors and the fact that this is the most appropriate solution today does not mean that it will be in ten years' time. we are therefore guided solely by the desire to ensure safe and sustainable management of radioactive waste in order to ensure effective protection of citizens. in this sense, an increase in research and development could be proposed if necessary, and we do not rule out other solutions, i insist, but on the contrary, we support further research in this field. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to confirm that the primary objective of the commission's legislative proposal is simply to ensure the highest possible level of security within the enlarged european union. and in addition to ensuring that high level of security, we want to make this matter more transparent to the public and, most especially, to this parliament. and also to deal with the problem of radioactive waste management in the nuclear sector, so that the various member states deal with this issue in a determined manner. i would stress that the application of this community legislation will provide the european community sector with stable and balanced general rules which will allow the sector to develop without discrimination or advantage to anyone. in this connection, i am pleased to note that the european parliament, the council and the commission are working together to provide the enlarged union with a genuine community policy on nuclear safety when the rapporteur. {es) mr president, this so-called nuclear package, which we are discussing tonight, has its origin in two stimuli: the first, enlargement of the union and the second, without a doubt, the green paper on security of energy supply. enlargement has brought into the union a number of countries with fission power stations, a different safety culture from that of western europe and different technological criteria from those common to the fifteen today. the accession process has achieved all the security objectives that these countries were required to meet, and so we can now be absolutely certain. however, since nuclear energy is unfortunately not only considered in strictly technical or scientific or practical terms, but is often imbued with ideology and too often with emotion, it was absolutely essential that europe should provide european citizens with a regulatory framework of a european dimension to reassure certain legitimate concerns. this nuclear package meets this need and we believe it does so adequately. the green paper states as one of its basic conclusions that for the future of energy in europe we must keep all options open and i stress the 'all'. the commission has already taken the necessary steps to ensure that the community's energy policy is properly implemented. it is precisely because of the emotional factors to which i referred earlier, the existence of a legally binding european regulatory framework which guarantees us that nuclear safety is a common objective of the union, dealt with by a shared methodology and with the due guarantees that any anomaly or incident will be addressed in accordance with the latest available technical advances, all this, mr president, is what the nuclear package also provides to public opinion in the union. it has been discussed, mr president, whether directives were necessary for this nuclear package, or whether recommendations, guidelines or weaker legal figures would have been sufficient. i must say that if this softer level of regulation had been used, the whole exercise would have been worthless because what european citizens really need is to be assured of their requirement of the highest standards for this type of installation and that is only guaranteed by a legally binding rule such as a directive. as regards the two specific legislative initiatives we have examined, all the concerns of parliament have been duly reflected in our respective reports. the flexibility of the timetable for the establishment of a final storage facility for high-level waste, the avoidance of a double layer of european and national regulations overlapping and undermining efficiency, the public participation in this whole process and the most complete information to citizens have also been guaranteed and i would not want to forget to mention that in the directive on waste it was essential, in our opinion, that although deep geological burial in stable formations is the most universally accepted option today, the door should be open to other lines of research in the future. commissioner, this nuclear package is certainly a step forward and although you are feeling cold in your skin today, the way you have approached this problem shows that the fire of decision is constantly burning inside you. in any case, this nuclear package proves something else and that is that when there is a problem which is difficult to solve at national level, as one of our great spanish thinkers of the 20th century said, 'in europe the solution is found'.

commission. - mr president, the commission would first of all like to thank mrs almeida garrett for her very good work on the commission communication on the framework for regulatory agencies. the fact is that there are currently 16 agencies which have been set up under the current treaties, in successive waves, and to meet specific needs on a case-by-case basis. the 16 agencies are now characterised by their diversity, both in their mode of operation, in the tasks assigned to them and in their names. as we stressed in 2001, we believe that the creation of new regulatory agencies contributes to improving the implementation of community rules. the 2001 white paper proposed that the commission should define parameters, more precise criteria for the establishment, operation and monitoring of these agencies. the first objective of our communication, the one which is the subject of your debate, is therefore to initiate a debate with you and, moreover, with the council, in a common framework, on the creation, operation and control of the future regulatory agencies which we define as actively participating in the exercise of the executive function at community level. as your rapporteur has just said, their action is indeed at the very heart of the executive power. to avoid any misunderstanding - i will come back to this in my reply to the debate, particularly on the point raised by the rapporteur - this initiative does not concern the so-called executive agencies which are involved in the management of community programmes. in short, what is the point of the commission's proposal? it is a balance between, on the one hand, strengthening the integrity and unity of the executive function - and we know that this is primarily the commission's responsibility - and, on the other hand, the autonomy that these agencies must be able to enjoy in order to ensure that their action is sustainable. it's all about finding that delicate balance. the agencies, on the one hand, are designed to relieve the commission of highly technical tasks and to enable it to refocus on essential tasks. however - and you reminded mrs almeida garrett - the commission must retain the final political responsibility for the implementation of the rules, since this is one of the things for which we are responsible to you and we need clearly identified officials to be present in your assembly. it is this difficult balance that needs to be improved, clarified and formalised, given that regulatory agencies are increasingly responding to a need for expertise of increasing level in a number of areas, irrespective of short-term considerations. in order for this expertise to be constant and to ensure a certain level of transparency, a certain degree of autonomy and of course control is also required. it is this balance that we are seeking and we await your debate to see whether the way we have formulated this balance corresponds to your own capacity to compromise on these tensions which are inevitable but which we wish to manage in a positive way.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. - question no 13 by reino paasilinna (h-0823/03):control of the blocking of spam e-mails: member states should have transposed the directive on the processing of personal data and the protection of privacy in the electronic communications sector by the end of october. on 5 december the commission announced that it was opening infringement proceedings against nine member states for their delay in transposing the directive. the majority of e-mails now consist of spam. what other measures does the commission intend to take to achieve the aims of the directive? the reliability of e-mail has been weakened and its development has stalled. how will the commission ensure that the member states take the necessary measures to put pressure on providers, for example, so that the main advantage of electronic communications, namely flexibility, can be guaranteed?
commission. it is true that unsolicited commercial e-mail, or 'spam', has reached worrying proportions: over 50% of e-mail traffic, according to many experts, is now 'spam'. the commission also agrees that 'spam' undermines not only privacy and consumer protection, but also productivity at work and overall productivity growth. consumer confidence in e-mail is falling, according to some studies. it is, however, a prerequisite for the successful development of e-commerce and the information society in general. the commission is reacting on several fronts. firstly, the european union has acted on the legislative front by adopting, in 2002, the directive on privacy and electronic communications – as mr paasilinna will know because he made a considerable contribution to the discussion. infringement proceedings were launched in november 2003 against a number of member states that had failed to take the necessary transposition measures. secondly, the commission knows that legislation is only part of the answer. the commission has discussed with interested parties a series of actions for member states, industry and consumers to take. these actions will complement legislation and seek to make the ban on 'spam' as effective as possible. they focus on effective enforcement by member states, self-regulatory efforts by industry, technical solutions such as filtering and security, and consumer awareness. on enforcement in particular, member states must not only put in place adequate complaint mechanisms, remedies and penalties, but also prosecute 'spammers' effectively and monitor 'spam'. cooperation between industry and public authorities is important in this regard. the commission is also taking steps to improve cross-border cooperation inside the union by meeting relevant authorities. since a large volume of 'spam' originates outside the european union, international cooperation will also be essential. several actions are under way in this regard. let me mention some of them. firstly the declaration and action plan agreed at the united nations world summit on the information society call for appropriate action on 'spam' to be taken at national and international level. secondly the commission will be hosting an oecd seminar on 'spam' on 2 and 3 february 2004 in brussels. thirdly, bilateral contacts are ongoing with third countries, including the competent authorities in the united states, since a large volume of 'spam' seems to come from us-based companies. these actions are the subject of a communication on 'spam' which the commission will adopt in the next few days. finally, the safer internet action plan and, to a greater extent, its likely successor, safe internet plus, will also fund activities relating to 'spam', including 'spam' sent to children. to conclude, however, let me stress one element: no one party acting in isolation will be able to solve the problem; success will depend on the firm commitment of all interested parties.
the commission. - question no 16 by alexandros alavanos (h-0837/03) subject: extradition agreement between the eu and the usa an agreement between the eu and the us on extradition in criminal matters was signed in washington on 25 june 2003. it has since been published in the official journal of the european union (oj l 181, 19.7.2003, p. 25). can the commission give us any assurance that the united states has no right under the agreement to demand the extradition of a citizen of a member state whose offence has been dealt with by the courts of that member state but is time-barred under the national law of that member state, or the extradition of a citizen who has already been convicted in the case in that member state? has the agreement entered into force? if not, what is the commission's expected timetable? question to mr byrne
the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on 23 june 2003 two agreements were signed between the european union and the united states of america, respectively on extradition and mutual legal assistance in criminal matters. these agreements were negotiated by the presidency of the council, although, as provided for in articles 38 and 24 of the treaty, the presidency was always assisted in the negotiations by the commission. as regards the question whether or not the extradition agreement confers on the united states the right to request from a member state the extradition of a person who has committed a crime in that member state which has already been prescribed by its law, the agreement does not lay down specific provisions on the matter. however, member states may invoke grounds for refusal relating to matters not covered by the agreement which are applicable in accordance with bilateral extradition treaties in force between a member state and the united states of america. this is the result of article 17 of the extradition agreement between the european union and the united states of america. the same applies to the second question of the honourable member, namely the situation of a person who has already been sentenced by the member state to which the request is addressed. none of the two agreements between the european union and the united states has yet entered into force, some member states have declared that they are obliged to respect their national constitutional procedures for the entry into force of the agreements and, in addition, written bilateral instruments between each member state and the united states of america are required for the implementation of the agreements between the union and the united states of america. these complementary bilateral instruments are currently being negotiated and once all the bilateral instruments have been agreed, they will have to be ratified by the congress of the united states of america.

commission. the commission fully shares the concern of the honourable member as regards the threat to the community citrus crop caused by the harmful organisms intercepted by spain. following the notification by spain of the preventive measures it has taken against citrus fruits originating in argentina and brazil, and in accordance with the relevant provisions laid down in the community plant health regime, the commission initiated discussions on the issue in the meeting of the standing committee on plant health on 11 and 12 december 2003. in the meantime, the commission has also urgently requested from argentina and brazil additional technical information in respect of the situation faced by spain, and about which the commission fully shares its concern. the commission and the member states agreed to review the position at the next meeting of the standing committee on 22 january 2004. the commission will then consider any action ensuring that organisms harmful to citrus fruits – like citrus canker, from which the community is free – are not introduced into and spread within the community. the commission expects to achieve a satisfactory solution before the next import campaign.

question no 22 by jan marinus wiersma (h-0797/03) subject: obsolete pesticidesthe problem of obsolete pesticides is a burden on the situation in ukraine, where there are 20,000 tonnes of such pesticides distributed in over 5,000 places as a threat to drinking water and the health of the local population. despite the adoption in june 2001 of the sixth environmental framework programme, which contains a specific section on pesticides, including specific measures to eliminate the risks associated with obsolete pesticides, three and a half years have now passed without any significant improvement in the situation. can the commission come up with a constructive financial solution or find a constructive financial instrument for ukraine? and question no 23 by robert goodwill (h-0798/03): the serious problem of obsolete pesticides in ukraine affects the health of the population and the environment, and urgent action is needed to deal with the more than 20 000 tonnes in at least 5 000 different locations throughout the country. in paragraph 74 of its resolution of 23 october 2003 on the proposal for the general budget of the european union for the financial year 2004, parliament referred to the risks posed to the environment by persistent organic pollutants (pops) and, in particular, by obsolete pesticides, and called on the commission to make the additional effort necessary to provide sufficient financial resources under the existing instruments for the elimination of pops in ukraine. in view of this, can the commission take steps to find an appropriate solution?
commission. we are aware of the threat to the environment and to consumer health that obsolete pesticides constitute in ukraine and aware, too, of the magnitude of the challenge that their elimination poses to that country. ukraine has taken a positive step concerning the elimination of some of the obsolete pesticides, in particular those that are persistent organic pollutants, by signing the stockholm convention regarding the elimination and reduction of those pollutants. the ratification of the convention is still pending. the commission urges ukraine to ratify the convention and to cooperate with the international community to work on this difficult problem. responsibility for dealing with obsolete pesticides is primarily for the country itself. while the commission is prepared to assist ukraine to the extent possible – and i should just note that our assistance to ukraine amounts to eur 126 million a year – current eu assistance programmes do not provide funding for the elimination of obsolete pesticides in ukraine. in fact, environmental issues have not been selected by the government of ukraine as a key cooperation area with the european union. however, tacis small project programmes could accommodate project proposals linked to the elimination of obsolete pesticides. taking into account the amount of pesticides to be eliminated, an eu contribution could only partially alleviate the vast problem. as a signatory to the stockholm convention, ukraine is eligible for funding from the interim global environmental facility, which is the financing mechanism of the convention.
commission. i totally agree with the honourable member that obsolete pesticides are a real and serious problem, not just in ukraine; they are a common problem in all too many post-soviet regions, as well as in some acceding and candidate countries. the estimate is that in ukraine there are perhaps up to 20 000 tonnes of these pesticides in 5000 locations and, as the honourable member knows, they can affect human health because of the contamination of groundwaters, soil, food and even air. the honourable member mentioned chernobyl: i was there recently. we have dedicated a lot of time and a great deal of money to that extraordinarily difficult and dangerous environmental issue. there we are working with the government of ukraine, which wishes to take that as a priority. it has not been easy even in those circumstances. what is more difficult for us, is to insist on our priorities through a programme such as tacis, in which the partner country is supposed to take ownership of the programme we are helping to support. i can assure the honourable member that we will continue to raise this issue and other environmental issues in the relevant subcommittee of the partnership and cooperation agreement. we will raise this issue during those meetings and if the government in ukraine says it would like us to focus some of our spending on this issue, we would be delighted to look at that. but the figures involved are very substantial. it is reckoned that it would cost at least eur 100 million for the elimination of the problem i described earlier, and that is why, in our judgment, it is probably more helpful to turn to the global environmental facility in order to secure an objective which the honourable member is quite right to highlight.
commission. the honourable member is entirely right to say that the issue we are discussing is of considerable concern to many groups in ukraine, and many of the environmental ngos which have begun to be active. the issue in which he has taken a particular interest – water contamination – has been of considerable concern to many people. i can only repeat that we will raise this issue with the ukrainian authorities. we will be willing, if they wish, to consider ways in which we could assist through the tacis programme. however, the need for funds for the overall elimination of pesticides in ukraine is beyond the present budgetary resources of the european union, though we can encourage ukraine to turn to other possible financing sources in order to deal with what is a horrendously difficult problem.

(es) mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mr moraes, on his efforts and on the good work he has done on a report on immigration, integration and employment, which i think deserves a clearly favourable opinion. these are matters in which personal feelings and opinions can easily emerge, as well as political temptations, and i have therefore wanted to refer to the content of the communication. immigration is a reality that needs to be regulated, and we cannot put our heads under the hood or look the other way. in europe, particularly in countries with lower birth rates (spain and italy, among others), immigration is a necessary remedy. if the population, as the rapporteur has said, is estimated to fall from 303 million to 297 million in 2020 in the european union of twenty-five and is further estimated to fall to 280 million by 2030, the decline in employment could have a negative impact on economic growth, insofar as it is the result of increased employment and productivity. that is precisely why immigration should not be seen as a problem but as an opportunity. an opportunity that, of course, raises some problems that we need to solve. without going into the details, i will mention the integration of foreign children of immigrants into schools; intercultural coexistence in neighbourhoods and workplaces; family reunification, with all the problems raised by the very concept of reunification in a broad or narrow sense; the regulation of the undocumented; the fight against illegal immigration and the mafias who exploit it; and, in particular, the specific situation of immigrant women. in conclusion, immigrants are necessary, but how many immigrants can we accept? all you want? it seems impossible. it would be like transferring to some of the member states the same problems that immigrants are trying to get out of. given that in countries with very low birth rates, without immigration, the relationship between active and passive workers would become unsustainable in the medium term, it seems to me that the right way is to integrate them. they are labour, but above all they are human beings who are needed by the member states. the tampere principles are therefore still valid: cooperation with the countries of origin, a common european asylum system, the management of migration flows and fair treatment of third country nationals. i believe that the charter of fundamental rights of the european union gives us the guidelines to follow in its articles 4, 5 and 14, or what is the same thing, the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment, the prohibition of forced labour and the right to education. since we are putting so much emphasis on the idea of employment, more specifically, article 15 proclaims the right of third-country nationals authorized to work in the territory of the member states to equal conditions with nationals. article 20 proclaims equality of persons before the law. article 21 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of other grounds, including nationality; article 23 guarantees equality between men and women in all areas, including employment, work and pay. the report by mr moraes describes situations and proposes measures which are generally acceptable in view of the often disadvantageous situation of immigrants in terms of wages, health and safety at work, working time and illegal work. in short, it is often, in more cases than desirable and in no case desirable, a situation of exploitation. we said that the first way of integration was employment, followed of course by cultural integration, but we must not forget that the same charter of fundamental rights of the european union, in its article 1, says: 'human dignity is inviolable. and it speaks to the dignity of every human being.
(es) mr president, commissioner, i think it is important that for the first time in this parliament - and a little late - we have a debate on the phenomenon of migration, linked to two important secondly, the possible posting of workers to a work centre or to an enterprise belonging to the group; and thirdly, the posting of workers from a temporary employment enterprise located in a member state which supplies them to a user operating in a member state other than that of the transferor. any of these situations can create disadvantages for posted workers, and of a different order: the first one that comes to mind may be their working conditions; hence the importance of directive 96/71/ec, which is a catalogue of minimum standards of protection under community law, although insufficient, since it does not in fact cover standards or aspects such as social security. i think the rapporteur has identified the problems well: unfair competition, a difference in social protection and therefore a detriment to workers, the need for a clear definition of the workers' statute. but it is also worth adding, and this has also been discussed here, the possible abuse of displacement and the problems arising from subcontracting and in general from the new forms of outsourcing, decentralization or decentralisation of production or, if you like, from the new forms of production organization. in conclusion, madam commissioner, i think that we have before us the opportunity, or perhaps the need, for a common core of mandatory minimum standards in all cases and at least guarantees, below which the condition of work or performance of the service is unlawful when the legislation of the state of the service is inferior to that of the place of origin of the displacement. without such a guarantee, in the scope in which it can take place, i believe that the possibilities of abuse and fraud are within the reach of the irresponsible businessman. and what would be worse, we could be inviting that fraud and that abuse.

significantly reduced the risk of fraud, in particular through new rules on the award of grants and subsidies, and contains strict rules on the exclusion of conflicts of interest. the new financial it is not its task to carry out central ex ante and ex post sample checks, nor does it have staff available for these purposes. the authorising officers by delegation are responsible for this and the directors-general are responsible for ensuring that the control systems are in place in accordance with the financial regulation and the sectoral rules. article 60 of the new financial regulation gives the authorising officer full responsibility for financial operations, and the prodi commission has thus implemented the recommendation made in the second report of the independent experts, which was supported by parliament. the main lessons the commission learns from the eurostat affair concern the exchange of information and inter-service cooperation, for example between the internal audit service, the internal audit capabilities and the horizontal directorates-general. indeed, it is necessary to ensure that information on irregularities reaches the political level and leads to immediate action. the committee on budgetary control of parliament has rightly placed the greatest emphasis on this throughout the debate. we have had a very difficult time over the past year because of the eurostat affair. i think that is true of the commission as well as of the work of the committee on budgetary control, and the president of the commission has spoken very extensively on all aspects here in this house on two occasions, and then we worked together to draw the necessary consequences and changes. i can assure you that the commission, which has started and is implementing the administrative reform with great commitment, will also implement the necessary additions to the reform consistently.

- the next item is the report (a5-0026/2004) by mr cercas, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the organisation of working time (review of directive 93/104/ec) (2003/2165 (ini)).
the rapporteur. {es) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the main purpose of my report is to examine two articles of council directive 93/104/ec on certain aspects of the organisation of working time. ten years ago this important directive was adopted, which regulates certain fundamental elements for the health and safety of employees, such as daily rest and holiday periods. the directive also sets the maximum weekly working time at 48 hours, although it allows its average calculation to be made over a reference period of four months. the adoption of this important directive - one of the most important in the community's social order - was not peaceful. the united kingdom's resistance was only defeated before the court of justice and, for ten years, two temporary exceptions had to be made to the reference period in which the 48 hours per week were calculated, and to the actual application of the 48 hours per week in those countries which wished to regulate this exception to the will of the workers, provided that this was expressed in a credible and free way: this is what is known as individual opting-out. the commission and the council should have reviewed these temporary derogations before 26 november. however, unfortunately, the commission did not communicate its analyses or proposals on that date. it was not until 30 december 2003 that it submitted a communication to us or opened a consultation period, and yet its text lacks concrete proposals on the most pressing issues. what the commission has done - and i am grateful for that - is to commission a study from the university of cambridge - by barnard, deakin and hobbs - on the use made of the opt-out by the country which adopted it - the united kingdom - which gives us a thorough insight into the negative consequences of its massive use and abuse in a labour market where it has been applied in a general way. my report was concerned solely with reviewing these two exceptions in order to answer, not with a tongue-in-cheek but with clarity, the mandatory question of the directive: ten years after adoption, does it make sense to continue extending the reference periods? does it make sense to maintain the principle that the 48-hour maximum does not apply through individual opt-outs? both questions, i believe in my report, must be answered in the light of the principles which defined the adoption of the directive: the health and safety of workers. these must be accompanied by a third element: flexibility, which the commission itself points out in its communication. we must ensure that the working and family lives of europeans are reconciled. my proposals are also clear. on the basis of our objective information, there is no reason to repeal the extension of reference periods which have proved useful and have not, at least for the time being, caused serious consequences for the health and safety of workers, but on the contrary, there is overwhelming evidence that the opt-out seriously infringes minimum rights to health and safety and is a serious risk to the reconciliation of family and professional life. the debate and the vote in the committee on employment have been very hard. i hope we can continue working and getting closer tomorrow. i have personally been open to the element of flexibility, including the problem of the doctor's watch which has been introduced into this debate. i've been flexible, as is the directive. i have not stopped saying, and i will continue to say until the end, that individual opt-outs set very serious precedents: minimum rights, mr president, are inalienable. if today workers are forced or allowed to waive basic rights, such as maximum working hours, tomorrow, with the same argument, they could be allowed to waive other fundamental elements of their health and safety, work in noisy, dusty environments, remove protective barriers on construction sites, waive maternity rights and many other things. and all in the name of individual liberty, which disappears when it is applied. it's a terrible precedent for this. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying that our charter of fundamental rights and article 137 of the treaty oblige us to curb the wishes of those who do not want european standards. opting-out is not a flexible rule: it is the absence of rules. by allowing someone to be exempted from a basic legislation of minimum fundamental rights, the absence of rules is being defended. and i hope that all colleagues will give this a thorough thought. we cannot offer victory to those who do not want to see the social europe built, to those who are allergic to the minimum standards which the workers of our continent have enjoyed for more than a century.
(es) mr president, commissioner, rapporteur, we are faced with a report which seems to me to be of profound social, legal and political significance. this is because the completion of the internal market must lead to an improvement in working conditions, because the community will support and complement the action of the member states in the fields of the protection of the safety and health of workers, as required by article 137 of the ec treaty, and because every worker has the right to limitation of the maximum working time, to daily and weekly rest periods, and to a period of paid annual leave, as well as to working conditions which respect his health, safety and dignity, as proclaimed by the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. the question is very simple, therefore, in a theoretical approach. the first aspect is that of the reference periods for the application of article 6 (maximum weekly working time): four months, as laid down in article 16 of the directive, or, where appropriate, possibilities of extension in the cases provided for in article 17: up to six and twelve months if this is done by collective agreements or agreements concluded between the social partners. the second aspect is the option not to apply article 6 if the worker gives his consent, that is the opt-out system, as has already been said here. the extension of the reference periods obviously has the consequence of extending the flexibility granted to undertakings. the only limit would thus be 11 hours of daily rest or 24 hours of weekly rest, but the directive would lose its purpose to regulate only the maximum working time every four months, every six months or every year, as the case may be. as regards the opting-out, the possibility of abuse is evident, particularly in the face of the situation of legal equality but not economic equality between the protagonists of working life. directive 93/104/ec is intended to ensure a better level of protection of the safety and health of workers, as reiterated in directive 2000/34/ec itself. it is therefore necessary to seek effective solutions for the situations and activities which require it, such as those referred to in the simap and jäger judgments, but with objective criteria or conditions, with general and non-abusive uses, and in any event without turning the exception into the general rule. i therefore believe that we should seek agreements before the vote to reconcile the legal guarantees for workers with flexibility, in the spirit of directive 93/104/ec.

(es) mr president, on 27 june 2003 the commission published a new proposal with the aim of ensuring the sustainable recovery of the northern hake population and its reduction within what is considered a safe biological limit, a precautionary biomass level of 165 000 tonnes. firstly, and this is something to be thanked for, the commission has finally decided to separate the cod and hake stocks into two different plans. it could not be otherwise after the obvious improvement in cod stocks, a direct consequence of the management measures applied by the sector for two years. but when we look at the proposed measures, we also find that the commission does not take into account the best available scientific information, nor does it dispel the doubts of the fishing industry, because, once again, there has been no dialogue with scientists and the proposal has been drawn up without serious involvement of the professionals. the commission is basing itself on scientific opinions, the content of which it does not specify and which, as the rapporteur mr souchet very well says in his explanatory statement, it has not disclosed to the committee on fisheries, despite our request. the precautionary biomass should have been established in the light of these scientific reports which have not existed. nor does this biomass appear to be proportionate to the status of the affected population, as the latest independent scientific reports and observations of practitioners show that it is not below safe biological limits. nor do we have any scientific assessments from ices to guarantee that the proposed reduction in fishing effort will lead to an effective reduction in catches, nor an assessment of the effects of the technical recovery measures - - question no 34 by mr pimenta question no 35 by gerard collins (h-0851/03) subject: measures to promote low-cost air travel can the commission give details of the measures it is promoting to support low-cost air travel in europe, given that the vast majority of eu citizens fully support and recognise the importance of low-cost airlines within the eu?
vice-president of the commission. (es) as a result of the liberalization of air transport in the european union in the early 1990s - which was also done on the basis of legislative proposals from the commission - we can see how competition has increased between the different airlines in the european union and how users benefit from lower fares and a better offer. in this same context, a new phenomenon has emerged: the so-called low-cost companies. the commission sees this as a positive development: it increases the supply to passengers, it means more economic activity, more opportunities for consumers and, moreover, it is raising the possibility of cheaper fares. the commission's action is to ensure this development by strictly applying the competition and state aid rules. in this respect, i have to say that it is not our job to support this or that sector, but to provide balanced rules which allow the development of the different types of aviation activity: the traditional companies with their type of business and the new companies, the so-called low-cost companies, which have a somewhat different market and which have undoubtedly considerably increased competition, supply and possibilities for the user.
vice-president of the commission. (es) i believe that, on the contrary, the solution and the answer which the commission has given in the ryanair charleroi case - which, rather than being about ryanair, is about the state aid given by charleroi airport, and that is the problem - opens up new possibilities for the promotion and development of regional airports, which are engines of regional development, and for the operation from these airports of the so-called 'low-cost companies'. i think the commission's decision is a balanced one. the commission has also concluded that the airport services agreement with ryanair was not in line with the market economy operator principle. however, it has placed some limits on them, in terms of time and above all in terms of the availability of such aid to any other company that is willing to carry out the same type of activity, in the interests of equal treatment for all companies operating in europe and transparency in this type of operation. but i would like to reiterate that the decision on charleroi is a bet on regional airports and low-cost airlines. it should be remembered that in the charleroi case we did not act on our own initiative but because complaints had been lodged with the commission and because the commission, as the honourable member knows, is obliged to resolve them. in fact, complaints have been made about other airports in various european countries. we shall deal with them in the coming months, when all the extremes that correspond in each case have been clarified. i think we are helping to clarify the situation, because there are a number of other regional airports which, thanks to the response to charleroi, will be able to offer airlines similar conditions, which will enable them to expand and develop their activities.
vice-president of the commission. (es) i would remind the honourable member that in the railway sector, as far as passenger transport is concerned, we have not yet achieved liberalisation. the railways in each country therefore operate as they see fit and have the support that each country is prepared to give them, based on criteria such as public service and the maintenance of the companies. so at the moment, low-cost companies may be competing with railway activity, but railways are benefiting from state support in virtually all countries. later, after a discussion on the third railway package, which i hope you will have for discussion shortly, and which i hope the next parliament and the next commission will be able to complete, we envisage the introduction of competition in rail passenger transport on international sections, not on national sections. at that point, we will have to see what effects this has on competition, but - i repeat - the aid we have authorized is limited in time and in amount. in no case may they exceed a maximum of 50% of the operating costs and, in addition, they must be decreasing for a maximum of five years. i think it is a balanced decision, which allows us to combine support for a regional airport, which - i repeat - is a source of dynamism and economic activity for a region. in the case of wallonia - an objective 1 region which is lagging behind the community average - this is what justifies the support for aid, not whether or not there are cheap tickets. an airline giving cheap tickets to people does not justify receiving public subsidies. the commission notes that the airport services agreement with ryanair was signed on the same day as the agreement with ryanair, and that the agreement with ryanair was signed on the same day as the agreement with ryanair. we have also agreed on the possibility of granting aid in the air transport sector when the public service condition is met. for example, in the case of the outermost islands and in the case of archipelagos, for reasons of internal public service. and in that case too, they must be subject to conditions of transparency, competition and equal treatment.

question no 37 by bill newton dunn (h-0026/04):on: drug smuggling how successful does the commission think the eu's five-year plan which expires this year has been, given how our streets are flooded with heroin and other drugs?
commission. the eu drugs strategy 2000-2004 provides a framework for a balanced and integrated approach on all drug-related activities in the european union. it has also been endorsed by the new member states and the candidate countries who have, in the meantime, set up national drug strategies and improved their capacities for taking action against drugs with the support of the phare programme. the union also has a number of drug action plans involving certain regions either producing or serving as transit countries for drugs, such as latin america, central asia and the balkans. research shows that a link between a particular drug policy line and the drug situation is difficult to establish. the availability and careful evaluation of relevant and reliable information are undoubtedly key elements in developing an evidence-based drug policy. the work of the european monitoring centre on drugs and drug addiction and the work of europol in this area form part of the basis for the commission communication to the council and the european parliament on the mid-term evaluation of the eu action plan on drugs. this mid-term evaluation was a first step in a larger process. by the end of this year we will have the final evaluation. without wanting to pre-empt the results of the final evaluation, the following developments on the eu drugs market can already be observed. heroin seizures have increased since 2001. our assessment is that street prices are generally stable or even decreasing. the number of heroin addicts seems to be relatively stable in the european union, although there are marked differences between the member states. cannabis remains the most widely-used illicit drug and its use is still increasing in many member states. the use of synthetic drugs such as ecstasy and the use of cocaine seem to be increasing in certain population groups, although the use of these drugs among the general population remains low.
commission. thank you for recognising that to a certain extent i am like the pope: i have no legions at all! indeed you are right, mr newton dunn, the main responsibility in this area lies with the member states. but there is a lot we can do, both in internal policy and external policy. when it comes to internal policy, one has to recognise that for years now europol has been playing a very important coordinating role in detecting the main transit routes. when we have detected the transit routes, we try to cooperate with such countries in order to prevent the entry into the european union of those drugs. we have made some progress in the balkan region thanks to cooperation with the countries in the area. thanks to the support of the cards programme, we have been developing specific law enforcement capabilities in those countries to fight against drug trafficking. i am less positive in my assessment as regards afghanistan. the figures i have at my disposal demonstrate that the poppies are growing and increasing, and it is quite clear that in afghanistan the political situation is not stable enough to guarantee close cooperation as far as law enforcement is concerned in order to tackle the issue of drugs trafficking. i believe this issue – and i know my colleague commissioner patten shares this view – will be at the top of the agenda in our negotiations with the afghan authorities in the near future.
commission. thank you for raising that question. my answer is very clear: no, it is not good at all. firstly, it is not good for people to become addicted to drugs. the european monitoring centre in lisbon is developing five key indicators that will allow us to have more reliable data, so that we can compare that data among the member states and establish a clearer link between the policy line of member states and the impact of that policy line on the pattern of consumption. these five indicators refer to figures for drugs used among the general population, the problem of drug use connected with infectious diseases, drugs-related deaths and the treatment provided by member states for those who ask to be treated for drug addiction. i hope that the work in progress with these five indicators will give us a clearer picture of the situation in europe. i would just add that my concern today is, above all, the proliferation in the use of synthetic drugs and the upsurge of a new profile of drug addict: the poly-consumption consumer. poly-consumption is a new pattern; it comes from a combination of illicit drugs and licit drugs. we need more research and more reliable information in order to be able to fight against this new profile that has arisen in the last few years.

should provide a constitutional basis for this cooperation. in any event, harmonious and balanced integration of the union as a whole requires that cooperation, particularly crossborder cooperation, be supported. this is what we are doing with the interreg iii community initiative, which contains a strand a specifically dedicated to this strengthening of crossborder cooperation. however, i am fully aware of the difficulties faced by member states, regions and local authorities in implementing crossborder cooperation projects under interreg. these difficulties are mainly due to the need for partners on both sides of a border to respect national law and the rules and administrative procedures of their own state. i say this, mr president, with a certain amount of experience, having been for seventeen years the president of a french border region and having led many projects which have experienced the difficulties i have just mentioned on the other side, in the val d'aosta in italy. regulations applicable to the next programming period of the structural funds. i think that this legislative proposal will be tabled in june. as you know, the commission is due to adopt next week, on 18 february, the third report on economic and social cohesion, which i shall be presenting to your house. this report will contain proposals for a reformed and strengthened cohesion policy after 2006. the creation of a legal instrument for crossborder cooperation, which mr vallvé calls for, should be one of the proposals that the commission will support in its third report on cohesion.

question no 53 by monica frassoni, adopted by elisabeth schroedter (h-0033/04) subject: exclusion of voters from the maltese electoral roll on 21 march 2003, the constitutional court of malta, at the request of an aggrieved party, defined the concept of 'residence' (cassolas case, judge tonio mallia, harry vassallo v. the electoral commission and john mary magro, no. 6/2003/1). the definition of the constitutional court of malta is as follows: 'the word 'domicile' does not mean physical presence in the country'. furthermore, the new law on the european elections in malta (act no. xvi of 2003, printed in the malta government gazette of 26 november 2003) expressly states that all maltese nationals residing in the 25 eu countries have the right to vote and stand for election in malta. is the commission aware that despite the constitutional definition and the existing legislation on european elections, the malta labour party (mlp) has again applied to have 1684 maltese nationals removed from the electoral rolls? these cases will come before the court in malta in the last week of january and maltese staff in the eu institutions are among those being targeted. what does the commission intend to do about the illegal attempt by the mlp to prevent maltese nationals from taking part in the forthcoming european elections in malta?
the commission, madam president, has already made a number of proposals. the constitution of malta recognises all fundamental and civil rights. the right of maltese citizens to vote in general elections is dependent on nationality, age and residence. in response to a recent complaint by a maltese citizen whose right to vote was challenged by a party, the maltese constitutional court has ruled that such requirements do not infringe the fundamental rights of maltese citizens. the european commission has no comments to make on the opinion of the maltese constitutional court. i would point out, however, that according to the maltese constitutional court, the concept of residence does not include physical presence in the country, but that temporary absence from the country is also included and permitted. if a citizen's right to vote is called into question by a political party in malta, the case must be dealt with by a competent maltese court and the interpretation of the maltese constitutional court must be taken into account. the right to challenge the electoral roll and the election results is an integral part of any transparent democratic system. it is certainly not the commission's role to interfere in the functioning of the maltese judiciary. the commission also notes that the recently adopted law on the european elections in malta provides that all maltese citizens living in the 25 member states have the right to vote and to stand as candidates in the elections to the european parliament in malta. this was possible because the maltese constitution covers general elections but not european elections. this is an interesting development which the european commission is taking note of with interest. it is clear that malta's increased involvement in international organisations is contributing to very desirable internal developments.
the commission i do so, madam president, but very reluctantly, because the european commission really has no business what any party in malta does or does not do. it's not true what you're saying that anyone here was removed from the voter roll. here one party has exercised its right to request cancellations. this is possible under maltese law - i have just explained this - and it is decided in a proper legal procedure. whether or not this system we have in malta is particularly beautiful is, i believe, not for us to decide. the only important thing is to determine whether or not the general right to free and equal elections is guaranteed in malta. that's the case. but it is certainly not the commission's job to pass judgment when any party does anything. i won't do that either.

the commission. mr president, mr bushill-matthews and mr pronk, on behalf of the epp group, have put a number of questions to which i shall reply. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the first question you asked is what the commission intends to do to achieve the lisbon summit objectives in terms of demographic change. the demographic problem is at present at the heart of our three main policies, economic policy - particularly public finance - employment policy and social cohesion policy. the question of ageing is now, as you will have seen, a key element of the broad economic policy guidelines and the guidelines of the employment strategy, with specific objectives. i would like to say in particular that this year, in the spring 2004 report, we have set three priorities, one of which is the promotion of active ageing, that is to say, the extension of working life. we have three categories of actions. the first concerns the abolition of economic disincentives which effectively discourage workers from delaying retirement. in many countries, the current system is that it is better for a person to retire than to continue working because of lower wages. so there's this serious issue of counter-motivation. the second is to promote access to training for all workers, but especially for older workers, and here we have set specific quantitative targets. the third is to improve the quality of work. in this context, the commission, in its efforts to put demographic ageing at the centre of its policies, proposes to extend the open method of coordination to the modernisation of the care system and the social protection sector. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of health care, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. the second question you asked concerns the flexibility of pension rules and is particularly timely. as you said, we have set ourselves specific objectives. we have set ourselves the lisbon targets of increasing the employment rate of the elderly to 50%, and the barcelona targets of increasing the average age at which workers leave the labour market by five years, and to do so by 2010. these objectives are monitored by the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we are currently examining with the social protection and employment committees how social systems are preventing or encouraging easy retirement. the final report is available to you, it will be presented again in 2004, and we can see in each system what are the problems with incentives for pensions, for disability benefits, for unemployment benefits, for older workers, for survivors' benefits and how the logic of incentives and not the logic of integrating these people into the labour market has distorted both the labour market and the individual's own attempt to enter the labour market. we believe that this report, which will be submitted to the european council, is an important tool in the hands of the member states as well. i should of course tell you that the european commission has been recommending the establishment of flexible pension schemes continuously since 1980 and the response has not been what we expected. as regards your third question on the wim kok report, we consider it extremely important, particularly because it is included in detailed recommendations for each member state. we have already included the kok report in the employment strategy and our recommendations to all countries will take account of this report. i think it is interesting that in cooperation with mr kok, the ministries of labour and the social partners, we are presenting the conclusions of the committee to the member states, trying to give them a lot of publicity and to (es) mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, at the end of the five-year term, as provided for in the treaty of amsterdam and the important tampere summit for the adoption of measures leading to the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice, and on the basis of what has been achieved so far, i would like, as chairman of the committee on civil liberties, to make an assessment and reflect on the future of this permanent challenge. i would say, as a general assessment, that we should not give a negative impression of what has been achieved so far, even though, for example, much of the progress is due solely to crises such as 9/11, and even though, in the particular field of asylum and immigration, we have not yet been able to find satisfactory solutions. all measures to develop the area of freedom, security and justice have a direct impact on the sovereignty of the member states, so the reluctance and difficulties are to some extent logical. in view of the progress made and, above all, in order to continue to make progress, why not consider a second tampere programme now? it seems that this may be the case - from what i have heard the commissioner say - and that is the feeling of this house too. i would also suggest that this new programme should be based on three key ideas: legitimacy, efficiency and solidarity. firstly, the legitimacy of the actions undertaken, the sole basis of which, in my view, should be the protection and guarantee of the rights and freedoms of citizens, for which the intervention of the european parliament is of vital importance. i wonder whether this has been the driving force behind all the measures taken or whether, on the contrary, it has been an exercise in defending the national interests of the member states, often bypassing parliament or sending it all the texts on which it has to decide too late. unfortunately, mr president, the reality is that the second hypothesis is correct. this is shown by the weak role played by the european parliament in key matters such as the judicial cooperation agreement with the united states or the programme to combat terrorism and organised crime, where the lack of consultation of parliament demonstrates a lack of transparency in decision-making and the relegation to the background of the genuine representative of the european citizens. it is fair to say, however, that there is one area in which parliament, the commission and the council have shown great determination and consensus: the fight against terrorism. let me also make a proposal on this point, mr president: the establishment of an international day dedicated to the victims of terrorism - which could well be 11 september - as the only way of bringing justice to those who are the real victims of this criminal scourge, which unfortunately is increasingly on the agenda, which attacks the most basic right of the human being, which is life and his physical integrity. i hope, mr president, that you will heed this appeal. secondly, an important element of reflection would be the effectiveness of the measures taken. the decisionmaking method used so far has undoubtedly led to a somewhat schizophrenic situation. this is demonstrated, for example, by the initiatives of the member states which are not adopted and which overlap with one another, by the blockages in the council as a result of the unanimity rule - as in the case of the normative development of the asylum procedure - or, above all, by the flagrant delays in the incorporation into the legislation of the member states of community rules, as in the case of the 'euro order'. that is why all the amendments to the draft european constitution are so important to avoid this situation. the last point is solidarity, which is perhaps the most serious lack of solidarity that is currently taking place in most member states. it is a fact that governments are more concerned about their domestic public opinion or their national budget than they are about achieving european objectives. or is that not what is happening in the councils of ministers in dealing with the serious problems caused by the accumulation of asylum applications or by the disorderly and irregular economic immigration which some member states are suffering, with tragic consequences? mr president, the worst thing about this strategy is that it ignores objective reality. in an area of freedom, security and justice without internal frontiers, it is useless to insist on defending strict national positions against other member states if the effects of the policy adopted by some have a direct impact on others. europe is a common project. the space we're discussing is a joint project. let us move forward together and the results will undoubtedly benefit us all.
