- question no 28 by mr pimenta question no 29 by bill newton dunn (h-0090/04) subject: equal treatment of suspects throughout the eu if the european arrest warrant and the proposed european arrest warrant are to function satisfactorily, equal treatment of suspects' rights must be applied throughout the eu. when does the commission intend to make a formal proposal for an eu agreement on legal guarantees for suspects? in other words, when does the commission intend to propose equal access to lawyers and interpreters, to combat police immunity and to ensure uniform interpretations of human rights, including the right to liberty, the right to a fair trial and the right to remain silent?
commission. very shortly the commission is planning to present a proposal for a framework decision on certain procedural rights for suspected persons in criminal proceedings throughout the union. the draft instrument is in its final stages of internal consultation within the commission. when it is finished and has been translated, it will be sent to parliament and the council. the draft framework decision covers five basic rights: access to legal advice; access to free interpretation and translation, ensuring that persons who are not able to understand or follow the proceedings receive specific attention; the right of foreign detained persons to communicate with their consular authorities; and written notification of their rights. as regards the right to silence, the commission has asked the law society of england and wales to carry out a study on gathering and handling of evidence, including how the right to silence is interpreted in all the member states and in the acceding countries. once the report of this study has been received, the commission will evaluate the need for any proposal in this area. police immunity is not within the competence of the european union, since the maintenance of law and order and the safeguarding of internal security are explicitly excluded from the ambit of the treaty on european union.
commission. i confirm that it is extremely difficult, because almost half the member states do not agree that there is a legal basis to deal with these issues at european union level. that is not the position of the commission. we think that mutual recognition, which is the cornerstone of judicial penal cooperation, requires mutual confidence among member states. to a certain extent, to create that climate of mutual confidence, we need a minimum degree of harmonisation or at least approximation of penal law, including procedural guarantees. we are not working in an empty field; the european convention on human rights lays down some standards. we think that we should go further at european level and be more specific about how to use the procedural guarantees already laid down in the european convention on human rights. we will present our proposal fairly soon and we will try to get it through the council. it will not be easy, but i am determined to follow that path.
commission. mr maccormick, i share your view that the situation is unsatisfactory but, nevertheless, there is no empty field, as i said. firstly, there is the european convention on human rights, which deals with fair trial rules, and which has been subscribed to by all member states and all acceding states. secondly, there are some specific procedural rules in the framework decision on the european arrest warrant as such and, thirdly, i am fully supportive of the idea of the charter of fundamental rights being legally binding, with constitutional status. as soon as we resolve the minor matters of the weighting of votes, it will come into force, i am sure.
- question no 30 by mr pimenta question no 2 by mr fischler
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the european council of 13 december 2003 gave the go-ahead for the establishment of a community fisheries control authority. the commission will present a proposal to this effect at the end of this month. in this proposal we will define the tasks of this new authority. the most important of these tasks will be to coordinate the joint use of control services in the member states. the controls will be carried out by multinational teams, among others, and the commission will define the inspection strategies to be used, such as benchmarking and common priorities. we will also involve experts from the member states in setting up the agency and consult the various stakeholders. we expect a study on the operational aspects of this agency to be carried out in september, the results of which can be discussed in the council in the context of the decision. the galician fisheries sector also gave me suggestions on a possible location during my recent visit to vigo, which i will of course have examined in detail and which are also the subject of the studies mentioned. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
i am aware, commissioner, as you can understand, of your visit to vigo, the city where i was born, and i know that the fishing industry in that city, which is very important in galicia, in the spanish state and in europe, has just made a number of suggestions on the functions and powers of this agency, to which i think the commissioner should give a concrete answer. moreover, i believe that we should promote an open dialogue with the industry before defining the agency's regulations, and i believe that this institution could provide the much-needed link between professionals and scientific institutions. in any event, i would like to ask you specifically whether the commission has already received the proposal from the spanish state for the seat of the agency to be moved to vigo and when do you think it will be finally moved?
the commission. we have not yet received the official proposal as to the precise location of this agency. but i also pointed out that there is still time for this because we must first of all establish a legal basis. and here we shall make the proposal without delay, but this proposal must also be incorporated into the legislative procedure.
(es) mr president, i would like to make a specific point in the context of the questions: as has been said, it is clear that it was the council which decided that this agency should be set up in spain, that this decision was approved and that the president of the 'democratically elected' government of spain, mr aznar, assumed that it should be located in the city of vigo. i think the commission has taken it on board too, since the commissioner himself was there. so i think there is no doubt about it. the sector is now naturally concerned about when this agency will start operating. i think that parliament will have to take a decision on the commission's proposal and that, once the new parliament is set up in july - and this is what i want to ask the commissioner - i think that in september it will be able to be, as he has said, in the operational phase. if parliament delivers a favourable opinion in the autumn, in september or october, does this mean that the agency could be operational by 2005 or that all the procedures for starting operations would have been completed, if all the procedures could be carried out from the new parliament constitution?
the commission. i would like to make it clear that the agency cannot start work until the legal basis is in place. i have pointed out that we will be presenting the proposal for the legal basis this month by the commission - we are moving very quickly here - and then both the fisheries council and parliament will have to take a position on it and take a decision. the council has not yet taken a decision on the matter, and i am not sure that it will be possible to reach a decision on the matter in the near future. it is only when this decision has been taken that the tendering procedures can be opened and then the staff can be selected, and that will take a certain amount of time next year. i'm sorry, but there's no legal or technical way to speed this up. we would also not be able to use the funds until the legal basis is in place.
- question no 32 by paulo casaca (h-0072/04):urgent measures to prevent predatory fishing in the azores watersbefore the introduction of free access to the azores waters, which is due to take effect from 1 august 2004, several dozen community vessels not registered in the archipelago have entered the azores waters under the pretext of holding licences issued by other member states. the portuguese authorities have proved incapable of controlling the fishing gear used, the quantities and the species caught by the vessels concerned. the azores authorities are concerned that predatory fishing will take place before the provisions of regulation (ec) no 1954/2003 enter into force. when will the commission, in the exercise of the powers conferred on it by the treaty and its duty to ensure compliance with the treaty, take action to ensure that these activities are brought to an end without delay? when will the commission state its position on the approval of the council's position in the light of the increasingly clear evidence that the said regulation is in breach of the fundamental principles of the peoples and the principles of the environment as laid down in the treaty?
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the commission is of course aware of the presence of spanish fishing vessels in azorean waters. however, there seems to have been a misunderstanding on the part of the portuguese authorities as regards the applicability of regulation no 1954 of 2003. article 5 of that regulation lays down the conditions under which fishing may be carried out in the waters around the azores, madeira and the canary islands. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be allowed to reserve fishing for local vessels within 110 miles of the coast. this has already been the case since 14 november 2003, when that legal provision entered into force. it is for the member states to ensure that these rules are then followed accordingly. the presence of spanish vessels in azorean waters outside the 100 nautical miles does not therefore justify immediate action, as you suggested, mr casaca, because these vessels comply with the access regulations. in this connection, i would remind you of the commission's statement on the adoption by the council of the 1954 regulation. we have also announced a ban on trawl fishing in azores waters to prevent damage to the delicate ecosystems on the sea floor. we have submitted a proposal for a regulation to the council on 3 february this year. the commission is also in constant dialogue with the member states concerned to ensure that the new rules are applied as smoothly as possible.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. first of all, i can assure you that we have consulted our legal services and that our legal services hold exactly the opinion that i have presented here and no other. we have decided in principle that: on the one hand we have established this new limit of 100 nautical miles, but on the other hand the fisheries protection zone has been extended to cover more species. in the past, there was de facto only protection for tuna fishing. i cannot therefore help you, even if you quote article 15. the spanish approach in the case you refer to was correct.
- question no 33 by maría izquierdo rojo (h-0091/04):on: recognition of actual spanish production in the future common organisation of the market in olive oil the reform of the common organisation of the market in olives in 1998 introduced a transitional period for the collection of reliable data on the olive oil sector to take account of spanish complaints that its quota was not correct. on the basis of this information and the evolution of the current market organization, it has been confirmed that it is inadequate and discriminatory compared to production in other member states. spanish and andalusian olive growers are thus the least supported, receiving on average 33% less aid over the whole period. in the future, a solution must be found to this discrimination. the new common organization of the market will enable the commission to adapt the spanish quantity to actual production conditions and thus avoid a permanent discrimination which would have serious budgetary consequences for the olive-growing regions and areas where this crop is of vital importance to their economies. will the commission carry out this necessary review and amend the spanish financial table to bring it into line with actual production?
the commission. i would like to begin by saying that we are going to discuss these questions raised in the last few questions tonight, because tonight is the debate on the reform of the olive oil sector, the tobacco sector, the cotton sector and the hops sector. the general principle of the reform of the common agricultural policy last june was that the national amounts of money should be equal to the average of the aid granted during the reference period. there is no reason why olive oil should be treated differently. the council of ministers has already decided to proceed in parallel with the june reform. a review of the national guaranteed quantities at this stage would also be contrary to the logic which led us to introduce these guaranteed quantities in 1998 and which holds member states responsible for keeping production increases under control. the national guarantees were then fixed at a level which, as subsequent investigations have confirmed, corresponded to the structural dimension of the sector in the individual producing member states at that time. as you probably know, spain's share of the total ceiling is 43%, between its share of the number of olive trees under cultivation of 39% and its share of the olive-growing area of 44%, compared with 1998. in this respect, what is at issue is a fair offer.
(es) mr president, commissioner, you know that the basis for this reform contains quotas which are out of date as far as spain is concerned. you know that spain is a specific case in this respect and that these studies and all the surveys show that the spanish production situation is indeed higher than has traditionally been recognised. spain has suffered a penalty in its production quotas, and this is obvious. this should therefore be recognised, because it is not the only member state in this situation. in view of the fact that the new cap reform is in fact a liquidation of the previous stage - and when it is liquidated, it is done according to the calculation of 'real realities', not that of outdated realities - and in view of the fact that during the whole of that stage which we are now liquidating, spain was comparatively penalized - and this is obviously demonstrable - by a mismatch in its production reality and, commissioner, recalling also that the spanish olive grove welcomed you very much always hoping that you would understand its reality and its potential in terms of health and environmental protection, i ask you: do you not envisage the possibility of reflecting the productive reality we have in the national budget? we ask for transparency and a tight quota.
commission. - mr president, i am sorry to have to correct you here. the situation is not exactly the same as in spain. it is not very wise for you, as the representative of greece, to argue in this direction, because the national guarantee quota for greece was in 1998 - as you rightly said - 419.5 thousand tonnes, which corresponds to 23.6% of the eu quantity. if you compare this with the number of trees you have, which is only 20% of the total, and with the hectares, which are only 18.8% of the eu area, it would actually be justified to transfer part of your guarantee to spain and not in the direction you have requested.
- as the commissioner has said, there is an important debate on agriculture this evening, and you will have an opportunity to exchange views. question no 34 is therefore withdrawn. question no 35 by carlos lage (h-0121/04):on the use of certain traditional designations of origin for wine by third countrieson 23 february, the commission adopted a series of amendments to regulation (ec) no 753/2002 oj l 118, 4.5.2002, p. 1. which allows the use of certain traditional designations of origin from third countries. these include 'tawny', 'ruby', 'vintage' and 'late bottled', which are exclusively used for port wine, as well as other terms used for madeira and various regional wines produced in portugal. there is no doubt that the amendments adopted by the commission will have a negative impact on the production and marketing of all the wines mentioned, but this will be particularly true of port wine, both because of the economic importance of this wine in a large region of portugal, namely the 'região demarcada do douro', where there are 33 000 wine growers, and because of the level of revenue, with more than two thirds of wine exports and about one fifth of food exports being made up of port wine. moreover, the generic use of terms which only refer to port wine, its importance and quality, may damage its international reputation. will the commission not, because of this error, rectify the problem and reverse its decision? what guarantees can the commission give that the reputation of port wine in the world will not be affected, particularly in terms of its origin, reputation and recognition by consumers?
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. you're probably familiar with the traditional english terms like ruby, vintage, tawny and late bottled. these names are protected at community level for quality wines produced in portugal and enriched with alcohol. in other words, these traditional terms can be used freely for other quality wines. however, in order to be allowed to use these traditional terms in portugal, a third country must meet certain requirements. the following conditions must be met: firstly, the name must be specific, that is to say, recognised as a quality name. secondly, the name must be distinctive or have a certain reputation, that is to say, the average consumer must be able to recognise the name as a distinguishing feature between a particular wine and another. thirdly, the name must be used in the territory of the third country concerned in accordance with tradition. fourthly, the rules laid down by the third country must not mislead the european consumer when the third country wine is on the community market. fifth, the official language of the country concerned must be english. so this is the case with south africa, with australia or the united states. if english is not the official language of the country concerned, the use of that language must be provided for in the legislation and english must have been used continuously for the traditional term for at least 25 years. since english is not the official language of third countries such as argentina, chile or brazil and since the legislation of these countries does not contain any provision to that effect, these countries cannot use the traditional names on the ec market. in order to use a traditional term in the community, a third country must submit a dossier to the commission, which will only allow its use if the numerous conditions i have mentioned are met. the management committee is involved in this procedure, which means that the member states are guaranteed a say. the amendment to the labelling regulation will not have a negative impact on trade, as the traditional names for fortified wines are limited, while third countries export mainly normal or ordinary wines.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. let me make this clear once again. of course, and i agree with you entirely, these are prestigious names and they also have a corresponding economic value in the marketing of these wines. it's perfectly clear. on the other hand, we have to follow certain rules. if we do not do this, we risk being sued and losing at the wto, and that protective system will be broken. i do believe that the regulations we have created are in any case sufficient to ensure adequate protection. the other question is the risk of misuse or falsification you mentioned. the risk of counterfeiting is not changed by these new provisions. the risk of counterfeiting is always there because it is attractive to use these prestigious names. in order to counter this risk, we must ensure that appropriate controls are in place and that such names are not misused, as has happened many times in the past. the first thing that is important is that cooperation with the import authorities works, because these imports cannot cross the border in this way, but must be declared.
- question no 36 by richard howitt (h-0126/04):on: mid-term review of the sugar regimein the light of the commission's recent opinion on the mid-term review of the sugar regime, what is the commission's response to the proposal by the least developed acp countries to maintain a share of their sugar exports to europe at current prices or prices approaching them?
commission. - mr president, you are right in theory that a higher price in europe makes the exports of the poorer countries to europe more attractive. but you must also be aware that the current price level is simply not sustainable for many reasons. we should have no illusions about our own beet growers or the beet exporters in the third world. our current internal market price is about three times the international price and we will certainly be faced with the fact that we will have to reduce external protection for sugar in the current wto round. this alone is sufficient to ensure that the price on the internal market will fall accordingly. there is no other way to do this. that is the problem we are facing. there are other questions: we can only compensate for the additional imports from the least developed countries by producing less, because sugar consumption in europe will not increase. then you must not forget that sugar is increasingly in direct competition with other sweeteners. you won't find sugar in coca-cola today. it contains isoglucose and nothing else. these sweeteners are also in direct competition with sugar. if we create a free market here, as the united states has done for a long time, then the quantities will increase accordingly. the result of all this is that in the european union, instead of production falling in the same way in each member state, it will simply be that sugar production in some member states will simply become unprofitable and that they will therefore withdraw from beet production. i'm sure you will. i think it's pointless to have expectations that we can't meet. in addition, there is the difficulty that we have to think about how we can help those developing countries with whom we have traditional sugar supply links, such as mauritius, if their sugar exports to europe are less attractive than they were in the past.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. when are the proposals due? we have said from the outset that we want to present the proposals before the summer, and that remains our view. at the very least, there could be problems because - and i did not mention this earlier - there is a panel in geneva against the european union on the so-called c-quota issue, and we should know what to expect from that panel. we must therefore also take into account the timetable of the geneva authorities. the second question: europe is of course an attractive market and many countries would like to supply europe. but we think that we should set clear priorities here, and these are: only the least developed countries should have free access to the european market. as you know, we have also made provision for a special arrangement for the balkan countries. the acp states and the rest of the world, with whom we have agreements, should have limited priority access with a clear tariff preference. if we give everyone the opportunity to supply sugar to europe, we do not need a sugar market regulation, but we need a complete liberalisation of the sugar market, which would mean that at least two thirds of european production would have to be abandoned.
- question no 37 and 38 will be answered in writing, since the time allowed for questions to mr fischler has expired. question to the commission question no 39 by marie anne isler béguin (h-0065/04) subject: negative human and economic consequences of pollution in the enlarged union a study published by the world health organization in september 2000 found that air pollution causes 31,700 deaths, 500,000 asthma cases, and 25,000 bronchitis cases each year in france alone, and contributes 1.7% of the gross national product. does this pollution-related deterioration of living conditions (health and life expectancy) in an eu of 27 member states not prompt the commission to speed up an epidemiological study of it in order to fully clarify the lethal impact (diseases and life expectancy) and economic costs of different types of pollution, especially in the future when combined with the effects of climate warming? does not the fact that such serious threats are facing european societies imply an obvious and urgent duty to carry out an epidemiological study, to disseminate its results in a way that reflects the risks involved, to make them known and to incorporate them into community policies?
the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. i am very pleased about this question, which gives me the opportunity to delve a little deeper into our message on the environment and health. this is one of my highest priorities as commissioner. i must admit that this is also one of the most difficult questions, because it cuts across the division of subjects and responsibilities which we normally have in the commission and also in the member states. it is necessary to work across all boundaries to link cause and effect, and that is not easy. nor is it easy to put a price tag on the health problems resulting from environmental pollution. i think that the world health organization has started a very important work to do just that, to show that environmental pollution has a very high price for society and that health problems in society also have a very high price. we are of course also attacking this issue together with the new member states. several of the conferences we have had to prepare our action plan have taken place in the new member states. we are mobilising their experts so that there can be no doubt that this is a pan-european way of working on these issues. we take this very seriously. we will continue to argue that the cost benefits are so great that it is actually profitable for both business and society to invest in environmental measures that also lead to fewer health problems.
commission. this is definitely part of our approach. there has to be a sound scientific base for any of the actions or measures we propose. we are working with the world health organisation to ensure that we have all the knowledge necessary and that we work on a scientific base. i should also explain that our environment and health strategy is called 'scale', which stands for science, children, awareness-raising, legislation and evaluation. this means that the action proposed will be based on scientific results. it will focus on children. we will also use legal instruments, etc. we include, where necessary, new epidemiological work, and we are trying to do everything we can to ensure that we have a sound basis and all the facts necessary to do it in a proper way.
- question no 40 by maría luisa bergaz conesa (h-0066/04):on: electricity supply to redes, a nature park and biosphere reserve (asturias, spain) the commission is considering whether the electricity supply line from lada to velilla, which runs through the nature park and biosphere reserve of redes, should be located as currently planned. will the commission require a complete plan for this pipeline network, which will bypass the nature reserves that are part of natura 2000, respect the areas where bears live and thus also respect community legislation? has the commission received the environmental impact study which the spanish authorities promised to send at the end of january at their meeting on 4 december 2003? if not, does the commission not consider that it is necessary to contact the court of justice now (the reasoned opinion was published in april 2003) in order to ensure that the spanish government and the region of castilla y leon, which has also been sued in this connection before the spanish courts, agree to draw up a plan for a pipeline network that is not harmful to the environment?
commission. the lada-velilla power line project mentioned by the honourable member would cross protected areas in the autonomous communities of asturias and castille and leon. in 2001, following a complaint filed in august 2000, the commission initiated an infringement procedure pursuant to article 226 of the ec treaty. this procedure, based upon obligations under directive 79/409/eec on the protection of wild birds and directive 92/43/eec on the protection of natural habitats and wild fauna and flora, reached the stage of reasoned opinion – the last step before bringing the case before the european court of justice – in april 2003. currently, the procedure is aimed at modifying the non-implemented part of the project in the autonomous community of castille and leon. in their answer to the above-mentioned reasoned opinion issued by the commission, the spanish authorities undertook to examine alternatives for the remaining part of the project – puerto de tarna to velilla – and confirmed in february 2004 that the necessary studies to comply with the requirements of article 6(3) of directive 92/43/eec will start soon. these include a full environmental assessment in order properly to identify the effects of the projects on the conservation values of the affected site; if these are considered significant, alternatives will have to be examined. if no alternative can be identified that is not damaging to the site, the project can only proceed if it can be justified on the grounds of overriding public interest and if provision is made for adequate compensation measures. in the event of significant effects on priority species identified under the directive, such as the brown bear, an opinion from the commission may be needed pursuant to article 6(4) of the directive. the spanish authorities explain that the necessary nature assessments will not be ready for ten months and that the resulting modified project will be subject to a full impact assessment procedure, in compliance with the provisions of directive 85/337/eec on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment. the authorities submitted to the commission, as supplementary information, a complete set of documents and studies concerning the original project and its likely effects on natural values. an examination of the details of the above-mentioned spanish answers is currently underway, which will permit the commission to decide what course of action it should take in regard to this case. with regard to the last part of your question, the commission would welcome and encourage a fruitful dialogue between the interested parties in order to reach an agreed solution, but it cannot interfere in the constitutional competences of the various administrations.
(es) mr president, commissioner, the people are concerned about the lack of transparency on the part of the spanish government and also about the lack of reliable information from this commission, which says one thing and then reforms and does another. i shall concentrate on three questions only: will the commission continue the infringement procedure instead of closing the case, as the spanish authorities intend to do by promising to alter only 30 km of the planned 90 km route, claiming that it is a new project? will the commission refer the matter to the court of justice of the european communities at the next infringement meeting without further delay if there is no new evidence after one year of notification of the reasoned opinion and four years of investigation of this infringement file? would the commission be prepared, if the regions of asturias and castile and león were to submit to it a new project which respects all natural areas and is in accordance with community legislation, to co-finance such a project, in order to avoid the economic losses which the region of asturias could suffer by dismantling the existing towers?
commission. the case in question concerns the part of the project that will not now be implemented. that part of the project will be replaced by a new one once the full procedure of identifying impacts and exploring alternatives has been completed. that means that it would, in any case, be a new project and that the old procedure may have to be discontinued. in that case, should the commission consider that the new project does not comply with european community law, a new procedure would be initiated afresh. the spanish authorities provided information on these developments in february 2004. the infringement covers only the non-implemented part of the project. we cannot take that case to court as it stands.

- question no 43, by james (jim) fitzsimons (h-0089/04):about: un conference on climate changein a un report of 11 december 2003 on climate change and human health, it is stated that climate change affects human health, that in 2000 it caused 2.4% of the world's cases of diarrhoea, 2% of the world's cases of malaria and that it caused 150,000 deaths worldwide in 2000. the un study adds that they affect weather patterns and air pollution and are responsible for poisoning water and food. how does the commission propose to respond to the guidelines issued by the un in response to these serious problems?
commission. i appreciate that the world health organization is now raising awareness as regards climate-change impacts on human health, in a cooperative effort with the united nations environment programme and the world meteorological organization. the commission can support the general recommendations and conclusions of this world health organization report on climate change and human health because, for instance, it focuses on the precautionary principle and the principle of sustainable development. within the commission we are taking this carefully into consideration in the formulation of our policies. the largest benefits of climate policies for human health can be expected from the reduction in the concentrations of ozone and particles. as climate policies in general reduce fossil fuel use, they also reduce related particulate emissions. additional health benefits can be gained by reducing urban concentrations of no2 and so2. thus, emissions-control strategies that simultaneously address air pollutants and greenhouse gases lead to a more efficient use of resources at all scales, also addressing human health concerns. the world health organization report confirms earlier statements that there are still many knowledge gaps involving likely future patterns of exposure to climatic environmental changes and the vulnerability and adaptability of physical, ecological and social systems as regards such climate change. therefore, we need better information to establish further the links between the pollutants and health effects, with a view to improving our climate change and health policies. the action plan on which we are presently working as a follow-up to the environment and health strategy is designed to integrate this information. while the action plan focuses on a set of defined exposures and diseases in its first phase, broader issues, including those related to the health impacts of climate change, can be taken up in future phases. moreover, the forthcoming thematic strategic on the urban environment, to be adopted by june 2005, and for which an interim communication is presently under discussion within the commission, should also help local authorities and member states to improve the environmental performance of cities. this in turn would also contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and make cities healthier places to live. we are also considering some projects under the sixth research framework programme. within the activities of scientific support to policies of the sixth framework programme, research is also funded on the physical and chemical processes of air pollutants, in particular on particulate matter at the urban to regional scales, in view of their impact on human health. under the last research framework programme, the ccashh project – climate change and adaptation strategies for human health in europe – was funded to assess the health impacts of climate change.

deputy to the co-commander maría rodríguez ramos. i should like to begin by taking up some of my time representing mrs rodríguez ramos, who, because of force majeure, is unable to defend her report on cotton as planned. mrs rodríguez ramos says that all the cap reforms in europe, from the mcsharry reform to agenda 2000, have always provided for a period of more than ten years for all the productions concerned to gradually adapt to the changes that come with the transition from a policy of price support to producer support schemes. mr commissioner, the current cotton reform was launched in 2001 and you now intend to make another reform without any environmental impact study, as we shall see, forgetting also that your purpose is completely unrelated to the policy indicated in the protocols annexed to the acts of accession of greece, spain and portugal, which include the objective of supporting cotton production in the producing areas. what you are trying to do is to achieve a total decoupling; we believe that your proposal leads to the abandonment of cotton production, the commission knows this, and, moreover, it is being done in the absence of valid studies on the sector. the commission is also aware that cotton production is concentrated in regions which suffer from a very significant backwardness, and that it will have a tremendous potential impact on the cotton sector and related services. and there is no alternative, mr. commissioner. what can these farmers do? the union states to a timetable. in the spirit of article 156 of the treaty, the guidelines for projects require the approval of the state concerned, and the commission must therefore oppose these amendments. other amendments propose axes in third countries. in this case, the commission cannot include in the transeuropean networks routes through third countries, but we are aware of the problem posed by the existence, after enlargement, of an enclave surrounded by the territory of the union. in june, in compostela, we will meet with the heads of the various pan-european corridors to review them, bearing in mind that two thirds of these corridors, after enlargement to 27 states, will be within the union and will be transeuropean networks, which are the ones we are approving today. in this review of pan-european corridors, specific and particularly dynamic attention will have to be paid to those projects which connect european territory through non-european territory, as is the case in some countries of the former yugoslavia in the balkans. ladies and gentlemen, certain amendments propose to withdraw or delete parts already included in the commission's van miert group proposals and approved by the council. these are amendments nos 1, 7, 20 and 25, which the commission cannot accept. the projects included in annex iii, i repeat, are based on economic studies and political approval by both the van miert group and the council. ladies and gentlemen, there has been a request for express mention of spain and portugal on certain motorways of the sea instead of saying 'the southern part of europe', as mr camisón has said. i'll check it out, but as far as i know, it's still in the proposals. the central crossing of the vignemal, the central crossing of the pyrenees, i repeat, must respect the will of the states. we must try to encourage them, but we must respect what the treaties say: that without the agreement of a state no work can be done on its territory. i would like to conclude, once again, by expressing my thanks to the honourable members and by saying that, as you can see, the positions of the commission and the council offer a certain flexibility to accommodate some of the proposals and contributions of this parliament which are an improvement on the initial text and which, moreover, presuppose respect for the balance between the two institutions. i ask this parliament to understand that there is this margin of flexibility, but that it is impossible to reopen the basis and the whole of the proposals for these new transeuropean networks from the top down, which we are urged to approve so that, from 1 may 2004, when we will be 25 and not 15, the ten new member states will be reflected in them, because they will be part of the whole of the union. i thank mr bradbourn and the whole committee on regional policy, transport and tourism for their work.

question no 2 by mr miguel ángel martínez martínez (h-0071/04) subject: book fair in cuba the annual book fair in cuba is a cultural and informative event of great international importance. this year the organisers had planned for germany to be the guest of honour. it seems that the german government has refused to participate, referring to the common position adopted by the council and the council's recent policy of cultural sanctions against cuba. nevertheless, the number of authors and publishers from germany or other eu countries participating has not been reduced. does the council consider that the common position and the sanctions mentioned are not only beneficial to cuban culture but also to european culture, or are they harmful to it? does the council feel that its authority is weakened when the invited european publishers and authors ignore the council's position and maintain their participation? several have condemned the eu's cultural sanctions policy as "meaningless, unreasonable and contrary to our interests".
council. – as both the council and the commission have repeatedly made clear in the european parliament, the decision of 5 june 2003 was part of a package of measures taken following the violation by the cuban authorities last year of international human rights standards. this took the form of the summary trial and lengthy prison sentences imposed on a large number of dissidents for exercising their right to freedom of speech and participation in public affairs, as well as the summary trial and the rapid execution of three hijackers of a ferry boat, in breach of international minimum standards for the implementation of the death penalty. the four measures announced on 5 june 2003 were symbolic and political in nature and therefore their implementation concerns only the governments of the european union member states and their officials. it does not affect the private sector or individual citizens, who are free to attend the cuban book fair and indeed any other cultural event organised by the government of cuba if they so wish. regarding the private opinions mentioned in the question, the council has no comment to make on what those attending the fair may have had to say. they have the right to express their views, even if their views are wrong. once again the eu calls on the cuban authorities to release all political prisoners without delay and to resume the de facto moratorium on the death penalty. the council reaffirms the continuing validity of the common position as the basis of the european union's constructive engagement with cuba, to be pursued through political dialogue so that tangible results can be achieved, particularly in the political, economic and civil rights areas.
(es) mr president-in-office of the council, dear friend, i am not prepared to fight over the use of a word. a few months ago, the european union reacted to certain actions by the cuban authorities with measures which you considered appropriate and which i - especially those adopted in the field of cultural cooperation - considered disproportionate, unfair and even absurd. i don't know what you want to call those measures. they say they're not sanctions. i would like to find another word, i don't know if they are restrictions, reprisals, pressures, retaliations, cultural blockade as the cubans themselves say. i would like you to tell us what word we should use to really get an answer to what we are asking. apart from that question, i repeat the question i put to you here: what do you think about the measures taken in the field of cultural cooperation helping or harming cubans and europeans? and secondly, does the president-in-office of the council consider that the behaviour of our civil society, participating massively in activities which have been, if not boycotted, at least obstructed by the european union, is a way for civil society to question the union's policy towards cuba?
council. – the words i used were very specific. as i mentioned, the measures were symbolic and political in their nature and therefore the implementation concerns only governments and eu member states. they do not have a direct implication so far as individual citizens are concerned. i also make the point that the measures which were announced on 5 june were taken only after the most careful deliberations. it was the council's considered view at that time that the application of the measures represented a balance between maintaining the willingness to engage in political dialogue to allow for tangible results, and the necessity to make it clear that grave human rights violations such as those that have occurred in cuba in the last 12 months were not acceptable. i am sure that mr martínez would accept that is the position. finally on a general issue regarding the eu and cuba: the measures adopted by the council were very carefully calibrated. some people might say that they are very mild, but the are proportionate in response to specific circumstances. the european union values this relationship with cuba and hopes that those relations can be improved. it is mutually beneficial to aim for an improvement in that regard.
(es) mr president-in-office of the council, i will not be the one to support, of course, the executions carried out by the cuban government. but i have to remember that there are many executions in the united states and also many targeted killings in israel. they're happening every day. i would like to ask in this connection whether the council is going to take any action with regard to the agreements with these two countries which i have mentioned.
council. – i am sure that everything the member has said is quite correct. i am sure cuba is an intriguing and interesting country. the diplomatic measures announced on 5 june were intended to send a signal to the cuban authorities that the new and grave violations of human rights simply were not acceptable. the measures were not designed to isolate cuba in any way. on the contrary, in reconfirming the validity of the common position on cuba on 21 july 2003, the council stressed that political dialogue should be continued with a view to producing tangible results, particularly in the political, economic and rights spheres. the council remains very much open to political dialogue. with regard to the point made about the impact, the cuban government is aware that the council acknowledges its significant achievements in the field of social rights such as health and education. however, it remains our earnest hope that the cuban authorities will come to realise the necessity to make similar advances in the field of fundamental civil, political and human rights. the same level of achievement in those areas as in the areas mentioned by the honourable member would be very welcome.

issued an injunction against the us navy to prevent it from using high-powered, low-frequency sonar in the pacific ocean, to prevent damage to marine life. as my predecessor, mrs korhola, pointed out, in 2002 nato military operations were carried out in the waters of fuerteventura and lanzarote, involving european union vessels, and as a result 14 whales were stranded. studies have been carried out by two professors, one from the university of london, mr paul jepson, and the other from the university of las palmas, mr fernandez, which were published in the journal 'nature' in november 2003, indication of the direction in which we are going. i have the impression that, following the study in the journal nature by professors jepson and fernandez, the impact of these low-frequency sonars on commission. – madam president, this is not the first time that this house has been asked to give its attention to this important and complex issue. from the very beginning, all those involved have recognised the difficulty of finding the answer to the question in front of us: what is the right balance between security demands and civil liberty? we tackle this against a rather sombre backdrop. just before the weekend, the european council agreed on a strong package of measures to reinforce the anti-terrorism efforts of the european union. i know that parliament will not want to send any equivocal messages about terrorism. at the same time, we all agree that the fight against terrorism cannot and must not be carried out at the expense of the protection of fundamental rights such as privacy. against this background, i would like to invite members to reflect carefully on what this resolution – if adopted – could possibly achieve and to check whether this corresponds to our objectives. i dare to say 'our objectives' because the commission and the parliament can surely agree on what our goals are. firstly, to cooperate to fight the scourge of terrorism without sacrificing fundamental civil rights and liberties. secondly, to free airlines from the threat of being caught between contradictory legal requirements with which they have to comply. thirdly, to make sure that such transfers are made in a clear and secure legal framework. fourthly, to foster a cooperative and balanced relationship with the united states. fifthly, and most importantly, to improve the protection given to air passengers and to their data that are transferred to the united states. for over a year, the commission has been negotiating with the united states with a view to meeting these objectives. i ask you frankly: does the motion for a resolution in front of us pay sufficient attention to the significant progress that has been achieved? the commission certainly wanted more and pressed hard for more over long months of tough negotiations. but, as members of this house know from their day-to-day dealings, the result of negotiations is rarely, if ever, perfect. we must also be honest with ourselves: our own delivery of our high data protection standards is far from being ideal. recent eurobarometer results show worryingly low levels of knowledge by european citizens about their rights and obligations. so let us be cautious before preaching to the rest of the world. the key question today on this file is: can we realistically achieve more? the resolution asks the commission to tell the united states that its concessions are not enough. furthermore, it seeks to open new negotiations with a view to reaching a better solution. the list of demands in the resolution is no doubt a very fine one, but will it take us closer to our objectives? in the light of my experience over the last 12 months i am afraid i have to inform the house that this is pie in the sky. the results of rejecting this package will not be a better package, but no package at all. having no package does not get us one inch closer to our objectives, which i thought we shared. it certainly does not lead to better data protection in the united states. we would be simply throwing away all those hard-won improvements. it certainly does nothing either for future eu-us cooperation. we can only influence the united states if we are credible interlocutors. credible interlocutors deliver results. delivering nothing after a year of negotiations does not meet the credibility test, and believe me, there are voices in washington only too ready to say to secretary ridge 'we told you that negotiating with these people is a waste of time'. there is therefore a real risk that the united states will leave the negotiating table and not return. defenders of the resolution by the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs may say that this is an unlikely disaster scenario and that the commission is just running scare stories to justify its own poor achievements. of course, the proof of the pudding will only be in the eating, but if i were a member of this parliament, i would not bank on it that the aims of the resolution are achievable. please ask yourselves whether it is likely that the united states will suddenly double the amount of change it is prepared to make and do so by june, as the resolution demands? members of this house have had their own contacts with american representatives over the last few months, and i am sure you have formed your own views about their openness to our arguments. the resolution and its defenders also point to obtaining passengers' consent to the transfer as the 'magic' solution while we skilfully negotiate a new and better deal. let me repeat the commission's full and active support for measures that ensure that passengers are fully and accurately informed and, where possible, give their agreement. but that should be in addition to – not instead of – the actions we have taken to improve protection in the united states. over the last year, parliament has been an extremely active and outspoken participant in this debate. in doing so, it has undoubtedly strengthened the commission's position in its negotiations with the united states. clearly, parliament should not be silent at this stage. i was indeed expecting some further expressions of concern and constructive criticism. of course nobody is asking parliament to say that it approves of and espouses the american system and approach. indeed, the commission itself does not espouse the american approach part and parcel, nor will we stop trying to achieve improvements in it. indeed, i am currently still in touch with the american authorities with a view to firming up and clarifying their commitments regarding the conditions under which they will be able to forward passenger data to third-country authorities. so, we are still working to improve the situation even further – and will continue to do so – before the commission takes its final decision on an adequacy finding. it is one thing to say that what is on offer is not perfect, and quite another to seek its complete derailment – as the resolution as it stands does. that is why i would ask you to reject this motion for a resolution. to conclude, i shall summarise the choice before parliament. rejection of the motion will allow the commission's proposed package – with the improvements in data protection that we negotiated with the united states – to go ahead. among these major improvements there are annual joint reviews to enable us to keep a close eye on things, and a clear cut-off date after three and a half years. it would also end legal insecurity and remove threats of sanctions for the airlines. i have no doubt there would be positive spin-offs for eu-us cooperation. that is the first choice. the second choice is adoption of the motion for a resolution, which would mean foregoing those advantages in return for a declaration of principle and a wish list that – i am sorry to say – cannot realistically be delivered.
(es) madam president, we are again in this house debating a subject which we are all very familiar with. since the beginning of the transfer of passenger data to the us authorities more than a year ago, with the united states as the final destination or transit country, parliament has expressed considerable concern about the totally irregular situation in which these transfers were and are still being made. today, however, we are again debating this question, but in somewhat different circumstances. firstly, because we already have a commission decision in which it qualifies as adequate the level of protection that the united states guarantees to the data transmitted to them, and secondly because the recent and tragic attacks of 11 march in madrid - among which i would highlight europol and eurojust - but also through cooperation with third countries and there is no doubt that we share with the united states the common objective and the firm determination to defeat the terrorist lacquer. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the agreement we are discussing today, which has been the subject of an overly critical report by the rapporteur, strikes a reasonable balance between the necessary application of security measures and the guarantee of civil rights, and provides citizens with the level of protection and legal certainty that we would lack if we decided to refer the decision back to the commission, leaving open a new period of legal vacuum.

- the report (a5-0135/2004) by mr bösch, on behalf of the committee on budgetary control, on the protection of the communities' financial interests and the fight against fraud - annual report 2002 (com (2003) 445 - c5-0593/2003 - 2003/2248 (ini)).
the rapporteur. ■es) mr president, mr commissioner - to whom i extend my warm welcome - ladies and gentlemen, in 1994 the european parliament adopted at first reading the commission's proposal on minimum safety and health requirements for workers exposed to the risks arising from physical agents. the different characteristics of the four physical agents - noise, vibration, optical radiation and electromagnetic fields - led the council in 1999 to take a new approach, advocating specific directives. after the vibration and noise directives, today we are dealing with the directive on minimum health and safety requirements for workers exposed to the risks arising from exposure to electromagnetic fields. this proposal is part of the package of rules designed to promote the improvement of the working environment, because, according to article 31 of the charter of fundamental rights, entitled 'fair and equitable working conditions', every worker has the right to work in conditions which respect his or her health, safety and dignity. at the outset, we should make it clear that the new directive is extremely careful about the possible socioeconomic impact, because it does not impose new obligations that were not already in the framework directive, but only specifies them. the directive only addresses harmful effects in the short and medium term and not harmful effects in the long term due to lack of sound scientific data. it does not address the risks arising from contact with live conductors. the protection is in this case in the framework directive. the proposal does not provide for exceptions in its scope, as this would constitute discrimination, as provided for in article 13 of the ec treaty and article 20 of the charter of fundamental rights. the directive is also a health and safety directive which aims to eliminate the risk at its source, although a specific directive - for example, 93/42/eec - requires the manufacturer to comply with essential requirements. the use may be incorrect and therefore the sources of risk may be multiple or varied. the commission's proposal is based on two concepts. the first is the exposure limit value above which work is not permitted. the second is the action value which gives rise to an action in the terms of the proposal. the contributions made by this parliament are mainly concerned with the obligations of employers in terms of assessment, measurement of the levels of electromagnetic fields to which workers are exposed, with the consultation and participation of workers and also with training and information, and also with a detailed specification of the content and monitoring of this light - article 8 - in order to prevent and diagnose, as quickly as possible, any adverse effects on health due to exposure to electromagnetic fields. when exposure exceeding the limit values is detected, a medical examination is required and, if health damage is detected due to exposure, a new risk assessment is mandatory. effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties are provided for in accordance with national legislation - obviously - in the event of infringement. if this report is adopted and the council accepts the parliament's amendments, the directive will be the result of a form of social dialogue, a political dialogue, in this case, because of the shared commitment of the ppe-de group and the pse parliamentary group, which, in the committee on employment and social affairs, understood that, through this directive, we could improve the working environment of european workers. the initial proposal was joined by mr crowley of the uen group. as rapporteur, i would like to thank him and all the other colleagues for their contributions and, most especially, the coordinator of the socialist group in the committee on employment, mr stephen hughes. without this agreement the directive would not be possible. if we get the necessary votes tomorrow, we shall have a directive, the fruit of the dialogue between the two political groups in this house, to improve the living conditions of workers, as their dignity as persons demands.
commission. mr president, i am very pleased to have the opportunity to take part in this debate and, looking at the speaking list, i am sure it will have been worth waiting for! it is very important for us to have the opportunity once again to discuss the european union's relations with latin america, and i am particularly pleased that we have the views of two very distinguished colleagues who know so much about the subject and who have committed themselves so enthusiastically and knowledgeably to strengthening our relations over the last few years. the agreements which we are discussing today mark an extremely important step forward in our relations with central america and with the andean community. i am therefore grateful for the strong support that the european parliament gave to them. as the house knows, the commitment to negotiate new political dialogue and cooperation agreements with each region was made at the madrid eu-latin america and caribbean summit in 2002. the european union has delivered on this commitment. negotiations were successfully and rapidly concluded after just two rounds in october 2003, and both agreements were signed on 15 december in rome. these new agreements are ambitious. first of all, they institutionalise and strengthen the political dialogue: the san jose dialogue with central america that was initiated in 1984 and the ministerial political dialogue conducted with the andean community that goes back to the 1996 rome declaration. secondly, they expand the scope of both the political dialogue and the european union's existing cooperation with the two regions, for example, by including some new areas such as migration, conflict prevention, good governance and counter-terrorism activities. obviously, having negotiated these agreements as rapidly as possible is not enough. we must also make sure that they enter into force quickly and i hope that ratification procedures on both sides will be speedy. this is important, because the new areas addressed by the agreements reflect the very real concerns of both regions. at the european union-latin america and caribbean summit in madrid it was agreed that the conditions were not right to launch negotiations for association agreements. these political dialogue and cooperation agreements were seen as an intermediate step: the aim of the agreements is to create the conditions which would allow the negotiation of association agreements, including free trade agreements, in the future. the heads of state and government also defined what the main requirements were for advancing towards an association agreement, notably the achievement of deeper regional integration and the completion of the doha round. i would like to take this opportunity to underline the importance of the recently negotiated agreements as an instrument towards our common goal of negotiating association agreements with these regions in the future. we are now two years beyond one summit, on the eve of another – the guadalajara summit – and we must re-assess our relationship with these regions. there are many questions we should ask ourselves. to what extent are the conditions we set out in madrid still valid in the light of recent developments? how should the absence of substantial progress in the multilateral trade negotiations affect our relations with these regions? how can we ensure that we do not inadvertently in any way undermine our principal trade objective of promoting multilateral agreements and completing the doha development round? otherwise, would we not risk the opening of such negotiations becoming a mere political gesture, as we want agreements with content that go beyond what can be agreed at multilateral level? is there an acceptable political formula to cover all these objectives? regional integration remains of key importance: it can contribute to fostering political stability, economic and social development and social cohesion within each sub-region. the commission considers that further progress towards deepening integration is a sign of political and economic maturity. how can we measure progress in regional integration? i believe the essential elements for measuring progress revolve around three fundamental elements: a fully operational institutional framework, the existence of a customs union and the reduction of obstacles to intra-regional trade. the next joint step should be to evaluate progress achieved by both regions with a view to preparing the ground for the opening of negotiations. i would underline that this process should be carried out in an objective manner and we should not set impossible standards that might only lead to frustration among our counterparts. the commission has always supported regional integration. we are convinced that it should continue to do so. this support is not only one of words: under our regional programme for central america, the commission has approved one project in support of the central american customs union worth eur 8 million in 2001 and a second one in support of the regional integration institutions and the involvement of civil society in the process of regional integration worth eur 15 million in 2003. a further project in support of the development and implementation of common policies to the value of eur 10 million is currently under preparation. in the andean community, projects on statistics, customs, competition and trade-related technical assistance, together worth more than eur 15 million, are being implemented and there are plans to strengthen this form of cooperation in the forthcoming revision of the regional strategy paper, adding another eur 4 million to the economic regional integration objective. central america, the andean community and latin america as a whole are not suffering from a lack of interest from our side. in the current financial perspectives from 2000 to 2006, funds for latin america are about 20% higher than in the former financial perspective. the community budget spends about eur 0.15 per capita in asia, while three times that much per capita is spent in latin america. perhaps of the greatest significance, we are now actually spending the money we commit. in 2003, 100% of the payments, as well as 100% of commitments, were used. i want to emphasise once again that relations with latin america are a geostrategic priority for the european union. i have been particularly pleased in recent weeks to be able to discuss our relationship with representatives of mercosur, with all the foreign ministers of the andean community and with representatives of central america. i very much hope that we will be able to have a successful summit to follow up the one in madrid, which will focus on regional integration and social inclusion. i also very much hope that the summit in guadalajara will be able to see a further development in our relations with the two regions with which we have only recently negotiated sensible agreements. (applause)
the rapporteur. i am glad to have heard the commissioner's words. they clearly show concern and a sense of priority, and i would like to tell you that the assessment of this political dialogue and cooperation agreement between the european union and the central american region will depend fundamentally on one factor, and that factor will be what perspective this period opens up, which the commissioner has described as a transitional period. from our point of view, and on the basis of the resolution of this parliament of 15 november 2001, this type of political and cooperation agreement must be the door to the preparation of association agreements including a free trade agreement, in accordance with the strong aspirations of our central american partners and, in my view, fully in line with the political, economic and commercial interests of the european union. in other words, the decisive factor will be whether a period of negotiations for an association agreement with the central american countries, including those of the andean community, with similar characteristics, mutatis mutandis, to those with mexico and chile, and the one currently being negotiated with mercosur, is actually opened as a prelude to a more general strategic perspective which should lead to a global interregional agreement and the creation of a euro-latin american free trade area. the third summit in may will now be an opportunity to demonstrate a sense of anticipation and foresight by opening up this perspective in an explicit way. there are changes in the region, a region - we all know - plagued by difficult, serious structural and cyclical situations, but there are certainly encouraging signs; there is a shared will on the part of the presidents of the region to make pragmatic progress in the field of economic integration; there is a new stage of the central american bank for economic integration, which is very promising from my point of view; there are open prospects for reform of the institutions of integration, in particular reforms with a certain depth of the central american parliament and, in this sense, the voice, the presence of the european union must help to show clearly that we do not only do diplomacy when there are situations of conflict, but that with the same commitment, with the priority of helping decisively the peace processes in the region, we continue with determination and tenacity in the perspective of improving the political and economic situation, in a region so devastated by the problems of the present and the history of the region itself. i would like, commissioner, that the may summit in guadalajara should clearly open a stage in which the implementation of this agreement is carried out with the greatest possible will, which also marks the maintenance of the trade facilities enjoyed by the countries of this region, within the system of generalized preferences and the special drug regime, and, above all, that a concrete perspective of compromise is opened up in the perspective of negotiating a real association agreement. and as we speak of the guadalajara summit, i would like to quote mr patten specifically on a subject which is not strictly central american, but which could be a success story of the summit in a specific field: there are several black holes in the current world situation, and one of them is called haiti. and the commitment to intensive and long-term aid from the european union, in agreement with the partners in latin america and in perfect agreement with caricom, the oas and the united nations, could be - i believe - a success story of the guadalajara summit, which will be fixed if the events are followed, afterwards, in a tenacious and long-term way by good intentions.
the rapporteur. {es) mr president, i would first of all like to thank commissioner patten for the efforts he has made, as far as i know, to be present at this debate, despite the difficulties on the agenda. i would also like to congratulate the commission, to remove any doubt, on its diligence in presenting the guidelines for the conclusion of these political dialogue and cooperation agreements - mr obiols was there and other members of this house who are present in this debate - concluded that a large catalogue of statements and pronouncements was not needed, but that it was sufficient, in order to achieve this bi-regional strategic partnership, simply a series of concrete proposals, which we set out in a decalogue. the decalogue is based on three main areas. in the field of political will and dialogue, because - - the next item is the report (a5-0172/2004) by mr goodwill, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on certain fluorinated greenhouse gases (com (2003) 492 - c5-0397/2003 - 2003/0189 (cod)).
commission. mr president, let me comment on the amendments and come back to the purpose and scope of the proposal, because a significant number of the amendments proposed by parliament, such as better or new definitions of terms, reinforce and clarify the commission's proposal, and the commission can accept many of them to a greater or lesser degree. the commission also welcomes a number of amendments that strengthen the provisions on containment and inspections and the training and certification of personnel involved in containment. it is important to say that this proposal is only a first step. the commission has indicated that it will look at a number of other issues, such as foams. consequently, it cannot accept the amendments on recovery, in particular in relation to foams. further action needs to be based on the careful assessment of the benefits and the costs. neither can the commission accept amendments that would either weaken the proposed inspection system of air conditioning and stationary refrigeration or put in place additional requirements as regards training and certification of personnel, both for the commission and the member states that have not been evaluated. an important part of this proposal is the reporting system, which will enable the commission to check the accuracy of emissions reported to the un convention on climate change and to support possible further action. the commission proposal tries to ensure that the necessary information can be collected without imposing too onerous a reporting system on industry, especially smes. in this context, the commission cannot accept a number of amendments. the commission believes that its proposal on use bans and the phase-out of some products and equipment containing fluorinated gases is based on a careful evaluation of all sectors and is balanced and cost-effective. consequently, it cannot support the amendment that would remove the derogation for small magnesium dye-casters using less than 500 kg per annum. the cost for this limited number of small and medium-sized enterprises to convert to an alternative would be high, hence the exemption. there are two other bans that deserve comment. the deletion of the ban on perfluorinated carbons in fire fighting cannot be justified since, apart from some minor uses, the market has already moved to other alternatives. as regards aerosols containing fluorinated gases, the new definition would exclude a number of novelty aerosols, while the inclusion of pharmaceutical aerosols in the exemption category could be a big loophole. on the sensitive issue of the phase-out of the fluorinated gases in mobile air conditioning in vehicles, the commission notes with interest the amendments to ban fluorinated gases, essentially hfc134a in mobile air conditioning in new vehicle models from 1 january 2009, and that a ban should apply to all new vehicles from 1 january 2014. the commission prefers to remain with its overall position on mobile air conditioning, given other amendments that reject the quota system and ban all fluorinated gases used in mobile air conditioning with a global warming potential over 50, rather than 150, as proposed by the commission. the latter would effectively exclude the use of fluorinated gas mixtures or hfc152a and favour co2 mobile air conditioning systems. finally, as regards the legal basis, the commission is proposing that the regulation be based on article 95 – the internal market – and cannot support amendments that propose that the regulation be based on a dual legal basis. the commission believes that while the environmental objective of reducing emissions of fluorinated gases is paramount, the main thrust of the proposal is more relevant to the functioning of the internal market and article 95. in conclusion, i should like to underline that the commission supports many of the amendments proposed for the first reading, and parliament, by acting so quickly, sends an important message to the council that there is now a need for increased focus on this proposal with the aim of reaching a final conclusion as quickly as possible. i will hand over to the secretariat a list summarising the commission's position on each individual amendment commission's position on amendments by parliament: see annex.. thank you for this debate.
