the commission. i would just like to take the floor again briefly and repeat what mrs avilés perea said. it asked again how it could be guaranteed that a case like eurostat could not happen again. that is the essential question. the eurostat case in particular has shown the importance of the measures taken by the commission in the reform, such as the rotation of directors-general. as the court of auditors has said, there can no longer be cultural principalities, but there must be equal standards. the financial regulation has several regulations that rule out that such a thing can happen again. we also drew the conclusions from the question of how we can prevent the flow of information from failing when something happens, as was the case with eurostat. we have set very clear rules that commissioners must be informed of olaf reports, that they must be informed of audit reports drawn up by their directorate-general or by the internal audit service, so that it can no longer happen here that someone is not informed in a timely manner. the proposal to amend the olaf regulation also aims to make it clear that the commissioners responsible will receive the relevant information when olaf is investigating something or has a case. i can only say once again that we have indeed learned the lesson from the eurostat case. mr prodi has been here twice and has explained what measures we are taking. he made commitments to parliament, to the committee on budgetary control, and we have fulfilled those commitments. i would like to thank you again for the debate, for the excellent report and, in general, for the intensive critical but constructively critical cooperation with the committee on budgetary control over the last few years. thank you very much.
commission. i hope you will excuse me if i speak for slightly longer than the two minutes, thirty seconds i am allocated, but the issues we are addressing this evening are extremely important and i would like to give them the attention they deserve. i want to say at the outset that i am very grateful for this opportunity of addressing you tonight on the subject of passenger name records. my friend and colleague, mr bolkestein, spoke to you yesterday about the case for a so-called adequacy finding on this issue. i want to underline once again the fact that the commission will carefully consider the points of view expressed by members in the debate in march, when my colleague also spoke, before making its final decision. another issue the house knows we will have to consider is the question of the onward transfer of passenger name records data by us customs. as commissioner bolkestein made clear yesterday in the plenary, these transfers are a matter of concern to us. commissioner bolkestein and i have been in contact with secretary ridge of the homeland security department on the kind of assurances that we want on the circumstances in which such transfers would take place. i spoke to secretary ridge myself yesterday evening. we look forward to studying his comments, and i can assure the house that his response to our questions will form an important part of our ultimate college decision on an adequacy finding. it is my task this evening to present the case for the other part of the package, namely the international agreement we have negotiated with the united states. it would provide a sound legal basis for allowing airlines to transfer passenger data to the united states. let me start by setting out briefly the background to this issue. none of us will ever forget the horrific attacks on the twin towers on 11 september 2001. the united states was profoundly shocked by them. in fact we were all shocked by those attacks. in europe we have suffered from terrorist attacks for decades – most recently the appalling bombing of passenger trains in spain last month. we stand, i hope, shoulder to shoulder with america in the fight against terrorism and i repeat that in my judgment if we had suffered anything like the attacks on the twin towers, we perhaps might have an even greater appreciation of how great us concern is over air transport. since those attacks the us authorities have taken a whole range of measures to provide their citizens with greater security. the requirement for the transfer of pnr data is one of these. we immediately saw a conflict between the requirements of the us legislation and our own data protection legislation. european airlines were faced with a dreadful dilemma: either to comply with the pnr requirement and risk being taken to court by their national data protection authorities, or not to comply, which would have triggered intrusive extra searches of their passengers. this would have resulted in enormous delays and a potentially serious loss of business for eu airlines to us airlines, which were supplying the required data. the european commission had a responsibility to do what it could to help our airlines and their passengers out of this situation. in the short term we made an arrangement with the us which provided for assurances on how the data would be used. this gave some comfort to the airlines, but we recognised that it did not provide a sound legal footing on which to proceed. that is why we have spent the last 15 months negotiating with the united states. as far as possible, we wanted to uphold the concerns of our citizens for their privacy to be protected. the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs understandably had a long list of objectives that it wanted us to secure. in the real world though, we were never going to be able to secure everything they would have wished. all negotiation involves compromises and, on this occasion, we had to face the fact that the us was already obtaining the data it wanted. as outlined in the commission communication of december 2003, the bilateral international agreement with the us that we are debating today is a necessary element in the framework that the commission is seeking to put in place both for legal and for political reasons. firstly, there is a legal reason related to the data protection directive. determining that there is adequate protection for personal data at the recipient's end is part of what a data controller needs to do before transferring data to a third country. in addition, the controller – in this case the airline – needs a legitimate reason for transferring the data, such as being required to do so by law. however, by law we mean community law or member state law. an obligation imposed by a third country cannot automatically justify processing of data within the community. this international agreement, which will become part of the community legal framework, creates such a requirement, but subject to one very important condition: the existence of adequate data protection in the recipient country, namely the united states. it is important to underline here that this agreement does not take for granted the existence of such adequate protection in the united states. the obligation on airlines is applicable only if an adequacy finding has been made, and for as long as it remains in force. on 31 march the european parliament adopted a resolution in which it disagrees with the commission that the current us undertakings represent adequate protection, and the college will decide in due course how to proceed. however, whatever the commission decides, this part of the agreement will only be applicable if there is an adequacy finding. therefore, there is no reason for parliament to reject the entire agreement on this basis. secondly, there is a legal reason for this international agreement, linked to international law. the european commission took the position of principle that us law enforcement authorities could only get access to databases situated in the community if they had been explicitly allowed to do so. through this agreement the community grants this permission, subject to a double condition. first, that there is adequate data protection in the us. second, that a 'push' system is not yet in place. i would make it clear that the commission shares parliament's view that 'push' should replace the current 'pull' as soon as possible and the date requested by parliament – namely 1 july – has been duly noted. we are doing our best to put in place the conditions that will make 'push' possible very soon. however, since the aim is to provide legal certainty today, we need to address this issue now and then work to change it as soon as possible. from a more political point of view, this agreement fulfils four additional important objectives. first, it ensures the future assistance of the us government on the basis of reciprocity in ensuring that airlines transfer pnr data to community authorities if the community or any of its member states were to introduce such a system. second, it also contains a statement that the us bureau of customs and border protection is implementing the undertakings that the adequacy finding is based upon, which is, as the house recognises, an important international commitment on the part of the united states. third, the agreement also enshrines the commitment to undertake joint reviews on matters relating to the agreement. last, but not least, the agreement protects travellers against unlawful discrimination on the basis of nationality and country of residence. before concluding, allow me to refer briefly to the report that has been submitted, which highlights two legal problems. the first is procedural. the rapporteur considers that parliament should have been asked to give its full assent rather than just being consulted. my reply would be, as commissioner bolkestein explained yesterday, that nothing in this agreement entails amendment to the data protection directive, which is the condition established by article 300 of the treaty for the assent procedure to apply. there is a second concern highlighted in the report, which stipulates that: 'the real scope of the international agreement will evolve at the discretion of the us administration without any legally binding participation from the european union side'. let me be clear that the essential link between the three elements of the package – international agreement, adequacy finding and us undertakings – is there to ensure coherence between them. no adequacy finding without undertakings; no legal effect on airlines as regards the agreement without an adequacy finding. so any unilateral change to the us undertakings that would lead to non-compliance with the principles of adequacy would also lead to a suspension of the adequacy finding. simultaneously, it would also lead to the non-application of the two key clauses of the international agreement, the obligation on airlines to provide the data and the authorisation to the us to pull without any need to modify or revoke the international agreement. this crucial safety valve is built into the agreement to prevent precisely what the report fears, i.e. the european union side being forced to accept any unilateral change to the us requirements for receiving passenger name records. to conclude, i would like to urge members to support the adoption of this agreement, despite their misgivings about the adequacy finding. for the reasons i have explained, this would not necessarily be incompatible with the position parliament has taken on the adequacy finding. the resolution adopted by the european parliament on 31 march calls for a wider international agreement incorporating a series of data protection principles. i believe that such an agreement is beyond what is achievable today. that is why i would ask parliament to back this agreement, not because it is perfect but because it is a great deal better for our airlines to operate under legal certainty and it is a great deal better for passengers to have much improved safeguards than the legal void that would result from a collapse of a package which we have worked so long and hard to negotiate. i apologise for speaking at such length, but i know this is an issue of considerable importance to parliament and i wanted to try to deal with the main issues that have been raised.

commission. mr president, i am only sorry that the house is melting away as we come to these important issues, but perhaps for the next few moments i will not find myself trapped between these passions as i have been recently! let me come to calmer matters. in february 2003, in response to the conclusions of the december 2002 justice and home affairs council, the commission presented a package of practical measures which seek to alleviate legal inconsistencies and practical difficulties in relation to the stamping of third country nationals' travel documents at the external borders of the member states. in november 2003 the commission presented a proposal for a regulation which seeks first to impose an obligation on the member states to stamp such travel documents systematically; secondly, to lay down the conditions in which the absence of an entry stamp may constitute prima facie evidence that the individual has overstayed in the member state's territory; and thirdly to ensure that the checks on individuals at external borders are only relaxed in exceptional and unforeseen circumstances. the obligation on the member states' authorities to stamp the travel documents of third country nationals systematically will make it possible to use the lack of an entry stamp as prima facie evidence of an illegal stay. this presumption of illegality may be challenged by any other evidence that the third country national may be able to produce. to allow member states time to put in place the necessary practical arrangements for implementation, the regulation will not come into effect until 1 may this year. on this date many of the practical implementation challenges will, in our judgment, cease to exist because enlargement will mean that the travel documents of citizens of the new member states will no longer need to be stamped. i hope that those honourable members who have delayed bedtime to listen to these remarks will find them helpful and i look forward to listening to the debate.

- the next item is the report (a5-0279/2004) by mr fernández martín, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation amending council regulation (ec) no 975/1999 laying down the requirements for the implementation of development cooperation operations which contribute to the general objectives of developing and consolidating democracy and the rule of law and respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms (com (2003) 639 - c5-0507/2003 - 2003/0250 (cod)).
commission. mr president, i am extremely pleased to have this opportunity to tell parliament why the rather technical commission proposal to which you will be giving a first reading today is so important. the regulation which you are being asked to extend by two years, until the end of the present financial perspective in 2006, is one of the two legal bases for the european initiative for democracy and human rights. as you are well aware, the initiative is an extremely important element of the european union’s overall policy on promoting human rights and democratisation in third countries. in 1999, the european parliament itself was fully involved in drawing up the regulations underlying the european initiative for democracy and human rights, moulding the objectives of the initiative and setting its priorities, as well as shaping the administrative procedures for its implementation. i am very pleased to see now that the honourable member's report fully supports the commission in securing an extension of the initiative beyond the end of this year, subject to some amendments. in the run-up to today’s plenary and decision-making, the commission proposal has triggered fruitful exchanges between a number of members of this house and commissioner patten and/or commission services. these exchanges have focused essentially on two important issues: firstly, how to more effectively involve the european parliament in political priority setting for implementation of the initiative and, secondly, how to further improve the performance and practical relevance of the initiative with a view to democracy building and strengthening human rights in the world. we have welcomed these exchanges, as we welcome today’s debate. the commission, like parliament, has every interest in supporting proposals designed to make the initiative ever more effective and relevant. as was stated at the february part-session, we have an open mind on the ideas that members of parliament put forward. however, this does not allow us to disregard certain constraints imposed by respective institutional prerogatives, nor must we lose sight of the key objective of the commission proposal before you today, which is to secure the continued operational availability of the initiative for the next two years. the commission has listened carefully to the views expressed by honourable members and is ready to examine in a constructive spirit all ideas that have been put to it in order to ensure that what we do, under the european initiative for democracy and human rights, is better focused and more effective. more specifically, i would like to state that the commission is committed to setting up a structured and regular dialogue on the initiative with the competent committees of the european parliament, led by the responsible commissioner and supported by his or her own services. this will enable us to exchange views in good time on planned multiannual programming documents, annual programming updates and work programmes, or amendments to them. it would, i hope, give parliament ample opportunity to provide comments and input into the commission’s thinking. it would also, crucially, be compatible with comitology rules and institutional prerogatives. moreover, the commission will examine with an open mind the suggestion, contained in the report's explanatory statement, to create specific mechanisms to allow greater involvement of civil society and ngos with a view to the promotion of democracy and human rights. in this respect, i would simply remind you, however, that this suggestion has to be seen in the context of the commission’s recent proposal on the future financial perspective, which envisages a simplified architecture capitals of culture has opened up new prospects for these cities by orienting them towards cultural industries, cultural tourism and cultural exposure. this is the case in a city like glasgow, for centres. if we work well in the future, as this parliament, whose last cultural debate is now, has done for the past five years, i have no doubt, mr president, that what your committee wanted, what your commissioner has always advocated, will be put into practice in the cultural cities of the future. i hope that the good examples of the past will be followed in the future and i wish all citizens commission. mr president, i am pleased to say that on this occasion i totally agree with mr posselt, which is not always the case. in reply to mr tannock, it is true that there is a big difference not on board, including the eu member state named during the debate. the most important and effective thing way of proceeding in post-conflict situations is, if possible, to have the two sides in a conflict join together in demining mapping. nicaragua was a good example of this, even though that was never a dirty guerrilla war. it was well-organised and both sides had mapped what they had done. commission. the european commission supports the strengthening of core labour standards and social governance in the context of globalisation. it has taken various policy initiatives in this field. it considers that more should be done to strengthen the social dimension of globalisation, and will contribute to the follow-up to the report recently presented by the world commission on the social dimension of globalisation established by the international labour organisation. with regard to the olympic games, the european commission financially supports the implementation of the charter of intent adopted by the organising committee for the winter olympic games in turin in 2006. this sets out the organising committee's commitment to dealing with ethical, environmental and social issues and to reporting on the social impact of the activities and compliance with the ethical standards. this initiative could also be very relevant for the 2004 summer olympic games. the european commission also contributes to the promotion of corporate social responsibility, workers' rights and decent work in the sports goods industry. it encourages the involvement and commitment of all actors, for example to combating the use of child labour in the production of fifa-licensed sportswear and footballs. a similar approach covering all core labour standards could be developed for the upcoming olympic games with relevant partners such as the global trade unions, broader civil society, the international olympic committee, the world federation of sporting goods industry, the different brands and companies and the ilo. the commission will continue its efforts to promote a more cohesive approach to harnessing globalisation, also tackling issues such as the application of fair rules in global supply and production chains. this is what the commission can provide in response to the concerns raised. however, with the organisers of the olympic games having given up the ideals of amateurism and voluntarily buried themselves in the deep dark hole of big money, there is a limit to what we can expect from them in the sphere economic ethics. they represent just another case in which we could discuss corporate social responsibility. in my view they are not a special case. they lost their innocence ages ago. the real problem is so huge that we must dig deep into our resources to continue the broader general struggle of ensuring decency triumphs in a world capable of producing child labour, etc. – with or without the olympic games.

- the motion for a resolution (b5-0194/2004 by mr andrews, on behalf of the uen group, on nigeria; - the motion for a resolution (b5-0203/2004 by mr tannock, mr corrie, mr sacrédeus and mr posselt, on behalf of the ppe-de group, on nigeria; - the motion for a resolution (b5-0205/2004 by mr rod, mr isler béguin and mr maes, on behalf of the greens/ale group, on nigeria); - the motion for a resolution (b5-0206/2004 by mr belder, on behalf of the edd group, on nigeria); - the motion for a resolution (b5-0209/2004 by mr van den berg, on behalf of the pse group, on nigeria); - the motion for a resolution (b5-0211/2004 by mr van den bos, on behalf of the eldr group, on nigeria); - the motion for a resolution (b5-0213/2004 by mr boudjenah, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on nigeria).
commission. mr president, the commission shares the concern at conflicts between communities in nigeria and condemns all attacks and violence, whether apparently ethnic, religious or social, etc. in origin. we caution against a simplistic analysis of the situation which focuses on just one area or religious group. the violence is often related to conflicts over access to resources or triggered by political tensions. in the case of plateau state, the causes of violence are related to both these reasons and the perpetrators have come from both sides of the community. it is factually wrong to describe this as something driven only by islamic fundamentalists. for information, i would add that plateau state is not a state which applies sharia law, and it is not likely to because it has an overwhelming christian majority composed of groups of indigenous people and settlers. in very many cases, there is a sort of social clash between incomer settler groups and the original inhabitants – a version of a conflict that we see in very many other places. the problem with understanding nigeria is that there are several layers of problems, and each layer is normally enough to create a conflict. therefore this complex situation is something we really have to respect in order to do something useful. for the second time this afternoon i have to say that i agree with mr posselt's contribution. we have similar views on this situation. his reference to yugoslavia is also very important because there we have assisted in a so-called solution which is contrary to what we, for very good reasons, find necessary for africa, namely to avoid changing the geography. even though we gave them nonsensical borders, europe and others rightly agree with africa itself that, as long as africa does not want to change the borders, we definitely should not advise it to do that, even if it is difficult. conflicts between communities in nigeria have been evident for some time and we have been following the situation as part of the early warning system for conflict which the commission is setting up. the commission has also adapted its cooperation programme to reflect that situation. support for human rights in nigeria is a significant component of our cooperation strategy for the country. nigeria was also selected as a focal country for the european initiative for democracy and human rights to respond to precisely the sort of concerns raised by parliament. three projects were approved last year, including one with a nigerian ngo working in plateau state and kaduna state to promote peace between muslims and christians. the project also covers improving the drafting and application of sharia law in conformity with the guarantees of religious freedom provided in the nigerian constitution as well as respect for the international conventions providing protection for human rights which the country has signed. in other words, reasonable co-existence between sharia law and the constitution of nigeria is an option. this is what the country is trying to organise. i mention this simply by way of a warning that we must not move blindly in one direction without really reflecting on the complexities involved. as i have already said, other conflicts relating to religious differences are very important and we should be careful not to overlook or marginalise these other aspects. if we fail to understand this, we will not be of much use in a dialogue aimed at stopping the conflicts. social, economic and ethnic problems – all these other layers of problems i have mentioned – have to be given a proper place in the analysis. at federal level the commission is working with member states to strengthen political dialogue with nigeria. this dialogue is one of the instruments provided by the cotonou agreement and the federal government is participating actively in that dialogue. we have adapted to the special realities of nigeria, where the states play a powerful role, and in fact the bulk of our work relating to water and sanitation is being done in six of the 36 states that make up the federal republic of nigeria. we have chosen the six states not on the basis of where it is easiest to work, but where need is greatest. although, in so doing, we are inviting problems, this is the most meaningful way of working on matters that relate to the core of the problems underlying what we are discussing here this afternoon. we share this house's call for the federal government to do everything in its power to protect its citizens, put an end to violence and promote respect of human rights, including of course freedom of religion. we hope that parliament's adoption of a resolution which is balanced on this issue will be seen as meaningful encouragement along these lines.

mr president, we are a large majority in this parliament, as in european society, who want a political europe and welcome the new member states, who want a constitution that will advance the union as a political entity united in diversity, to consolidate this historical experience, unique in today's world, in a continent which, even in the last century, has seen terribly tragic experiences. the stateless nations, like mine, galicia, are not yet recognized as such in the draft constitution. as we want a political europe, a europe of the peoples and citizens, we will continue to fight for this recognition and for self-determination within the union. if we want a political europe, mr president, we must say that it will not exist without a social europe, the achievement of which is particularly urgent with the integration of brotherly peoples whose per capita income does not exceed 40% of that of the union of the fifteen. in this situation it is paradoxical and irresponsible for the wealthier states, which say they want a political europe, to try to impose a reduced budget of the european union, which amounts to only 1% of gdp, even though, with enlargement, the inhabitants of the territories eligible for objective 1 (which have less than 75% of the average per capita income) will double, or rather, will increase from the current 63 million to 153 million in the coming years. the budget is not going to be solved if it is limited to the 1.14% proposed by the commission. if we continue along this line, we shall not be moving towards social europe. per capita funding in the objective 1 regions will be cut in half, thus undermining the cohesion policy that has helped to shape the whole of the union. and this will be negative, both for the union of the fifteen and for the union of the twenty-seven in the enlarged union.
the commission. mr president, if we could characterize tonight's debate and give it a title, we would say that it is a debate on solidarity. it was indeed the word that was heard more than any other tonight and, of course, the need to strengthen it was stressed many times and i hope, as mr libicki and mr kroupa said earlier, that we will be able to make europe and our countries better for us and followed the debate very closely, and i can say that it has become clear that economic and social policy cannot be dissociated from each other. the approach we adopted last year, deciding to modernise and combine these two policy areas, is therefore the right one. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the slow economic growth in the early years of the lisbon strategy, and therefore of the social policy agenda, may raise doubts, as mrs lulling has said before, about the underlying logic of the modernisation approach adopted in 2000. the fact that several intermediate objectives will not be achieved in 2005, such as unemployment, as mrs ainardi and others have pointed out, and the increase in the employment rate of older workers, which is much lower than the rate we have been aiming for, can all feed criticism. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. we must not only remain faithful, as mr marini has stressed, to the principles on which the european economic and social model is based and which are contained in the lisbon strategy, but also be committed to the objectives of that strategy. this does not exclude that adjustments may be required in respect of the specific policy measures and their methods of implementation. but it is clear that the european union should take advantage of the economic recovery and the enlargement momentum to give new impetus to the lisbon strategy, focusing in particular on certain priorities such as improving investment in networks and technological knowledge, as highlighted by many, including mrs grossetête, mr szabó and many others, strengthening the competitiveness of industry and services and extending working life. in general, the new member states face and are facing the same challenges in implementing structural reforms as the old member states. of course, as many have pointed out, such as mr krasts, mrs šlesere, the new member states are certainly having greater difficulties in some cases. of course, some countries, such as poland, as mrs ciemniak said, have high growth rates, 6%, and have achieved faster reforms in the area of structural reforms. in this area of structural reforms the new member states must focus particularly on creating conditions to boost productivity growth, as productivity levels are generally very low, and on tackling the high levels of structural and long-term unemployment mentioned by mr siekierski. i would also like to mention at this point a point raised by mrs jensen at the beginning of the debate and taken up again later, the question of the free movement of workers. it is known that transitional arrangements are in place. this translated into different national practices covering the whole spectrum from 0 to 7 years. but regardless of any gradations in the transitional periods, which i hope will prove unnecessary and be abolished as soon as possible, or restricted as much as possible, i must stress that freedom of movement and the right to settle and work in another member state constitute fundamental freedoms protected by community law. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would also like to stress again what i said in my initial speech, that highly integrated and interdependent economies, which share a common market, need effective coordination of economic policy formulation and implementation, both at national and european union level. all the components of the economic coordination framework are closely linked to this overall strategy. i also agree with those who have stressed, like mrs thyssen, that the only way to accelerate progress is to make further reforms. we must extend our coordination beyond budgetary matters to cover broader economic policy issues and we must take into account both the social and environmental dimension which mrs myller has spoken of and has mentioned what i have said and emphasized before and i make it clearer now, namely that countries which provide high social protection, such as denmark and sweden, manage to be highly competitive. we must find, mr president, the political will to extend our coordination to all the areas covered by the lisbon strategy, so as to achieve greater growth and more employment.

the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking you for this last opportunity to address parliament on the development of the area of freedom, security and justice in an enlarged europe. the commission and parliament have been together for five years, and the contribution and constructive cooperation of this parliament, sometimes in very difficult circumstances and with very tight deadlines, will undoubtedly be one of the major milestones of this legislature. recent eurobarometer surveys organised by the commission demonstrate the general desire of citizens for more europe. these expectations are even greater in the context of an enlarged europe of 455 million inhabitants. the new citizens of the union want to live freely in a world of security, just like everyone else. security is not just about fighting crime, security is a means of ensuring freedom. these two concepts are inseparable and the commission has always sought to strike a balance between freedom and security. the third element of this area is, of course, justice, which contributes to the protection of freedom and to the guarantee of security in an area where the mobility and interrelationship of people and businesses across national borders are an increasingly present reality. today, many citizens of the union still fear the security consequences of enlargement. it's important to address those fears with rational argument. the enlargement process has strengthened the capacity of the new member states to contribute to the development of stability and security throughout the european union, not only by receiving the acquis communautaire but also by improving the police and judicial capacity that the commission has supported over the past five years. negotiations with the acceding countries were concluded only when it was mutually agreed that a satisfactory level of alignment with the existing legislative framework and an adequate enforcement capacity by the new member states had been achieved. in all cases, further progress is still needed. the commission will play its normal role as guardian of the treaties and will continue to provide substantial financial assistance following the phare projects, which will continue until 2006, and thereafter through a schengen mechanism and the transition facility itself. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union's budget. another aspect that has been conveyed by the media concerns the fear of a massive movement of new citizens across europe. as i have already had occasion to say here, these fears are unjustified. the commission has carried out a study which shows that in the next five years about 1% of the total working population of the new member states will exercise the right to move. this means less than 220 000 people a year in a union of over 450 million people. i would like to remind you, even in my own personal capacity, that on the eve of enlargement to include spain and portugal, similar fears were raised, which proved to be completely unfounded. the treaty of accession provides for the possibility for the present 15 member states to apply transitional measures. they are sufficient and i hope they are indeed merely transitory. enlargement also represents a real challenge for certain specific policies, notably the strengthening of external border controls. we hope that the external borders agency will be operational from 1 january 2005 to support the efforts of the 10 new member states to improve border control. as parliament knows, the internal border controls of the new member states will only be abolished following a specific evaluation process and a subsequent council decision. but this two-stage process will only be completed once the schengen information system, the so-called 'second generation' sis, has been established. the timely development of sis ii is therefore a priority for the commission and will require the active involvement of all member states. in the field of judicial cooperation, the enlarged europe makes mutual trust even more indispensable to ensure the full operation of the principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions. in this connection, certain procedural measures need to be improved, for example those provided for in the framework decision on procedural guarantees in criminal proceedings which the commission has just presented to the council, and mutual trust between all the member states of the union needs to be strengthened through better mutual knowledge of their legislative and judicial systems. at the request of the european parliament, the commission is in the process of setting up an exchange programme for judges from all member states, both in civil and criminal matters. finally, as regards justice and home affairs policies, we are faced with a number of challenges. one of them is the visa policy and, in particular, the principle of reciprocity in this area, which has been the subject of careful attention by the commission. in an enlarged union, for the area of justice and home affairs to work, it is essential that the constitutional treaty comes into force, that the structure of the pillars is abolished, that the co-decision process is generalized to ensure full democratic accountability for decisions in this area. judicial control needs to be improved by extending the jurisdiction of the court of justice and giving the commission the powers typical of infringement proceedings. the draft constitutional treaty responds to these challenges by proposing the introduction of qualified majority voting in the area of the common policy on immigration, asylum and external borders and the strengthening of the provisions on the integration of third-country nationals legally resident in the european union. the principle of solidarity, which is already in place, will be more clearly enshrined in the constitutional text on border control, asylum and immigration. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to remind you that 1 may marks not only the date of accession of the 10 new member states but also the expiry of the deadline set by the treaty of amsterdam for the completion of the first phase of the gradual development of an area of freedom, security and justice. the commission will shortly present a communication assessing progress over the past five years and including initial guidelines for future priorities. these priorities will be built on the common values of freedom, security and justice of an enlarged europe and should be based on the progress that we all hope will be provided for in the future constitutional treaty, which must be swiftly adopted for it to enter into full force.

council. mr president, i will be brief, but i wish to thank members for their constructive and positive comments. there were some comments on the shortcomings of our presidency, and i shall take these in the spirit in which they were made. i want to thank mr poettering, mr hänsch, mr duff and many others who welcomed the agreement on the european constitution. the agreement on the constitution was historic: agreement would not have been possible without all the participants working together to achieve it. the important thing is that the union has shown that win-win solutions are possible if we work towards compromises, as many people have stated. it is impossible for people to set down what they alone want. via compromise, this unique system can create positive outcomes that benefit everybody. all of you who have just been engaged in the election campaigns and earned the privilege of being in this parliament know how important the european union is for the prosperity and well-being of europeans. at the same time, you, more than most, know the difficulty of making european union agenda heard above the clamour of what some people often mistakenly consider to be more pressing bread-and-butter issues. i say 'mistakenly' because the european union is about vision and a vast array of practical issues of great importance. many members, from different countries and different perspectives, have mentioned those issues today. we must explain to people what is in the constitution. it will be important to provide a space for informed debate in countries that will and will not be holding a referendum. the period between now and the entry into force of the treaty will give us the opportunity to describe and explain what the union does and does not do. we can articulate the values and objectives that underpin the union. although we should not underestimate our task, we should not underestimate the text of the european constitution itself. a clause that states that the union's values are respect for human dignity, liberty, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights is one that can be clearly understood by all our people and should be sold to them on the basis of those values. when the constitution states that the union's aim is to promote peace, its values and the well-being of its peoples, this too will resonate with everybody. at the same time, however, there will be genuine concerns and many opposing views will be raised. these concerns must be heard and the issues must be addressed in a measured and reasonable way. a fear without foundation is still a fear, and all fears must be addressed, as i have discovered over the last six months. those of us who support the european union and the constitution whose values it embodies must remain passionate advocates of it. at the same time it is important that those who support and those who oppose the new european constitution approach the debate with moderation, reason and accuracy. i just wish to touch on a few of the issues mr poettering raised. he and some others mentioned the issue of christianity. the preamble of the text acknowledges europe's religious inheritance. we would have preferred to see an explicit reference to its christian heritage, but it was not simple to achieve a consensus on a suitable wording. however, an important new article recognises the special contribution of churches and, for the first time, provides for open and regular discussion with them. this has been widely welcomed by church and faith organisations. so although there is no explicit reference in the preamble ­ which i personally would have liked ­ it was important to include that new clause. a number of members mentioned the nomination process, which i know is very important to mrs frassoni. back in the convention, the irish government proposed a radical way of nominating future presidents of the commission. our vision was to involve this parliament and the parliaments of all the member states in the process of electing the new commission president. i would ask the new members of parliament to look at our proposal. we received no support when we advocated it, so i hate to hear the people who did not support us now criticising us, but that's politics! members should consider the proposal for the next time around: it may be complicated, but it is a good idea. remarkable work was done in the convention on the european social dimension. mr katiforis led the working group on social europe. it is an area of particular concern to me personally and to the irish presidency because we value the social solidarity that is the central feature of the european project in ireland. we are a country that fully involves employers and trade unions ­ a 'voluntary pillar' ­ in all legislative decisions. we have been doing that for 17 years. i have to remind my good friend and colleague mrs doyle of that ­ the point has obviously passed her by over the 17 years. we value the concept, and president prodi is quite right: we have adopted a positive, progressive aspect of the constitutional treaty. this is the european people's constitution. we must remind our citizens of that fact. i agree with mrs doyle's point on small business: we have to continue to try to do that for small business. mr czarnecki spoke of the issue of freedom of movement. from day one we in ireland have opened our doors to all parts of europe and we did not distinguish between people from old and new member states. we are proud that we have done that. mr goebbels and a number of other members underlined the importance of the lisbon agenda and regretted that more of the goals involved were not achieved. i am the first to acknowledge that the lisbon agenda is work in progress. we have to intensify efforts and improve our delivery if we are to reach the goals we have set ourselves for 2010. that is why we set up such a thorough process in the mid-term review. we have set out what we would like to do in the future, but we have also said what we have done. as regards practical delivery over the last six months, and to give one concrete example as to what i was asked to do, people should just look at the details set out in a chapter of a report we drafted dealing with working together for growth and employment. i have been asked to look at the financial services area, which was most effectively steered forward under the leadership of minister mccreevy. by securing an agreement on the financial services instruments, the market directives and the transparency directive, minister mccreevy and his team - with excellent cooperation from parliament - completed this services action plan. this is a critical area for the future growth of the european economy and one i can cite as a practical example of what is being delivered on the lisbon agenda. indeed, i have underlined the importance i attach to the lisbon agenda in nominating minister mccreevy as commissioner. i am sure his experience will help there in the future, because the lisbon agenda is all about delivering growth and jobs for europe, and the minister knows about delivering those two things. i would invite you to look at ireland's record on these issues, which is would be of some value. mr de rossa is correct that we should discuss domestic issues at home, and i will be very glad to do that with him at any time. our finance minister has liberated irish workers from the punitive tax rates established when the administration with which mr de rossa was associated was in power. i always find it interesting when a socialist mentions a 'right-wing person': definitions are always interesting. mr de rossa says he is left-wing and socialist and he gave under two euros to old people. mr mccreevy is right­wing and he gives 10 euros every year to old people. work out the definitions for yourselves: they are quite interesting. i have only been in politics for 27 years: i need to be around a while longer before i understand the definitions of right and left, which i believe are rather nonsensical in any case. it is a true honour to be here reporting to the house. i believe that 2004 will be seen as a highly significant year for the european union. we enlarged to 25 member states. we have agreed a constitution. we have renewed our commitment to achieving the lisbon agenda goals. we have reinforced our relationship with our global partners. while the work of the irish presidency is done, the work of the union obviously continues. i wish mr balkenende and the dutch presidency every success. i also wish president prodi every success for the remainder of his term of office and hopefully the same will apply ­ with the house's support ­ to mr durão barroso in the future. i wish you well too, mr president. on this first working day, i wish everybody here happiness and success in their political work in the european parliament. go raibh míle míle maith agaibh. because i think that all of us europeans have a fundamental interest in the stabilization of iraq, in seeing a truly independent iraq, an iraq at peace with itself and at peace in the region. if i am of the world, globally considered, to face the great challenges on a global scale, namely terrorism, threats to the environment, major epidemics and underdevelopment, which cannot be overcome by europe alone. europe alone is not enough. we need to bring our main partners along constructively, and among them are, of course, the united states of america. but now i would like to make it clear that i am european, portuguese and european with a lot of honor. if i am elected president of the european commission, i will defend the general interest of europe, the common european good, and i will not accept that europe is treated as a second-rate power, regardless of which power it is. i would like to see that there is no doubt about this. the third question concerns our conception of european security and defence. in this context, i would like to say that i stand today for what i stood for before i took up this position as a candidate for the presidency of the european commission. i understand that it is useful and i think that we need to build a european security and defence identity. i think it is important and that is why, as prime minister, i supported all the steps to strengthen this european unity and, moreover, i had the honour, as minister for foreign affairs, of signing some of the acts in which portugal was involved in building this same identity, namely our accession to eurofor or euromarfor, which were the first steps of my country towards actively participating in a european security and defence identity. the second question concerns the role of the commission, the european parliament and the european council. i would like to repeat on this point what i have already written and said before i took up this position. i have always defended the role of the commission as a supranational institution, as a truly community institution. the positions i took at the intergovernmental conference were to give the european commission the greatest independence and credibility. i did not know then, i did not even imagine that i would find myself in this position, but i believe, and i believed then and i still believe, that the community method is essential. more than ever, now with 25 countries and in the future with 27, 28 or more, if we enter into a purely intergovernmental logic - i will weigh the words but i will say it - it could be the end of the european union. if we follow a purely intergovernmental logic, it could be so. we can have a logic of groups, a logic of balkanization between groups in the european union, the strongest against the weakest, the richest against the poorest, the centre against the periphery, the largest against the smallest. the only solution is the community method as advocated by the founding fathers of the european union, jean monnet, robert schuman, konrad adenauer, alcide de gasperi, paul henri spaak, and so many others. that is why i said in my speech that we are not going to change the values, but we can change the attitude in the implementation of these values. the community method and the role of the commission are therefore essential, and in this sense i think the positive complicity i have mentioned in the relationship between the commission and the european parliament is important. a prominent mep, daniel cohn-bendit, argued that meps should punish the council and for that, the candidate for president of the european commission should be shot. i would like to say that if you want to punish the council, mr president, there are other ways of doing it that are much more practical and less painful than punishing myself. there are many other occasions in this parliament to do so. however, the commission can be your ally, it can be the european parliament's ally and i have already said that i will do everything to ensure that this is the case, with due regard for the powers of each institution. i have tried to show my respect for parliament here today, as i have done in the hearings with all the political groups. i have tried to do the same as i did in my country with regard to the assembly of the republic, our national parliament. i promise you loyal cooperation in accordance with the principles of transparency which have been mentioned here by several members, particularly from the liberal group, but not only from the liberal and democratic group. so i think that if i am elected we should make a dynamic coalition of those who are at the forefront of this european project. that is why i said that although my party is of course and with great honour part of a political family, i believe that the president of the commission should not be the president of a faction, but should seek consensus among all those who share essentially the same european project. i can see here in the different political families, from the socialists to the liberals and democrats, in the epp family and in other members, the same european conviction. that is why, in reply to some members of the european socialist party and also of the liberal group, i would like to say that my approach is neither dogmatic nor factional and i think i have shown that when i was the only head of government to support a socialist politician as a candidate for president of the commission, but i did so because i was convinced that he was a good candidate for president of the european commission. would you like better evidence of a non-dogmatic spirit and a non-sectarian spirit? if i am elected, i will work with the various political families, and of course with those who believe in this european project, and i will end by making the following request: on the social question, please do not make caricatures of my position. as prime minister i had to act on what i considered most urgent, but what is considered most urgent is not necessarily what is most important. in my scale of priorities, the social and cultural come before the economic. but i have had occasion to say that in order to achieve social justice objectives - which i believe are above others - we must act immediately from the economic and financial point of view. this is my vision for europe. that is why i consider that the lisbon agenda is not just the agenda for competitiveness. competitiveness, no doubt, but also social cohesion, sustainable development, including environmental protection, and a european policy of environmental leadership. that is why in the agenda i have proposed to you today, in general terms, a partnership for europe, i have spoken of three essential vectors: prosperity, solidarity - i stress solidarity - and security. solidarity between the different regions, in order to respond to the new members of our union, but also solidarity between the different groups and social classes, paying particular attention to the most disadvantaged. this is my vision. i think it's possible to reconcile these elements. i repeat, i am a reformist from the centre who wants to work loyally with this parliament, who believes that europe can be built with a lot of will and who needs your support to give authority and credibility to a commission, not to defend the commission's own ground and any institutional selfishness but because the commission is the body that represents the general interest of the european union and the european common good and therefore has this natural complicity with the european parliament, which is the voice of all european citizens. if i can earn your trust, that's the direction i'm committed to working towards. mr president, mr durão barroso, first of all, let me congratulate you on your appointment as the future president of the european commission, and i would also like to make a few comments on three points which i think are important. firstly, on the role of the commission and the appointment of its president, secondly, on the common foreign and security policy and, thirdly, on diversity, subsidiarity and shared sovereignty in the european union. firstly, the role of the commission and the appointment of its president. you have just been appointed by the heads of government, by the european council, and it is for this parliament, this house, to approve your appointment, which will eventually be ratified, together with that of the other members of the commission, by the governments of the member states. with the new constitutional treaty, which will come into force in these five years of your next mandate, and also that of this house, this question will change, and it will be the european council which, taking into account the result of the elections, will propose to parliament the candidate to be elected president of the commission, who will be elected by the european parliament. i think it is a step forward, although i still do not consider it a decisive step. i would like to ask you, mr barroso, whether you think that, with the new constitutional treaty, the commission will really become a real executive government of the union; whether you think that, when the citizens have to cast their vote in the elections to the european parliament, they will really feel that their vote is decisive and that with it they will be electing the president who will govern the union in the next term. we have had an experience which has been absolutely negative, because there has been a large abstention. i think it's because the citizens haven't felt that their vote was for this. second, you hosted the meeting in the azores that led to the invasion and the war in iraq. i would like to ask you whether, in your new role, in a similar situation you would allow members of the european union to take such a decision without first consulting the council, without there having been a joint position of all the member states of the european union. and thirdly, with regard to diversity, this constitutional treaty speaks of the competences of the european institutions and also of the state institutions. it speaks of exclusive powers of the union and of shared powers, but there is a real diversity within the union which has not been taken into account: the stateless nations and the constitutional regions, which have powers over which the central governments of the states cannot decide. what do you intend to do in your mandate to make the european union truly integrate its real, institutional and cultural diversity?

president of the commission. i would like to thank all the questions that have been put to me and i will try to answer all of them, some of which i did answer yesterday. i would first like to address the greek members who were very active in the debate and, in showing my fair play, congratulate them on their victory in the european championship hosted by portugal. i want to tell you that organising a championship of that size is a big task and that is why i wish our greek friends the greatest success in organising the next olympic games. even to those who will not vote for me, i want to say that i will show the same fair play that i showed in relation to the victory of greece in the last championship. as regards the specific questions i have organized, the cluster responses, in this matter i am in favour of clusters. international issues: to answer questions from mr watson, mr de sarnes, mr schultz, mr ortuondo larrea and mr kristovskis, among others, on a strong europe in the world, i am in favour of europe maintaining its leadership on environmental issues, particularly on climate change issues with kyoto. i am in favour of europe maintaining its leadership in favour of open and fair markets in the doha negotiations and promoting a multilateral perspective on both political and trade issues. i am in favour of europe taking an active role in development policy, particularly in the fight against poverty in the world. africa, of course, is a priority. but also against epidemics like aids, malaria, tuberculosis. i think europe has a social duty here which it cannot abdicate. that is why we must also have resources that are compatible with our ambitions in the new financial perspective, while also trying to fulfil our commitments in the united nations declaration, the so-called millennium declaration, and also our commitments in monterrey with regard to development assistance. as regards more specifically foreign, security and defence policy, and in this context i am referring to several questions, in particular those from mr deus pinheiro and mr wiersma, i think we must develop a defence identity in europe. the new constitution, the new constitutional treaty will help us to consolidate this security and defence identity. i also think we can work with the high representative, the future foreign minister of the european union. in fact, i'm already prepping that job with javier solana, because i think there's a job to be done here. i now turn to the question of iraq, which i raised yesterday, but on which i would like to say a few more words. the truth is that the iraq question has shown that there is still no common european policy. it was not my country that broke the unity of the european union. there were several members of the european union who are even members of the united nations security council who took different positions. this is the reality. it is not the european commission that has to define the foreign policy of the european union, it is still, in our system, an intergovernmental matter. what i can tell you is that as president of the european commission i will try to work, in particular with the new foreign minister of the european union provided for in the new treaty, so that there is gradually a coherent policy of the union, so that the european union speaks with one voice. now, the truth is that on the iraq issue it has been found that this is not the case yet and that is why i understand that it is not useful for us to be here today to talk about who was right. we must now look for ways of getting closer together, and the latest resolution adopted unanimously by the united nations security council already provides the basis for such a convergence. our interest in working together on the iraq issue, our interest in seeking a common vision, namely for the stabilization of iraq, of that region, for an independent and sovereign iraq, for an iraq at peace with itself and at peace with its neighbours. i therefore try to answer the questions put to me by mr wurtz, mr swoboda, mr antónio costa, mr napoletano, mr wiersma, mr frassoni, mr gruber, mr paasilina and all the others, by saying that in the future, if i am confirmed by you as president of the european commission, i will do my best, together with the member states, to ensure that there is a common vision, a common vision which has not visibly existed between the member states, nor, let us be honest and sincere, even within our respective political families. it was a painful issue and we have to get past it in the future. but i want to say the same thing to you yesterday about the question of iraq, and more particularly about relations with the united states. i am very proud to be european. if i am confirmed by you as president of the european commission, it is my duty to defend the general european interest, the common european good, and not the foreign policy vision of country a or country b. i shall not be bound by the foreign policy position of this or that government but by the search for a foreign policy of the european union. as regards relations with the states - a question raised by several members, including swoboda, mussolini, schultz, evans and others - i think it is important that the european union does not define itself as opposed to any country or any region. we have our own identity. we do not need to define ourselves as opposed to the united states, china, russia or any other global power. i think it is in our interest to involve the united states of america constructively in the major global issues, namely environmental issues and the fight against underdevelopment and major epidemics. that is what i will try to do if i am elected president of the european commission. another issue that has been raised here has to do with turkey, which is one of the most difficult issues we have to face. mr grossetête, mr de sarnés, mr martinez, mr molder and mr belder, among others, have spoken on this subject. it will be a key decision for the european union. before any decision is taken in december, both the european commission and the council must hear the european parliament's opinion on this matter. i cannot now assume or presume what the final outcome of this process will be. i do not yet know what the commission's position will be on the report which is still being prepared by the prodi commission, but i can tell you that i agree with you when you say that this is an important matter for debate and that any decision which is taken must be known and explained to everyone, starting with the members of the european parliament. i would also like to say that it must not be a decision based on religious considerations and i am referring to some members and i say to you my conviction that we are a union, a community based on law, based on human rights, and never a union based on any religious prejudice. this point is essential to me! i would also like to say that, regardless of the question of turkey, we must have a special policy towards our neighbours. our neighbours to the east, in the balkans and the mediterranean. that's why i made it a priority yesterday. i think that the european union's foreign policy cannot be everywhere at once, and not everything is a priority. when everything is a priority at the same time, nothing is a priority at all, and what we must do is a constructive policy to spread prosperity and stability to our immediate neighbours in the east, the balkans, the mediterranean, in addition to our active contribution to global multilateral organisations, in particular the united nations. we must therefore strengthen our relations with our immediate neighbours, because our own security and stability depend to a large extent on them. in the institutional questions that have been raised, in particular the procedure for my appointment, this question was raised by mr schultz, mr swoboda, mr martin, mr cohn-bendit, mr ortuondo larrea and also by mr dehaene. i understand the reservations about the method currently used to elect the president of the commission. but the truth is that the treaties were kept. in any case, to show my concern about this issue, i myself have been available to appear in all the political groups that exist in this parliament, and i have therefore gone well beyond the obligations imposed by the treaty to show my respect for the european parliament. it is up to you, and to a large extent to the european parliament, to seek with the council a more concrete way, particularly in 2009, of making the political choice or criterion count in the selection of the president of the commission. i want to be clear and say that i am not just seeking to be the council's candidate, although i am of course very honoured to have had the consensus, the unanimity, the support in the council, but if elected i will be the candidate chosen by the council and by this parliament. that's why i'm here to present my positions and answer your questions, and that's what i'm going to do. i would like to reiterate that if elected i will defend the common european interest by seeking to counter, if necessary, the particular interests of the states, by seeking a balance between all the member states, large, medium and small, since all are important. dignity is exactly the same, no matter what size you are. as regards the question raised by mr swoboda, namely that i have submitted my resignation as prime minister, this decision was a sign of respect by this parliament. it was not right in our system, particularly in the portuguese system, where the president of the republic has certain powers, for portugal to wait a month to find out whether or not its prime minister was elected president of the commission. that's why i'm not here to introduce myself as head of government. i am a member of parliament, a member of the portuguese parliament. i'm here as one of you, presenting your ideas and submitting to your vote. it is a sign of respect for this parliament. another issue which has been raised here by many members, notably de villiers, bonino and carlos coelho, was the problem of commission-parliament relations and i want to use the expression i used in my speech, 'positive complicity'. the european union advances when these two institutions, the commission and the european parliament, work hand in hand, respecting their own powers, of course, without the commission seeking to replace parliament, nor, of course, parliament entering the european commission's powers. but when these two institutions work hand in hand, europe moves forward and that will be my guiding principle. as regards the debate on the future of europe and ratification - a problem raised by mr schultz, mr grossetête and mr dehaene, among others - i would like to say that this is a debate which must be won at national level and all politicians, whether they are members of the european parliament, members of national parliaments or others, can take part in this debate. as an institution, it is the commission's responsibility to provide credible and reliable information on what is going on. so the task of communication will be an essential task, but i think this is a job that requires us to have the political courage to fight against the apathy that mrs bonino and other members of this european parliament have been talking about. i will personally be available for this debate wherever and whenever you want me, but again, it is a debate that must be won at the national level. another question that was also raised has to do with the choices of commissioners, namely whether or not there are supercommissioners. this question was put to me by a number of members, including mrs ludford. i would like to say that i do not want to have just one supercommissioner in my commission, but i would like to have 24 supercommissioners, because i think there is an essential principle, which is the principle of collegiality. the european commission needs to uphold this principle. i have not yet made a final decision - i will only make it after your confirmation - on the structure of the european commission, but i want to say that this is a responsibility of the president of the european commission, not a responsibility of the european council, and for that reason i will exercise my responsibility as regards the allocation of the different portfolios within the commission. the principle of collegiality applies here too, we do not fall within the competence of other institutions, but the council cannot fall within the competence of the commission either. it's my responsibility, and i'm gonna do it. the question of transparency and openness has been raised by several members, including evans, bonde, ludgren, martens and others. i am committed to an open, efficient and accountable european commission. i think the european parliament's role in monitoring the work of the commission is very important. in order to do this supervisory work, members need information and i am prepared to give you that information. the positive work
