the next item is the commission statement on the recent environmental disasters (fires in southern europe).
commission. mr president, we are seeing an increasing frequency in natural disasters here in europe and around the world. as we have seen recently, floods and forest fires wreak havoc, causing human and economic problems and also serious damage to our environment. of course we are trying to combat these problems. with regard to forest fires, a series of common measures in the field of prevention, protection and restoration have now been put in place. our rural development programmes provide support for a wide range of forest activities, providing funds for prevention of fires and restoration of forests damaged by fires, according to priorities decided by the member states. in portugal approximately eur 149 m from the european agricultural guidance and guarantee fund is available for prevention and restoration for 2000-2006. in spain the total budget allocated for forestry measures for the same period amounts to eur 820 million. the recently created eu solidarity fund was established to respond to major disasters which caused direct damage of more than eur 3 bn or exceeded 0.6% of the affected country's gross national income. only in very exceptional circumstances can the solidarity fund be mobilised for disasters that remain below this high threshold. it has already been mobilised following the huge fires last year in portugal and spain and, at their request, it provided eur 48.5 m for portugal and eur 1.3 m for spain. the commission has not yet received any requests for 2004. as you know, the forest focus regulation is our most recent instrument to monitor and to implement prevention measures in the field of forest fires, as well as to detect the reasons for their frequency. the financial framework for the implementation of the forest focus scheme for 2003-2006 is fixed at eur 65 m, of which eur 9 m can be used for fire prevention measures. our civil protection assistance mechanism is also proving its worth. in 2003 and 2004 portugal sent requests for assistance to the eu monitoring and information centre, which then coordinated support offers from other participating countries. thanks to the mechanism, it was possible to ensure the rapid despatch of aerial forest fire-fighting means to portugal. in 2003 portugal accepted the assistance of two aircraft from italy and three aircraft from germany. in 2004 spain supplied three aircraft, france two, germany two, greece two and italy one. additional assistance was offered by the uk and norway but was not taken up by portugal. four years ago i expressed my concerns about the increasing number of forest fires and the damage they cause, stating that the risk for forest fires and the vulnerability of our forests have now reached a level beyond which further fires would seriously endanger the ecosystems and their sustainable management. sadly we saw this happen during last year's heatwave, which hit southern europe in particular and which culminated in the destruction of large parts of the portuguese natura areas. i wish to conclude by saying that the commission has taken your resolution of 4 september 2003 on the effects of the summer heatwave into account, and it serves as a very useful compendium for actions and measures on which to base future initiatives.
mr president, i have to agree with the commissioner when she says that in the european union the problems of fires are causing great environmental tragedies. there are 45 000 fires in the european union every year and more are going to be burning every day because drought, which is a structural problem in the european union, is going to cause ever greater environmental problems, not only in southern europe but also in the north. the united nations experts also tell us that this problem will continue to increase with climate change, and we find that in the face of these 45 000 fires a year, the european union lacks a genuine common policy for fighting fires. measures, means and money are lacking. i would remind you of regulation 2158/92, the expiry of which led the european commission to show that it wanted to abolish the fire-fighting helplines. this parliament, when the forest focus was discussed, managed to extract nine million euros from the european commission until 2006, a ridiculous figure. on the other hand, we have the forestry chapter of the rural development regulation. that regulation has not worked. i agree with the commissioner when she talks about 820 million euros, but they are under-utilized. they are misused because there is no interregional or interstate coordination. the member states act as they wish and improvise. yes, the french may have brought two planes to help fight the fire in portugal, but it was by no means in a coordinated way. and the coordination is not interregional either. an example of this is what has happened this year in spain. there is a region in northern spain - galicia - where the largest forest area is found. 99% of the fires that occur in this autonomous region are controlled within 24 hours. in galicia, forest fires are being fought effectively and forest activation plans are being put in place. its rate of fire is five times lower than the average for the spanish state. and yet, in andalusia, we have seen 42,131 hectares burned because the means available were not used. this is a drama and this should be a good opportunity for this to be fixed. how did you do that? i would like to put a little common sense into all this, because the european commission is due to present the european forestry strategy in the coming months, and this should be an opportunity for it to reflect in depth on this problem. and that a forestry policy be introduced in the european union which takes seriously the measures to protect forests against fires and, above all, which helps to coordinate administrations so that, at least and without extending the means, the scarce instruments currently available are properly used and that an episode like the one that the junta de andalucía has experienced and played in this summer and has been experienced in the european union never happens again.
mr president, commissioner, the fact that we are debating fires again in this parliament shows that we are not doing something quite right. the figure for the area burned is a real ecological catastrophe. in my region alone - as has already been said here - in andalusia, more than 40 000 hectares of forest have been burned in a total of 753 fires so far this year. in view of the consequences of the fires this summer, we should honestly ask ourselves whether the commission's opposition to the increase in budgetary appropriations under the forest focus regulation was justified. the commission should also seriously ask itself whether it was right to shift the burden of fire prevention to regional and rural development funds without establishing adequate control mechanisms to ensure that they are used precisely for prevention, reforestation and regeneration in this area. the reality today is that our countries are in urgent need of help. i therefore ask the commission to clarify whether it is considering the granting of any additional funds for the restoration of the funds concerned. the union should not take a single step backwards in its climate change policy. the question is very clear: does the commission consider that the european union is acting in an appropriate way to protect its forest heritage? does the commission think that it would be possible to allocate extra funds from the solidarity fund or some other much more flexible mechanism to mitigate the effects of these fires, which are destroying a natural heritage from which all of europe benefits?
mr president, the greens are very concerned that there is no preventive war against fires. the greens call for a pre-emptive war against fires. the present abandonment of the rural world, depopulation, the demographic bleeding, have a disastrous result. european funds do not reach those responsible for managing the mountain. the people who have lived off forest resources like cork, or the oak fruit, for example, in andalusia, have lost their livelihood. this is not just an accident, but the clear result of a policy which relegates the rural world to the last place, which does not organize resources, which is oriented towards planting species such as eucalyptus and pine - precisely what some people in this house are now criticizing and used to defend - leaving a legacy of ignorance which then produces fires. this situation calls for investment in civil and rural society, both in programmes such as the laeder programme which is now being considered for abandonment and in other rural programmes which reflect a civic fabric of the peoples of europe.
mr president, i am well aware that mrs wallström knows that she has given us a political answer with data and statistics, and she is well aware that, at the moment, the european union's aid to the forest fires is simply money handed out here and there. there is no such thing as a complex strategy, because it is a complex problem, and it is interdisciplinary and involves cooperation between institutions. and politicians are there to solve complex, difficult problems. in this sense, i think we need to make a model of risk management, management and cooperation, because we have issues from the judiciaries, because there is a lot of terrorism, to the issue of the police, the issue of the civilian population, the local authorities. models must be made, the same as was done for agenda 21. the european union is capable of doing that. but above all i am concerned about the need for strong shared technological development, because the principle of subsidiarity requires the european commission to do what countries or regions cannot do. and the problem of technological development is very important. for example, the transfer of military technology, the development of gis and many other things that in some regions are being applied with great success and that would need a technology to be shared among the 25 countries, among all the regions, among all the local authorities, because, of course, without that technological advance, we can only achieve human efforts and a lot of good will, but little success.
mr president, there is no doubt that the first responsible for the forest fires are the authors. in 96% of cases, the causes are attributable to man and that is why the spanish government has already announced a series of measures, including the tightening of penalties for this crime or the prohibition of building in affected areas. it is also true, as has already been said, that other causes cannot be forgotten. the transformation of the socioeconomic structures of rural areas seems to be the most fundamental, but so too is the lack of success of european rural and forestry development policy. most fires start in neglected forests, a consequence of the abandonment of traditional agricultural activity, the ageing of the population and the demographic crisis. but, mrs wallström, you cannot put the entire weight of this serious problem on the eaggf or rural development policy. the serious environmental consequences of forest fires call for european action. the difficulties you have experienced in implementing the solidarity fund should be alleviated by the creation of a specific rapid intervention mechanism for these smaller scale and smaller scale disasters than those foreseen by the solidarity fund. at the same time, european forestry policy should be reoriented by recognising the uniqueness of the southern forest and by drawing up a specific plan for its protection and for the comprehensive environmental recovery of burned areas. i would like to conclude by saying - and i hope that this is not misunderstood - that i believe that party politics should be absent from this debate, and that we should all seek a consensus position. if that is not the case - it rains in galicia and it does not rain in andalusia - then perhaps some members might begin to wonder where the €820 million that commissioner wallström has told us about has been spent.
commission. mr president, this debate has illustrated the complexity of this issue, which affects us at all levels. we know that climate change will probably increase these types of extreme weather events and it is quite probable that we will see more of these problems occurring, as the international panel of climate change has told us. that underlines the responsibility that is shared between the different levels. the european union, the commission and the institutions will have to act in a coordinated way to ensure that we have the necessary capacity. member states will also have to be sure that they have done everything for prevention and that we have a higher level of preparedness to deal with these forest fires, extreme weather events and catastrophes. it is a matter of resources - such as fire brigades - and being able to mobilise them quickly. it is also a matter of having resources for prevention activities. so there is a whole spectrum of activities and responsibilities. we are addressing that. you know as well as the commission does that member states in general are very reluctant to engage in a debate on a common forest policy for europe, so we are also touching upon very sensitive political issues and responsibilities. even if we set aside more money, it is not always true that this would help immediately, unless there is better coordination of activities, unless there is better planning for prevention and preparedness on the part also of member states. i just want to underline that as welcome as more money is, it is not always a matter of only having more money; there also has to be better planning and coordination in member states. thank you for this valuable debate on an issue that we risk having to raise again in the near future. i appreciate the interest you show in finding common solutions to prevent forest fires, to fight them and also to mitigate the damage they cause - because the funding has often been a matter of mitigating and trying to come in after the damage has been done - as well as to help member states restore their potential for forestry production. i have noted several suggestions that i will also take into due consideration after this plenary part-session and there will be a follow-up. i believe we could further increase transparency concerning the application of existing instruments. we will also examine the need for additional prevention measures when implementing the forest focus regulation as we will do when considering the proposal for the council's rural development regulation. as a first modest step, next november the commission will hold a conference entitled 'citizen participation from restoration to prevention - good governance for the restoration campaign to follow forest fires in france, greece, italy, portugal, spain, slovenia and cyprus'. so it will also take into account the experience that we have gathered. it will focus on restoration and involvement of civil society because, as you said, the causes can be anything from climate change to the human factor. we must seek to identify the lessons learned from last year's events, raise awareness among citizens and local and regional authorities, and collect suggestions for the future. so there is also work to do to improve our activities in this field. i am happy that we have found today a common view on possible actions that we should focus on for the future. i once again thank you for this debate.

commission. the emissions from aviation are increasingly significant. according to the sector's own analysis, the world passenger aircraft fleet could double by 2020. that means an increase from 12 000 aircraft to roughly 25 000 aircraft by 2020. this has a significant impact and, therefore, what we do is important. the commission was aware of these problems months ago. there have been discussions with coreper since july and there is definitely a common position between all 25 member states and the commission to keep all options open. we believe that this is the only way forward. the next discussion in coreper on the future strategy will take place next friday. the commission and member states, with the uk taking the lead, are now working on alternative texts, as it is important to do the practical work. the commission will also study the technical feasibility of introducing aviation emissions trading schemes into a general scheme and will look at different solutions in this area. the conclusions are expected in nine months, on the basis of which the commission intends to propose measures. our position is clearly to keep all options open in order to be effective. we are grateful for the support of the european parliament.

we now come to the next item on the agenda: the debate on the commission statement on the consequences of the sinking of a ship containing toxic ash off the turkish coast.
commission. mr president, according to the information currently available to us, the ship that sank recently in turkey had originally sailed from spain in the year 2000 with a cargo of ash from a coal power plant in spain. in may 2000 the turkish authorities informed the spanish ministry of the environment that they had received 2 200 tonnes of ash that had been exported without authorisation. the turkish authorities classified the waste as hazardous due to its chromium content. the secretariat of the basel convention was also informed. according to the spanish authorities, they immediately began to investigate the case. the information from the port of avilés showed that the documents that the ship was carrying were forged, hiding the fact that the waste was originally destined for algeria but had been rejected there because it was wet and therefore unusable. the company exporting the cargo stated that it had not intended to send the waste to turkey, but to algeria, and that the captain of the ship had acted without its consent. the spanish authorities took action against the company and required it to take the waste back to spain for treatment. the company appealed against the decision and administrative proceedings went on until the end of 2002. in 2003 and 2004 discussions continued as to how to return the ash to spain. in july 2004 the turkish authorities informed the spanish authorities that they could proceed with a plan drawn up by the company to transfer the ash to another vessel and return it to spain. however, before this could be done, the vessel sank on 6 september. we have strict rules in place that regulate the movement of waste within and outside the european union. exports of waste for disposal are prohibited. exports of hazardous waste for recovery to oecd countries, including turkey, have to be notified to the competent authority in the country of export and need the consent of the authorities concerned. if an eu member state discovers that a shipment has taken place without notification, it has to ensure either that the waste is taken back within 30 days or that it is taken care of in an environmentally sound manner. according to the information available, spain was willing to take back the waste and fulfil its legal obligations. unfortunately, legal and administrative problems delayed a solution until it was too late. this problem should have been prevented at source. therefore it is one of our priorities to work further towards improving implementation of community legislation. we are holding regular meetings with national authorities to discuss problems of implementation and possible solutions. a key issue in this respect is increased cooperation between port authorities in order to tackle, among other things, the problem of port hopping. furthermore, may i remind you that the role of non-eu countries in cases such as this is defined in the basel convention on transboundary movements of hazardous waste and their disposal.
mr president, mrs wallström, thank you for your statement. we are faced with a new maritime accident, this time in the mediterranean, which highlights the present fragility of the common network we are building to ensure the greatest possible maritime safety. the erika and prestige accidents in community waters have taught us the hard way about the urgent need for legislation and control of maritime traffic in the european union, and have painfully brought about a set of very advanced legislative measures whose transposition, implementation and rigorous application are helping to advance the process of strengthening maritime safety and preventing marine pollution within the union. in the case of the mv ulla accident in the port of iskenderun, alexandria, turkey, we find another type of need, which has to do with coordination between the authorities of a member state of the union which has always complied with international and community legislation and the authorities of an associated state which aspires to be part of the union and which should therefore make every effort, as it already does in other areas, to comply with what we call the community acquis on environmental prevention, and with the contradiction between the two aspects involved in this type of accident: the urgent practical measures and decisions to deal with the environmental emergency and the much slower legal requirements, the conflicts and the difficulty of identifying the last responsible parties which the interests of the maritime traffic chamber cause, and which it is constantly denouncing. in this case, we can say that the spanish authorities have complied from the outset with the requirements of the basle convention, by opening a sanctioning dossier against the company and obliging it to repatriate the ashes and also by carrying out all the necessary coordination with the turkish authorities and providing all the necessary assistance and technical assistance so that the repatriation of the ashes could be carried out. unfortunately, delays, especially those resulting from an embargo imposed on the vessel by the turkish authorities, have meant that, in the last period, from 7 july, when that embargo is finally lifted and the company, therefore, due to pressure from the spanish authorities, has recognised the need and its requirement for repatriation, the turkish authorities finally have free access to the vessel. it is too short a time and the ship, which was already in a rather difficult condition, as has been shown by the various arrests it has suffered in the past, ends up sinking in circumstances which are still to be clarified. it must be said that the spanish authorities have raised the need for this assistance from the outset, that a technical assistance mission is currently on its way to turkey and that, in this case, it will once again be necessary to consider how other actors operating in this tangle of legislation and maritime traffic have responded or not to their obligations: the company, other authorities, the captain, etc.
mr president, i think we're at the tip of the iceberg. it is not a coincidence, it is not an isolated incident, we are talking about the number one company in the construction materials sector: lafargue-asland, we are talking about its spanish subsidiary dragados, which has already been fined 18 times for not declaring the content of its waste. we are talking about a four-year period, whereas the deadline for returning the waste should be 30 days. what has happened in these three and a half years and more? what has the european commission done? we ask the commission to adopt a zero-tolerance policy. at this moment - as i speak - there are probably dozens and dozens of ships in the same situation. what is this company doing, which is exporting the same material to algeria on a massive scale, and has been fined 18 times, when there has been no public transfer, when the commission has not been informed? we believe that the european commission should take action in this matter by adopting clear sanctioning measures against infringements. an infringement procedure must be opened to find out the causes and responsibilities of the disaster. we cannot expect the pedagogy of catastrophe in this matter, we cannot accept a litigation that goes on forever.
commission. mr president, honourable members, we have a common interest in keeping our seas safe and preventing environmental catastrophes of this kind. i would, of course, never contradict the commission's statement – probably supported by all institutions – that we should learn from accidents of this kind. we should also do everything to prevent this continuing to be only the tip of the iceberg. we also know that there is a lot of money involved in wasted shipments; but i do not accept that the commission should take the blame for everything that has happened in this particular case. it is not the responsibility of the commission alone. we have a responsibility, we will accept that to the full; but in this case, i repeat, the problem should have been prevented at source. it is not entirely a legal problem or to do with something missing in the legislation, but it is a combination of illegal actions and legal and administrative problems, which delayed a solution until it was too late. we have to concentrate on implementing environmental legislation to the full, thus avoiding problems of this kind. of course, we will see if there is anything to be learned from this. can we act in a better way, can we prevent this happening in the future? it is also very clear from the existing legislation where the responsibility lies. it is not that this case opens up enormous gaps in the existing legislation, but rather how the legislation is being interpreted, implemented and enforced in different member states. the issue was raised about the "polluter pays" principle, which is one of the fundamental principles in eu legislation and in eu environmental policy. but in this case the pollution has taken place outside the eu where, of course, the commission has no competence to apply eu law. we have to get the facts right. i hope this discussion will prove fruitful for the future, because it is in our common interest to make sure that this does not happen again and that we learn lessons and can keep our seas safe. it is very important that enforcement is also carried out, to make sure that the signal goes out to all actors in cases like this. thank you for a good debate.

ladies and gentlemen, i would now like to use my privilege as president to address you. first of all, i would like to thank you again for the confidence you have shown in me by electing me as president of our parliament. i have already announced that i will leave the presentation of my strategic vision for the first half of this legislature for this plenary session. it is not a question of presenting a political programme or of presenting my own ideas on european integration. my purpose as president is only to outline and guide the priorities of our agenda. in doing so, i want to share with you the pride of belonging to the greatest multinational parliamentary institution, a symbol of peace and democracy, respectful of diversity, a forum for debate and decision-making which affects the daily lives of all europeans, even if many are not sufficiently aware of it, and the future of the world in which we are going to live. this feeling of pride in all of us goes hand in hand with a sense of responsibility. responsibility in the exercise of our powers, in our position on international affairs, responsibility for the proper functioning of this enlarged parliament. a parliament through which flows one of the two sources of legitimacy on which our union is based, the one that flows and represents the european citizens, which does not have to always coincide with the other, the one that emanates from the member states. a parliament in which 25 different parliamentary traditions already coexist and which is expressed in 20 official and working languages, with the complexity and cost that this entails. these are many languages, but they do not yet represent the full linguistic diversity of europe. i am reminded of this fact often. in the exercise of this responsibility, i have spent the last few days of the summer, in the name of all of you, issuing continuous statements of strong condemnation of the attacks and terrorist acts which have struck, in the most savage and cruel way, in different parts of the world. the european parliament has thus joined the democrats in their feelings of sadness and solidarity with the families who have been so unjustly and brutally bereaved by this tragedy, from which no country is unfortunately exempt. to emphasize this, to express this feeling in the most solemn and collective way possible, i have addressed the 25 heads of state and government of the member states of our union, suggesting that today, together with us, the representatives of the european citizens, the schools of the eu should observe a minute's silence in memory of the children of the children who were victims of the beslan school massacre and, in general, of all the children who are the victims of terrorist violence in the world. i can anticipate them, since several countries have announced that they will join this initiative, an expression of the feeling of the europeans in the face of these terrible events. ladies and gentlemen, our parliament condemns and rejects all acts of terrorism, because terror, in any form and in any country, is contrary to the values on which the european union is founded, whose citizens expect european unity to be a way of fighting more effectively against a threat which is today one of their main sources of concern and insecurity. let me tell you that it is not enough to express the horror we feel. repeated condemnation causes words of pain to reflect frustration and helplessness. there is no excuse or reason for such abominable events as those we have experienced western and developed world, is not about condemning it but about how to combat it. certainly, suicidal fanaticism is not going to be stopped by reasonable arguments put forth by educated and intelligent people. but we cannot claim to eradicate all its causes by the simple and indiscriminate use of force, by avenging on other children the harm done to our own and creating an unbearable escalation of violence. we're not going to win the battle against terrorism by thinking of it as a conventional war. this parliament must develop the area of security and justice, actively promote a counter-terrorism strategy based on international police, judicial and intelligence cooperation, and combat the underlying causes that fuel murderous and suicidal fanaticism. analyzing is not justifying. the debates and resolutions of this parliament can never be mistaken for a justification of terrorist violence. the fight against terrorism requires us to reflect on its causes in order to reactions to our deliberations may be. ladies and gentlemen, the news this summer has also reflected another source of concern and insecurity in europe. i am referring to the increasingly frequent phenomenon of companies moving their activities within an integrated economic area in search of better working and tax conditions, which we call delocalisation. you will have seen how this phenomenon generates defensive reactions in some countries which can affect the union's solidarity policies. it certainly raises the question of the relationship between economic competitiveness and social cohesion in a conflicting way, objectives which, in our view, must be complementary and which are proclaimed in the european construction and, in particular, in the lisbon strategy. everything is more complicated than it seems. the simple nominal comparison of labour costs is perhaps not the only explanation for this phenomenon. this debate is certainly of interest to europeans, who expect a the commission's proposal for a regulation on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use (emah) is a very important one. as with any political agreement reached after long discussions between the governments of the 25 member states, the result of its first reading is meritorious, worthy of consideration, but, in our view, completely inadequate. the council has taken a strictly accounting approach in its first reading. if parliament were to accept - and i am not going to accept - this view of the council in its present form, we would be faced with the triumph of national accounts over european policy, and i do not think that would be good for the union or for the member states that make it up. we in the european parliament are well aware of the national budgetary constraints that are inherent in insufficient economic growth, and we know that the stability pact imposes very clear rules on the containment of budget deficits. but the figures are clear: in recent years national budgets have grown by 22%, while the community budget has grown by 9% over the same period. that is to say, austerity and budgetary rigor are a plant that grows much better in the european parliament than, sometimes, in the national parliaments themselves. we in the european parliament - and this rapporteur too - know that community policies have a high added value in terms of growth and employment, whether in the structural funds, research or external cooperation, to name a few. we fear that the council's approach at first reading is simply to create artificial margins in categories which do not correspond to the real needs of the union, nor to the commitments made to third parties, nor even to the political will expressed annually in the budgetary vote in december. in general, in order to give a more reasoned opinion on the european parliament's reaction to this council draft, the rapporteur prefers to wait until the amendments have been adopted in the committees responsible and in the political groups. i would like to make a few points, however. firstly, as the general rapporteur, i assume that the reduction of the ceilings in the categories must be a condition for the union budget. the european commission had already incorporated this reduction in its preliminary draft budget and, in general - though not in all respects - we share the commission's analysis. the margins created by the commission in categories 3, 4 and 5 are, politically, much more realistic than the margins created by the council, which is a paradox. secondly, the situation of the agencies. it is time for the council to face up to an undeniable fact: decentralised agencies need sufficient funds to get started and to function normally. if the political decision to create agencies is made, the political decision to maintain them must be made. the council's position is inconsistent here, and the rapporteur is prepared to propose innovative solutions to resolve once and for all this double political language between commitments and compliance. thirdly, the question of payment appropriations. to keep it below 1% of the union's gross national income - something so desired by some member states - the council has cut eur 4.3 billion. commitments outstanding at 31 july amounted to eur 122 billion. in relative terms, the categories with the most outstanding amounts to be liquidated are, in this order, 7, 4 and 2, the latter being the largest by volume. any responsible institution would want to put an end to this situation. the n+2 rule mentioned by the commissioner was created to improve implementation and accelerate project completion. to absorb this ral (residual liquidation) would require an increase in payments not a decrease, unless simply savings for national treasuries are sought. since the 2000 budget, €44.5 billion has been returned to member states in unspent appropriations - more than the entire 2005 budget in structural funds - and this return should not be seen as a saving for anyone. to return appropriations to member states because they have not been able to spend them is to waste the added value of spending on community policies which have been adopted to contribute to growth and employment in the union. ladies and gentlemen, this is the first real budget with 25 member states. the union has more challenges to meet and more needs to meet than in previous years. it is the responsibility of the three institutions and of course of this rapporteur to do more with the money we need than in other years. i wish the three institutions a successful dialogue and i would like to acknowledge the good spirit shown so far by the dutch presidency. the next item is the statement by the council and the commission on the humanitarian situation in sudan.
mr president, the situation of tension in sudan has been known for many years, not just one. once again we are experiencing a humanitarian drama which, in fact, is masking a political drama. it is precisely this drama that must be faced: a humanitarian emergency, which may be even worse, is still to come. according to estimates by many ngos, between 100 000 and 350 000 people could die from widespread famine. this requires us to take swift action and i therefore welcome the fact that both the council and the commission are taking action in this direction. it is necessary to continue humanitarian aid, it is necessary to put pressure on the khartoum government to disarm the militias and, if that implies the need for sanctions, they must be imposed. the number of international observers, specifically african, must also be increased. i would like to draw attention to the importance of emphasizing the need to address the political causes of the country's poverty, which have allowed the authoritarian regime in khartoum to exist for many years and which have also allowed, among other things, european countries such as the united kingdom, spain and cyprus to export arms to that country in violation of the arms code of conduct, which means that we must put the need for a review of this process on the table and again demand a complete embargo on this issue from the united nations.
council. mr president, the european union and the council of ministers are deeply conscious of the worsening situation. we are following the situation very closely and i share your concerns. i have listened very carefully to the suggestions you have made and to your calls for action. i also agree with those speakers who have stressed the fact that what we need is a political solution, not a military solution. military force would only lead to further bloodshed and we want to avoid that. it is in that context that we believe that the african union, which has taken the lead, should continue to be in the driver's seat. at the same time, however, we see how important it is that a cohesive and coherent effort be undertaken so that the african union, together with the united nations, the european union and the united states, exert increasing pressure on the sudanese government as we have done from the beginning - notably as the dutch government, but also as the european union over these past months. we will also continue to push the african union to implement the suggestions that have been made by the united nations. i listed a number of possibilities: increase the number of observers, increase the military force supporting these observers, increase the civilian presence, send a police force - even a european union police force, if the african union asks for one. it is very important that we cooperate very closely and that the african union tries to find an african solution to an african problem. we must lend all the support we can muster. i believe that we should follow a twin-track approach on the calls for action. on the one hand, i share the feelings of all those who have said that continued, strong diplomatic pressure on the government of sudan is an absolute requirement. we have done this and will continue to do so in the context of the meetings we have. for example, next week we have a meeting the united nations. i have also met with ministers: at the end of july i invited minister ismail to the netherlands. there was a strong exchange of words on the situation. promises were made, but - as we have seen - they were not kept. that is why there should also be another track, and that track, as many of you have said, consists of sanctions. the european union is currently examining all the possibilities for imposing sanctions very carefully, but we think that sanctions should be effective. they should really hit the government and they should also be all­encompassing, so, together with the commission and the council secretariat, we are drafting a comprehensive review of which sanctions are possible. among those sanctions, we are considering an oil boycott, an arms embargo and many other possibilities to make it crystal clear to the sudanese government that we mean business. on the other hand - as commissioner nielson mentioned - we should not forget that humanitarian aid is of the essence. if one talks to mr lubbers or mr pronk - as i have recently - it is very obvious that one aspect is the situation in respect of the sudanese government. the other aspect pertains to the humanitarian aid situation, which is terrible at the moment. there too, the european union is doing everything it can. as far as mrs bonino's suggestion on the international criminal court is concerned, you will understand that i wholeheartedly agree with this. the international criminal court with its seat in the hague is something we endorse whenever we can. however, we should not forget that what we need first, in the united nations, is to discuss the situation on the basis of mr pronk's report. subsequently, the united nations security council should make a request, and then we can act to initiate proceedings in the international criminal court. i can only repeat that we are very concerned about the situation. we take everything you have said into account and take it very seriously. we are deeply aware of the suffering of the people there and of what has happened. whether you call it genocide or not, the situation is very serious. we have to be willing to take action. in the meantime, we are waiting for the outcome of the discussions that are to take place shortly in the united nations.
commission. mr president, i would warn against jumping into the terminology of genocide. at the moment there is no authoritative evidence that this is the correct way of characterising the events in question. this is an impossible discussion because, once the word is there, any attempt to clarify and analyse it is only seen as an attempt to cover what it looks or sounds like, an attempt to make it easy to understand. this is very serious: rushing to use certain words, and acting and speaking as if these words are the actual facts, is not the way to clarify to the public that what we see is unacceptable and has to be stopped. taking that step and using certain terminology at this stage can be, in my opinion, problematic. we need to establish the facts, and i expect this to happen. there is a risk here that myself and others are seen to be taking this matter too lightly. even with that risk, i would like to make the point that in relation to the tradition of impunity in these matters, i find it important that the african union has been encouraged to do something and is not sitting passively waiting for the government to comply. the african union is totally publicly committed to putting pressure on the government, and at the moment is making an effort to increase its engagement in darfur, both quantitatively and qualitatively in terms of the mandate. this needs to be supported. it is a new experience for the so-called international community to be able to relate to and support something like this, which we have never encountered before in an african crisis. we need to do more. the un's role is absolutely essential. the commitment throughout africa, via the african union, to use the newly created peace and security council has created a basis for the un to act. without this there would have been little grounds for optimism. even that word is perhaps out of place in this instance. what can we do to exert maximum pressure? i still have not signed the country strategy paper for sudan. more than eur 400 million is available via unspent funds – which could not be used for normal development cooperation activities during the many years of fighting between north and south – and new money from the ninth edf. this large amount of money cannot be made available until we see a comprehensive peace agreement. it is a political fact of life, which comes as no surprise anywhere - not here and not in khartoum - that the situation in darfur must be seen as part of any definition of peace in the country. this pressure is a major element in our effort to push things in a better direction. in the coming year we will face not only the demands relating to humanitarian aid, but we will also have to prepare to secure the livelihoods of the people whom we hope to assist in returning to their homes as soon as possible.

the next item is the statement by the council and the commission on the beslan hostage crisis and massacre and the fight against terrorism.
mr president, what happened in beslan fundamentally confirms that islamist terrorism is already the main problem affecting and will affect the coexistence of europeans. it is not just an emerging problem, but we have to have the conviction that it will be a growing problem. the greatest risk we europeans face in this phenomenon is that european citizens will interpret inaction, paralysis, doing nothing as the fundamental identifier of our inaction. that is the biggest risk, the biggest difficulty: not knowing how to deal with this terrible risk from our own principles, convictions and values. from my personal experience, in dealing with a terrorist scourge, the first, the most important - in my opinion - the definitive thing is awareness, awareness of the seriousness of the problem. legislative and operational measures will be important, but the most important thing is awareness. this awareness has a twofold perspective: firstly, we must dare to put the fight against terrorism at the top of the list of priorities, at the top of all problems. that is why we must say, reiterate and affirm in all the union's documents, in all our public statements: terrorism is the main problem. today i dare to say that the main shortcoming in the european union's counter-terrorism policy is not a lack of measures and initiatives, but that we do not sufficiently identify terrorism as the main problem facing europeans. secondly, the second objective of awareness is the conviction that we can defeat this phenomenon. we cannot begin to fight terrorism without being sure, from the moral strength of our convictions, that we can defeat terrorism. terrorism is essentially fear, it creates fear. and that fear of failure that we have when we face a problem of this nature is the first thing we have to know how to overcome and then defeat the terrorist organization. it takes time to combat a terrorist phenomenon. there are no shortcuts, no magic solutions. but the conviction has to be present in each and every one of us from the very beginning. the fight against terrorism is neither left-wing nor right-wing; it is essentially a moral imperative. that is why i think we have to devote more time, more monograph sessions in this parliament to tackling terrorism. i think we must reiterate more often that terrorism is the main problem facing europeans and we must encourage a debate between governments to find out in certain circumstances, when there are attacks close to elections, what defence instruments those governments have, delaying or not holding elections, to prevent terrorists from achieving their objectives. in short, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that we have a moral imperative of the first order. the next item is the statement by the council and the commission on the situation in iraq.
the council, the president-in-office, has for some time been very concerned about iraq, and this has also divided us. although we are concerned about developments in iraq, it is of the utmost importance that the european union continue to support the iraqi people and that we do not abandon the iraqi people, but rather continue to provide that support. the continuing violence is a matter of concern to us, but the past few months have also created scope for coherent and united eu support for iraq. i shall come to the question of what support the eu might possibly offer in a moment. but first, a quick look back, if you'll allow me. june in particular was an important month for the long-term future of iraq and the iraqi people. first, on 8 june the un security council adopted resolution 1546, and on 28 june the temporary occupation of iraq was ended and sovereignty restored. the inauguration of the allawi interim government marked a major turning point in the history of iraq. the new resolution also restored unity in the international community and, moreover, allowed for a renewed role for the un in iraq. this is certainly an important fact in view of the organisation of elections in january 2005. equally important, the developments in june made it possible to bridge the differences of opinion that had existed within the eu up to then on certain aspects of iraq policy. this was made clear in the conclusions of the first general foreign ministers' council under the dutch presidency in july. the council endorsed the european union medium term strategy of high representative solana and commissioner patten, as well as the commission communication on iraq the eu and iraq- a framework for engagement. these documents provide a clear framework for the european union's involvement in general and also in some details. in addition, as i said, these conclusions contain a number of very concrete points for action. the eu will actively cooperate with the un in iraq, and will engage in a dialogue with the iraqi authorities to see where the eu can further support iraq. to further investigate this, a reconnaissance mission has been sent to iraq. i'll get back to you on their findings in a moment. it is clear, in any case, that the eu needs to be involved in supporting the reconstruction of iraq and the internal iraqi political process. in this connection, the national conference must not remain unmentioned. despite the great difficulties in its preparation, this meeting was a success. all layers of iraqi society were represented, including many women. and finally, it was possible to reach agreement on the delegates who will sit in the national council. the formation of this council is an important step towards the elections. unfortunately, along with all this good news, there is also a lot of bad news. the abductions and murders of foreign citizens, including eu citizens, are a terrible example of this. our condolences go out to the victims and their families. but let us not forget that many iraqis are also victims of violence, especially those iraqis who have taken responsibility for the reconstruction of their country. the continuing attacks on oil pipelines are also a serious threat to the recovery of the iraqi economy. not only is iraqi society and economy threatened by the continuing violence, but so is the political process in iraq. the situation in fallujah is very worrying and the past few months have shown in najaf and baghdad that violence is bubbling under the surface and can erupt suddenly in the shiite parts of iraq as well. in this context, we welcome the recent agreement which was concluded in najaf. partly thanks to the courageous efforts of ayatollah al sistani, there is a prospect of restoring order and security in najaf under the leadership of the iraqi interim government. let us hope that this is a step towards better relations in iraq and improved security conditions. the fact is that sectarian violence is clearly not in the interests of the ordinary iraqi, whose country's reconstruction is being unnecessarily delayed by terrorism. the security situation is, of course, a determining factor in the extent to which the eu can effectively help in the reconstruction of iraq. and it's clear that that situation is not good right now. nevertheless, the dutch presidency has taken up the conclusions of the general affairs council in july and this has already led to greater eu involvement in the political process in iraq. i myself visited iraq in august to underline the european union's support for the economic, social and political reconstruction of iraq. i have therefore held talks with the president, the prime minister and the foreign minister. i also had a meeting with representatives of the united nations in iraq. all iraqi interlocutors underlined the importance they attach to a clear and visible eu role in iraq. in this connection, they advocated the opening of a commission office in baghdad. i also expressed, on behalf of the eu, our concern about the reintroduction of the death penalty in iraq. mr allawi, who had recently visited iraq's neighbours, stressed the importance of stability in iraq for the region as a whole. i said that the eu was keen to help with regional security and stability. i also told him that an invitation to the eu to participate in the next neighbourhood conference would be very much appreciated. the eu is already regularly addressing the responsibility of iraq's neighbours. the un representatives during my visit indicated that eu support for their activities is vital, especially as regards the electoral process. i also introduced the eu reconnaissance mission to iraq. this scouting mission has now returned. delegates from the presidency, the commission and the council secretariat examined the possibilities for concrete involvement of the european union in the context of civilian crisis management in the following areas: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation in the member states. the mission held talks not only with the iraqi authorities but also with representatives of the united nations, the united states, nato, the multinational force and the electoral commission. the mission concluded that the following activities could be considered: - i will summarise these areas briefly with your permission: first of all, police training. secondly, in the area of the rule of law and human rights: training of judges and prosecutors; technical assistance for the establishment of an iraqi special tribunal; forensic expertise and assistance in exhuming victims from mass graves; assistance in setting up a national centre for human rights and democracy; education in the legal field. thirdly, the civil service; capacity building in various ministries and in the prison system. fourth, the elections: election assistance and observation. fifthly, development of arms export control legislation, demobilisation programmes for militias and support for the property committee. all in all, there are plenty of areas where the eu can act. it is important that the activities undertaken by the eu respond to real iraqi needs, add value and complement any activities that may already exist. in addition, synergies between eu instruments and activities should be closely monitored. the commission has also been asked to present a report on the implementation of the new financial perspective for the period 2007-13. it is now important that a fact-finding mission be sent to iraq to give a more concrete picture of the possibilities for action by the european union. the council secretariat, in consultation with the commission and the presidency, will begin to plan such a mission. i would also like to mention the importance of the un presence in iraq, which, as i have already said, is very important, especially in view of the elections. if the un is to function properly, it is vital that there is adequate protection. resolution 1546 provides for this. the secretary-general of the united nations has asked the governments of the eu to make a financial contribution to the second ring of protection, the so-called un protection force. it has been shown that the member states attach importance to an eu contribution to this. will be able to make a concrete offer of aid to iraq in the reconstruction of the country. commission. it is almost exactly five years since i appeared in this parliament for my confirmation hearings as a commissioner. since then i have been fortunate to take part in literally scores of debates – more, i am told, than any other commissioner: such is parliament’s interest in external relations. i would like to thank parliament and its members for the courtesy that i have invariably been shown. i have enjoyed coming here. it is important, in my view, to try to establish democratic roots for foreign policy. it is not an area of public policy to be left to the diplomatic experts, whose record is at best somewhat patchy. anyway, as i ride off into the sunset, i should like to record my appreciation for parliament’s role in developing, not by leaps and bounds but – perhaps inevitably – by lurches and shuffles, europe’s common external relations policy. the worst shambles to have overwhelmed us in the last five years has, of course, been the row over iraq. i do not want to go back over old arguments. if we needed reminding that you cannot have a common policy if the larger member states are deeply divided, then here was the evidence. other evidence also speaks eloquently for itself. as someone once said, 'stuff happens'. is the world today safer than before the overthrow of the appalling saddam? is global terrorism in retreat? are we closer to building bridges between islam and the west? is the world’s only superpower more widely respected? have the citizens in our democracies been treated in a way that will encourage them to give governments the benefit of the doubt next time they are told that force needs to be used pre-emptively to deal with an imminent threat? i simply pose the questions. honourable members will have their own answers. but here we are: saddam overthrown, violence raging across much of the liberated land, the regime changed, with an interim government preparing the way for democratic elections. whatever our past criticisms, we are all now up to our ears in this endeavour. if iraq goes badly, we all suffer. so we have to try to work together to hold the democratic project in one piece. what are we pledged to do as a union, leaving aside the contribution of individual member states? we have already pledged, and are working hard to deploy, eur 200 million this year. i very much hope that we will be able to secure agreement for a further eur 200 million for next year. we are developing a good record in disbursing this assistance, having paid more than eur 200 million into the united nations and world bank trust funds over the course of the past year. we are working well with the united nations and the world bank, helping to ensure that our resources are disbursed quickly and well. we have focused our assistance this year on three areas: on essential public services – health, education, water and sanitation; on poverty alleviation and the development of livelihoods; and on governance and civil society. i would not pretend, however, that all is well. how could i? the hazardous security climate – evident not least in the appalling series of kidnappings, most recently of humanitarian workers dedicated to the wellbeing of iraqis, and evident also in yesterday’s appalling atrocity in baghdad – obviously limits the pace of disbursement, as does the fact that we are working with an interim government that is still feeling its way in public administration. that is life – at least in iraq – and we will continue to do our utmost within the constraints of the situation on the ground. what i can say, firmly, is that i am convinced that our decision to take the multilateral, trust fund route was absolutely the right one. a comparison of our disbursement rate with that of other bilateral donors, including the largest donor of all, only confirms this. when we proposed to parliament committing eur 200 million to the reconstruction of iraq, bringing to over eur 300 million the amount we will spend in 2003-2004, some honourable members argued that we were being parsimonious. they argued that we should do more: they suggested that we should spend at least eur 500 million, though they were coy about telling us where the extra money should come from. this morning i was interested to read a report by the bbc from washington: 'the us administration wants to reallocate billions of reconstruction dollars for iraq and spend them instead on security and other short-term needs. us officials say this new strategy has emerged after months of review.' the report goes on: 'the shift is also being interpreted by critics as proof that grand long-term plans to reshape the economy just were not realistic. they also charge that the intensity and level of violent resistance was severely underestimated.' i think we were right in our judgment about the amount of money that we could sensibly put into iraq, and i think parliament was wise to support that judgment. in the coming months, we will continue to implement the proposals set out in our communication of 9 june, which has received widespread endorsement. in particular, we will focus on the essential issue of support to the electoral process. once the independent electoral commission and the united nations have identified exactly what they need, we stand ready to help – as i shall explain to the iraqi president when i meet him later today. but i should be clear that, under the current circumstances, we cannot and will not propose a conventional election observation mission – that would be simply impossible, as honourable members in this chamber who themselves have taken a lead in election observation missions will know. but we will seek ways to ensure that we play our full part in assisting free and fair elections in iraq. in the longer term, we will need to consider how best the commission can be represented on the ground. opening a delegation would obviously be difficult, expensive and potentially dangerous. but we are prepared to consider that route, if it is clear that it would add to our effectiveness in helping the iraqi people. so let me be blunt: we will work for a better future in iraq whatever the bitterness of past disputes. there is, though, one other general point that i would like to make, triggered by these reflections on iraq. i hope that the house will be generous to me in allowing me to stray a little on what is, almost certainly, my last outing in this mother of parliaments. when, just over two years ago, some of us expressed concerns that the united states was abandoning the sort of multilateralism which had characterised its foreign and security policy since the second world war, we were strongly criticised. america, we were assured, still wished to work with allies, provided they shared washington’s view of how to cope with a dangerous world, and by and large kept any reservations to themselves. some allies did indeed accompany america to baghdad, a venture not yet blessed – as we have noted – with the easy and benign consequences that were famously predicted and promised. liberation rapidly turned into an occupation – or what was seen as an occupation – bitterly resisted, with atrocity after atrocity. democracy failed to roll out like an oriental carpet across the thankless deserts of the middle east. above all, peace in jerusalem and palestine was not accomplished by victory in baghdad. so, partly because american neo-conservative unilateralism had clearly failed to establish an empire of peace, liberty and democracy, we have been more recently advised that allies and multilateralism were back in fashion in washington. even the united nations was deemed to have its uses. vivat the state department. all done and dusted then? sighs of relief all round? can we now look forward to the restoration of that old-fashioned notion that allies have to be led not bossed, and that multilateral institutions have their important uses, even for the world’s only super-power – that, pace machiavelli, there is much to be said for being admired and not just feared? the rhetoric of the present united states election campaign inevitably raises a few questions. i do not seek to take sides. america elects its president and its congress. the rest of the world looks on. we in europe should work as well as we can with whoever wins. we are not partisans in the process, whatever our private opinions. moreover, i am not so naïve as to confuse campaign rhetoric with a platonic dialogue. i have, after all, been a party chairman myself. but campaign rhetoric reflects something and what is reflected here is pretty unsettling. if you want to get a cheap cheer from certain quarters in america, it seems that all you have to do is to bash the united nations, or the french, or the very idea that allies are entitled to have their own opinions. multilateralists, we are told, want to outsource american foreign and security policy to a bunch of garlic chewing, cheese eating wimps. the opinions of mankind, which the founding fathers of the united states thought their country should note and respect, are to be treated with contempt unless, i suppose, they faithfully reflect the agenda of the american enterprise institute and fox tv. what are we to make of all this? first, multilateralism is, above all, in the best interests of the united states, a point which previous administrations would not have questioned and most political leaders would have subscribed to for the past 60 years. second, surely the national interest of the superpower is to put its traditional allies on the spot, not challenging their right to consultation, but probing what they have to say and how they intend to turn their rhetoric about cooperation into effective, not effete, multilateralism. how, to take one obvious point, do we intend to go about not just draining the swamps in which terrorism breeds – to borrow the cliche – but also shooting some of the crocodiles? further, how and when will we in europe countenance the use of force to support the international rule of law? that is a question which we in europe regularly duck. if the political culture of american exceptionalism excludes the notion of working with and talking to foreigners, if unpopularity overseas is taken as a mark of distinction, a source of pride, too many mr president, i am speaking in support of the commission communication entitled 'strengthening economic governance and clarifying the implementation of the stability and growth pact'. it is important to return to economic governance because what we are experiencing comes from the maastricht treaty, in which the decision on economic and monetary union was taken: monetary union was described and implemented, economic union not so much. and the stability pact, which is now about ten years old, was conceived out of a certain distrust of certain countries that seemed not to be able to pass the test. the capacity of the european union to create shows that those who were the examiners are now the most virtuous and, curiously, those who imposed virtue are the ones who have sinned the most. in short, this gives hope for the construction of europe. since then, we have introduced the euro, we have decided on the lisbon strategy, we have drawn up a constitution - i would like to recall that all the government representatives went to the working group of the convention to oppose the development of economic governance. the stability and growth pact must therefore be revised and updated, because in many respects it is not working - especially in the growth aspect - and because we have had to go to the court of justice to have some states apply it. i think that is what justifies both the commission's action - which we clearly support - and the council's positive reaction, because just as the european central bank has to be monetarist, the council has to be concerned with the functioning of the economy.
council. i am very grateful that you have given me the opportunity to say a few words now. i apologise for leaving earlier but the problem is that i am not only president-in-office of the council and speakers, why did we have problems with the pact? the basic mistake in the past has been that we did not make use the good times for consolidation. i believe that both mr poettering and mr klinz said a few words in that regard. my colleagues in france and germany also concluded that if they had been in surplus or in balance before the downswing started, they would not have breached the 3% limit and all these troubles would not have arisen. i think that is an important consensus. those who now criticise the pact for its rigidity are probably not the same people who advocated more rigid consolidation in the good times. perhaps they felt that the good times were so nice that we could spend even more than the governments planned. that is my experience, at least. we must be consistent during the entire cycle. if we consolidate firmly in good times then we can be more relaxed when the economic cycle takes a downturn. stablilisation over the entire cycle – that is one of the lessons learned. i hope, as i am sure you do, that we are now at the start of the upward part of the cycle. if we use that time well, the inevitable downturn will not, once again, lead us to the problems that we have previously encountered. we do not need any change to the text of the pact in that regard. as has been remarked by some speakers, the stability and growth pact is not a solution to everything.
