deficits, the fact that the deficits were not high enough, are the real problem in relation to the lack of growth in europe. we have to look at the necessary reforms and also set the right priorities in our budgets, so that we really spend the money within a budgetary framework and on the issues that are important for the lisbon process. i must point out that if we were more relaxed on deficits, interest payments would gradually crowd out other expenditure, such as expenditure on r&d and education, which we all want. in the medium and long term, higher deficits are certainly not a solution for any lisbon objective. they may even conflict with the lisbon objectives. a few of you were a bit afraid of an ad hoc approach, that we would not apply equal treatment to all the countries based on clear criteria. we discussed that in the council and stated that we need a rules-based system for the future. there were some questions about the golden rule. as such, the golden rule is a pro-cyclical system. it was used in the 19th century in many countries. i do not think it would be good for economics today. other questions were asked about the role of mr juncker. he will be president of the euro group. there are some advantages to having a longer-term president, who will also be its face vis-a-vis the outside world, for example in the g-7. if people see a new minister of finance come from the euro group every six months, it will not make a very strong impression. such a president also organise and plan for a longer period than just six months. i hope that in the coming weeks and months we can work further on this issue. as i said, the commission proposals are a good basis for discussion. they will probably not be accepted lock, stock and barrel, but i do not think the commission ever expected that. we already have some basis for consensus in the paper i presented to you today. i hope that we will get full consensus on an operational pact that is really implemented.
mr president, commissioner almunia has given a masterful performance of shakespeare. as in the funeral oration of mark antony, it sings a song of austerity but at the same time it announces that it has laid the necessary burdens to blow up the pillars on which it stands. the commissioner is advocating simple rules, but at the same time he is telling us that we will have to take account of the national circumstances of each country, which means that there will be 25 different rules. what we said yesterday about the stability pact is still true today. it is absolutely true that the austerity pact must be maintained in order to maintain price stability; that budgetary austerity serves to free up resources for education, research and development to make the lisbon process possible; and, above all, that it is necessary to deal with the implicit, hidden, unbudgeted obligations arising from the ageing of the population. what we said yesterday is still true today. and if we are saying different things today, it is simply because we are giving up the stability pact. the stability pact was good, its breach was bad. secondly, commissioner, all those who have always been in the stability pact are those who have today applauded its measures and all those who have always been in favour of the stability pact are those who are against the flexibility, inequality and discretion which the commission proposes. thirdly, commissioner, the applause of the governments is not a disinterested applause. the stability pact is not a pro-government pact, it is a pact against governments, to limit the action of governments, to prevent them from sterilizing the actions of the central bank and to maintain price stability. and if it is a pact against governments and in favour of the citizens - and i agree with what the chairman of the committee has said - it will have the support of my group to strengthen the powers of the commission, as opposed to the council, and the powers of parliament, as the representative of the citizens, to defend that budgetary stability which will enable the citizens to enjoy lower prices, lower interest rates with which to pay their mortgages and which will serve to guarantee our pensioners that in the future we will have resources to meet their needs, which we will not have wasted by paying interest and paying off debt. the epp group will be with the commissioner in that debate. but if the aim is to establish rules of discretion, inequality and, in short, injustice in the application of the pact, recalling the principle 'pacta sunt servanda', the commissioner will not have us on his side.
the commission mr president, first of all i would like to thank all the members who have contributed to this debate, sometimes in support, sometimes in criticism and sometimes simply in criticism. all of them seem to me extremely useful for the future development of my responsibilities as commissioner responsible for carrying out, in my area, this adaptation and improvement of the stability and growth pact and, in general, of economic governance, and they seem to me extremely useful for conveying arguments and objectives from parliament to public opinion on a matter as important as that concerning the economy of the member states of the union and of the european union as a whole. i would like to reiterate - as i did in my opening statement, as has been made clear in some speeches, but i want to repeat it in this final statement - that the treaty is not at issue, nor is what the treaty says about public finances and budgetary stability. the 3% of gdp ceiling for government deficits in the member states of the economic and monetary union and the 60% of gdp ceiling for government debt remain in force. countries which are not complying with these limits have the obligation and the commitment to do so. they are still in force, not by chance, but because one of the objectives of economic and monetary union must necessarily remain budgetary stability as a sine qua non for the effectiveness of the very important political decision we took when we launched economic and monetary union and, in particular, the creation of the single currency. and it is still necessary to preserve the objective of budgetary stability and those reference values through a system of rules - as has been said on many occasions throughout the debate. but it is also necessary to bear in mind that the ultimate objective of economic and monetary union, of budgetary stability of economic policies, is to ensure more growth and more welfare for some of our citizens. and some of you have expressed the view that a debate on the reform of the pact could even lead to some effect on the stability of our currency, the euro. i do not think so if the debate is conducted, as in the council last weekend and as in this debate in parliament today, within the limits we have set for it. what is being said is that the euro area and the european union as a whole are growing less than other parts of the world. we have more stability, thanks to the decisions we have taken in the framework of economic and monetary union, but we have less growth. and that is indeed an answer that we must find not only with the instrument of the stability and growth pact, but also by re-reading it, revising it and adapting it, introducing more economic rationality into it, taking into account the heterogeneity of a european union of 25 following enlargement, taking into account that the treaty also speaks of the need to preserve the sustainability of public finances and not only to preserve and ensure budgetary balance in each of the financial years, through the monitoring of the public deficit, and taking into account that, throughout the years of application of the stability and growth pact, it has always suffered, in terms of credibility, because the existing rules have not been adopted and the one who must do so in the last instance, which is the council. we therefore need to strengthen the pact, the budgetary surveillance framework and our economic governance instruments. and how is that to be done? more flexibility or more rigor? with both. in some respects we must be more flexible, because experience shows that the margin of manoeuvre which we have for the reasonable interpretation of the rules we ourselves decide is not sufficient to take account of very powerful arguments deriving from economic rationality, from the concrete situation of the economy of a country at a given moment. and in other respects we must be more rigorous, for example in monitoring the evolution of public debt levels or in the mechanisms for implementing the pact, both in the preventive and in the corrective part of the pact in the excessive deficit mechanism. we must take account of the economic cycle, preserve equal treatment for each and every country - and this is a task to which the commission feels particularly committed - and ensure better compliance. we need to link the pact instrument better with the other economic governance instruments - as has been said in many speeches this afternoon - of the lisbon agenda of economic growth objectives to make the economic and monetary union of the european union the most competitive area in the world, and at the same time more socially cohesive and more environmentally sustainable. does that require a debate? the commission takes it for granted. should this debate be limited to a certain point? of course, and that is what the commission's communication says. should we seek cooperation and the greatest possible degree of consensus in our dialogue and cooperation with the council? it seems to me an imperative we cannot ignore. the debate - and so has the president-in-office of the council, mr zalm, who has also spoken - should lead us, and i trust it will lead us, to the conclusion that, in november, at the second ecofin review of the adaptation and improvement of the stability and growth pact, the degree of agreement and consensus between the member states, at council level, and between the council and the commission, will be even greater than the very appreciable degree of agreement that has already been shown over the previous weekend. it will require regulatory changes, the least possible. in any case, the key point in the debate should not be whether or not an article, a provision or a paragraph of a regulation should be changed. the touchstone will be whether the reason why it is necessary to change that regulation has been agreed, is reasonable and is in line with our objectives of budgetary stability, of maintaining a framework for fiscal and economic governance and of that framework serving us to preserve the stability and growth of the economic and monetary union. finally, mr president, a word on the subject which has been mentioned many times in many speeches by france and germany. the court of justice's judgment of 13 july basically upheld the european commission. the council was unable to act as it did last november. we now have to apply the treaty, as interpreted by the court of justice. the council must respect the commission's right of initiative. the commission is the guardian of the treaties and must therefore ensure that the rules of the treaties are respected and that they are developed through the existing stability and growth pact, and we are committed to this and will act on the basis of the judgment of the court of justice. how are we gonna do this? we are following very closely the development of public finances in many member states, but particularly in france and germany during the year 2004, and the budgets which each of the two governments is beginning to draw up and which will be sent and discussed in their parliaments in the coming months, before the end of the year. at the end of october, with the knowledge we have at that time of the content of the budgetary policies formally announced by the two governments and pending the final decision of their respective parliaments, the commission will publish its economic estimate and forecasts and we will estimate what the evolution of the public deficit in france and germany in 2004 may be - we could almost say precisely now, but i prefer to reserve until october - and our estimate for 2005. on the basis of the commission's economic forecasts and the precise information we will have in the weeks following the publication of these forecasts on the actual and concrete content of the budgetary policies committed by each of these two countries for 2005, the commission, in exercising its right of initiative and assuming all its responsibility, will tell the council what its proposal is. the council will have to take the appropriate decisions, of course, in a climate of cooperation, but, of course, with the utmost respect for the principles and rules laid down in the treaties and the regulations in force on budgetary stability.

commission. mr president, the commission is gravely concerned about the situation in burma and, since 2001, has been using the asia-europe meetings of the asem process to reiterate this concern to heads of state and government, ministers and senior officials from the ten south-east and north-east asian countries which participate in the asem meetings. i do not have to impress on the honourable members of the european parliament how important the asem summits are in the eu political dialogue with asia, being the only occasions when eu heads of state meet south-east and north-east asian heads of state in a group-to-group dialogue. it is absolutely clear that all members of the european union remain highly critical of the military regime in rangoon and the european union will continue to repeat our demand for the immediate and unconditional release of daw aung san suu kyi and other leading representatives of the burmese national league for democracy. unfortunately, so far the burmese government has shown no sign of fulfilling this, or the other two conditions of the tullamore gymnich. great efforts have recently been made to find a solution which would allow the asem summits to take place. the commission is of the opinion that we have been able to find a compromise which is acceptable to all. we have been able to reach this agreement, because we value eu relations with asia too much to allow our asem dialogue to be taken hostage by the behaviour of the regime in rangoon. the eu has reached an agreement on the participation of burma in the asem summit, together with the 10 new eu members, cambodia and laos, but the european union expects burma to participate at a level lower than head of state and government. at the same time, in order to send a strong signal to the burmese regime that we do not agree with its policies, the european union has decided to strengthen the targeted measures against the burmese regime if it has not fulfilled the tullamore conditions by the time of the asem summit. ministers have agreed to expand the visa ban list to include serving members of the military of the rank of brigadier-general and above, and members of their families, and prohibit eu-registered companies or organisations from making any finance, such as loans or equity, available to named burmese state-owned enterprises. in addition, eu member states will vote against extending loans to burma from international financial institutions. the commission is also looking at ways and means to take concrete action against illegal logging, while extending assistance to the burmese population, especially on health and education, via international organisations. since the solution to the political situation in burma will have to be generated within burma and within the region, i am convinced that our dialogues in asem contribute positively towards future reform in burma. the commission therefore looks forward to the asem v summit in hanoi on 8 and 9 october, which in the context of wider discussions will allow a discussion with asian leaders on human rights and prospects for reform in burma and allow us to communicate our concerns to the burmese representatives there. working closely with the eu member states and especially the successive eu council presidencies, the commission is committed to all the appropriate efforts, whether they are diplomatic, political, or developmental, that might facilitate and accelerate the democratic and human rights reforms within burma.

maldives government, and to a strong public statement calling on the president to release prisoners, lift the state of emergency and continue with constitutional reforms. the president was clearly stung by these statements. he sent the minister for tourism to the united kingdom, germany and italy to explain the situation. he reassured the european union that he intends to continue with his promised constitutional reforms. he agreed that amnesty international and the red cross should visit the prisons. in shaping our response for the future, we should also recognise that the president undertook some reforms before the summer – discussions in the majlis assembly and the establishment of the human rights commission – but that he was clearly moving too slowly for the citizens of the maldives. building on this, a resolution from the european parliament that would underline the main messages already passed by the eu would be very valuable. it should also push the president to move on his offer for the red cross to monitor the prisons, stress that the european union will continue to monitor the situation closely and, if warranted, take up the president’s offer for the eu representatives to return to the country for further dialogue. however, it would, in our view, be premature to consider travel restrictions, suspension of aid and other more punitive actions at this the next item is the statement by the president of the commission on the balance sheet of the prodi commission.
president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is with great emotion that i stand before you for the last time as president of the european commission. in fact, in a few days, a journey that has seen us walk together for five years will come to an end. five years marked by major political and institutional changes and major events in europe and the world. i would like to begin this meeting by reminding you of the situation in the european union in 1999. in the institutional field, many wanted to limit the reform to the so-called 'left-overs' in amsterdam, proposing a limited institutional agenda that was not up to the new challenges of the union. in an unfavourable economic situation, fears, doubts and scepticism about the real possibility of physically introducing the euro were very strong. equally strong were the uncertainties about when to achieve enlargement and the number of countries to be involved. many were pushing for enlargement limited to a maximum of six countries. there was no defined time horizon or rules and the press and public were very much afraid. the risks posed by the balkan situation to the continent were even greater, in the absence of a clear and convincing european strategy in that region. finally, the commission itself was in crisis, shaken by the events of 1998 and 1999. its credibility and authority were reduced to the bare minimum and it was therefore necessary to revive its image by initiating for the first time a serious and profound reform of the administrative structure. we have accepted the challenge. together with you, we have put forward an ambitious agenda for europe. the key to this agenda, the unifying factor, which gave impetus and coherence to our action, was enlargement. the unification of europe, through enlargement to ten new countries, a clear timetable for the other candidate countries and a concrete prospect of full integration for all the balkan countries, represent the greatest contribution the union could make to the stabilisation and political, economic and cultural growth of the entire continent. to meet the challenge of enlargement, we had to find the right balance. we could not go too slowly, at the risk of losing the drive towards europe, which was very strong in the candidate countries. but we could not move too quickly without securing the consent of the citizens of the union. we have therefore strongly supported and accompanied the reform processes under way in central and eastern europe and, at the same time, we have taken on board the concerns expressed by europeans about the costs of enlargement, population movements, environmental risks, nuclear safety and corruption. the public opinion in the new member states was more than expected, as the success of the various referendums showed. we have shown that negotiation and dialogue, although sometimes difficult, complicated and detailed, are the only democratic way to export democracy and stability. at the same time, the ambition of enlargement to meet the demands of freedom, security and democracy of half our continent required that we take up the issue of reviewing our institutional set-up with equal ambition. that is why, first isolated, then supported by a consensus that has been growing continuously, we have pushed for a reform that meets the needs of governance in a europe of 25 or more member states. during these five years we have thus experienced a permanent institutional negotiation: the european council in dublin in december adopted a resolution on the situation in the community. thanks to the joint efforts of parliament and the commission, the convention method has finally become a reality, bringing more democracy and more transparency to europe. however, the scepticism surrounding this proposal, which i have defended since the night in nice, was very strong. never before have two visions of europe clashed as they have in this period. a strong, political europe, capable of meeting the global challenges we face, and a weak europe, understood as a mere space of prosperity, stability and regulation and not as a real political entity. europe has changed a great deal since the 1980s and 1990s, and the attitudes and policies of the various governments towards europe have also changed a great deal. in recent years, alliances between governments have very often been ad hoc, pragmatic, linked to specific proposals or to the domestic and international political situation, nor have there been groups of countries consistently pushing for greater integration. for our part, we have always fought to make our union stronger, more democratic and more effective. we have put forward very innovative proposals - think of the union's foreign minister for example - both at the european convention and at the intergovernmental conference that followed. we have now come to the end of the play. in a few days' time, a constitutional treaty will be signed in rome, which is undoubtedly a great achievement for europe, bringing more democracy, simplicity and transparency, even if it has other aspects that are less satisfactory - think for example of the cases where unanimity remains. this is a task to which we, and especially you, honourable members, have made a fundamental contribution. i have spoken to you, honourable members, about enlargement, institutional reform, growth policy and peace. none of this would have been possible if, in all these areas, we had not restored order, strength, prestige and pride to our institution, the european commission. no change is possible without a thorough reform of administrative structures and apparatus. the first positive effects are already being felt in various areas, such as decentralised financial control or external aid programmes. but above all, the reform contained strong political messages and aimed to restore the commission's legitimacy, independence and efficiency. it is enough to mention the example of the rotation system for directors-general, after many years in which some directorates-general were regularly filled by officials of the same nationality, or the nationality rules for commissioners and their cabinets, or finally the decision to bring commissioners closer to the services than their employees. but above all, there is one element that has characterised my commission and of which i am particularly proud: the commission has already done so. i could count on a cohesive, highly professional team, working in great harmony. today, some of the members of this commission already occupy very important posts in national governments and parliaments. i also see these as concrete, strong signs of the revival and growth of the institution which i have had the honour of presiding over for more than five years. and i am sure that the commission will be able to become even stronger under the presidency of josé manuel barroso, to whom i wish every success. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the process of continental unification is a great opportunity to extend the stability and prosperity of the union to the whole region around it. so we didn't just move the division, the "wall", a few hundred kilometers further east or south. for years, people have been talking about the frontiers of europe, but no operational proposals have been put forward. we have proposed a new vision of the union's frontiers, through the neighbourhood policy, aimed at achieving a genuine special relationship with the whole range of countries from russia to morocco. the european constitution itself acknowledges the need, which we have emphasized, to establish a new relationship between the union and its neighbours. at a time when everyone is talking about a 'clash of civilizations' - and i am convinced that it is above all a 'clash of ignorance' - we have also given a strong impetus to intercultural dialogue and mutual knowledge, particularly in the euro-mediterranean area. i am not sure that the commissioner has been able to give us a clear answer to this question. two days after the lifting of sanctions against libya, those moments seem really far away. but it is only four years of quiet, steady and intensive work that has brought about important changes in that country and paved the way for its readmission into the international community. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, over the years we have always made a very clear and strong choice in favour of multilateralism. more global and regional governance, a closer partnership with the united nations and less disparity between north and south were the objectives that inspired our action. we have not just "talked" about multilateralism: we have used it to serve our own objectives and political choices. i will give just a few examples: we have linked the objective of trade liberalisation to the need to take greater account of the legitimate demands of civil society and developing countries. we have played a central role in the enlargement of the world trade organisation to foster more effective global governance. we have focused our cooperation and development and humanitarian programmes primarily on poverty reduction. we have strengthened links with other regions of the world, such as latin america and asia, and helped new processes of regional integration, such as the african union. we have also made a concrete contribution to a stronger transatlantic relationship. in fact, after the iraq war, many people said that the gap between the two continents was now unbridgeable. i have never believed this, because i am convinced that in areas where europe really exists, where it is not paralysed by national vetoes, important results can be achieved together with washington and with equal dignity. we have therefore worked hard and effectively with our american partners on concrete issues of great importance, both in the field of security and the fight against terrorism and in certain areas of the world, such as the balkans. i said it before and i 'll say it again . in this difficult, often tragic world, europe has been able, and has been the only one able, to export democracy. in the economic field, the euro has undoubtedly been the protagonist of our mandate. the euro was to be the cornerstone of the new europe from the outset. that is why we have seen the euro from the outset as a major political project and not just an economic one. a project of policy makers and not just central bankers; a project that needs vision, authority and coordination. throughout the mandate we have insisted on the need to strengthen economic governance, because the cost of non-europe in this area is still too high. to this end, we have put forward various proposals to adapt the stability and growth pact to the new needs and the new economic reality in europe, finally opening a debate which was called for by many parties but which no one had the courage to launch. i must confess that i smiled when, after much criticism of my position, a well-known french newspaper wrote that 'with its recent proposals, the commission was making the pact more intelligent' ... we have also consistently contributed to the lisbon strategy and put forward the various proposals needed to achieve the objective of making the union the most competitive and dynamic economy in the world by 2010. think, for example, of the european research area, the emphasis on business innovation and the information society, the new programmes for lifelong learning and the opening up of our universities to the world. the reform of competition policy itself is one of our most significant contributions to greater competitiveness. in the social field, the 'social policy agenda' has provided the framework for a whole range of interventions in the fields of employment, social protection, health and safety at work, equal opportunities and social inclusion. in this area, however, we must be honest and admit that many objectives have been missed. above all, we have not achieved those objectives for which the community method could not be used and which were bound by the unanimity vote. the example of the difficulties encountered in the elementary case of the community patent, repeatedly blocked for linguistic reasons, is perhaps one of the most eloquent. if the member states do not change their behaviour, the lisbon strategy is at risk. the results achieved and the proposals put forward are numerous in terms of achieving the area of freedom, security and justice, improving environmental protection, the energy and transport sectors, and strengthening health and consumer protection. think of the implementation of the tampere agenda and the effort made to respond to the new challenges of international terrorism after the attacks of 11 september 2001. think of the sustainable development strategy in gothenburg, the johannesburg summit and european action in support of the kyoto protocol, which now seems to be able to bring its final results. in these areas, we have truly assumed world leadership, demonstrating in a concrete way the added value of european action in a multilateral context. we have combined strategic choices of the utmost importance for the future of the union, such as the european satellite navigation system galileo or the global strategy for the single european sky, with ready responses to emergencies, such as the shipwrecks of the erika in 1999 and the prestige in 2002. at the beginning of our mandate, there was another area where it was crucial to restore consumer confidence after the mad cow crisis: the food sector. the integrated 'farm to fork' strategy, accompanied by instruments such as the european food safety authority, was our response. the reform of the common agricultural policy itself is designed to respond to new challenges, both domestic and global, by aiming at a more sustainable strategy that pays more attention to rural development. finally, we presented our political project, our vision, for the union after enlargement, with our proposals for the new financial perspective. a political project aimed at the practical realisation of a genuine european citizenship for a union which has now become continental in scope and which must assume new responsibilities towards its citizens and its own responsibilities on the international scene. because that was our ambition too: the european union is committed to making europe a world player, to allowing europe to make its voice heard and to act in favour of a world of peace, security and balanced development. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to conclude by mentioning one last point which i believe should be placed on the balance sheet of this commission and the european parliament. it concerns the conclusion of a framework agreement between the two institutions for the entire duration of the legislature. our agreement has given added value to joint initiatives, such as the practice of communicating the commission's major initiatives to the european parliament as a matter of priority and solemnly. these agreements have strengthened the political role of the commission and the basis of its democratic legitimacy, which lies largely in the european parliament. this is an undeniable democratic advance, which i hold dear and for which i thank you. finally, i would like to point out the great agreement between the european parliament and the commission on legislative matters. conflict situations can be counted on the fingers of one hand. we should be glad of that. the commission's proposal for a directive on the coordination of certain provisions laid down by law, regulation or administrative action in member states concerning the pursuit of television broadcasting activities is one of the great merits of the codecision procedure and of the fairness with which the three institutions involved have handled it. at the end of these five years i am therefore pleased with the development of the constructive relations established between the commission and parliament. i hope and believe that these can continue in the future. if that is the case, it will mean that the outgoing commission has not only developed its relationship with parliament but has also laid the foundations for further strengthening democracy in europe. i am firmly convinced that we need even more europe and even more 'union' in europe. we must fully embrace the european political project and take it forward with strength, conviction and courage. that's what we've been doing these past few years, and i'm really grateful for all the help and support that you've always given us.
thank you very much, mr. prodi. before i give the floor to the spokesmen for the political groups, i should like to thank you, on behalf of parliament and myself, for your work as president of the commission, and to recall that you took office at a particularly difficult time in european history and that five years later, when you leave office, europe has undergone some historic transformations. yes, really historic. this is, without rhetoric, the right word to express what has happened in europe during your term of office. the effective implementation of the euro, the effective implementation of the monetary union - long dreamed of and hard worked to bring about - will be known as the 'prodi commission'. the greatest enlargement of the european union - which will surely never be repeated - has also taken place under your presidency. this is one of the structural changes in europe that history will associate with your name and the commission you have chaired, and also with your rich and intense participation in the work of the constitution which will be put to the vote. just by mentioning these three issues, mr prodi, you leave the commission presidency with a bag full of money. they are full of political assets which are profoundly transforming european reality and are driving its unity. my predecessors have told me that you have always listened to the european parliament, that you have always been a listening ear. although you may not always have followed his advice, you have always distinguished parliamentarians by your kindness and your constant accessibility. and above all, and above all, with its european commitment. it was this 'widely recognised' commitment to europe that made you president of the commission. you can be satisfied, above all, because by leaving it, that commitment to europe is even more recognised than yesterday. mr president, as the school of culture and peace at the autonomous university of barcelona points out, the situation in israel and palestine has not improved in recent months, quite the contrary. the international court of justice's ruling on the israeli-built separation wall, israel's refusal to comply with the ruling, the impression in diplomatic circles that the quartet roadmap is on the verge of failure and the protests by palestinian groups over corruption in gaza are just some examples of these steps back. it is also clear that we cannot dissociate the delicate situation in palestine and israel from the international context and the dire consequences of the absurd way in which the united states and some of its european allies are dealing with terrorism on an international scale, an attitude which, in my view, is increasingly fuelling the fanaticism of al qaeda. the european union must therefore take a much more forceful stance on what is happening in the middle east. i make two proposals: to follow and support the proposal to put in place all the necessary means to ensure that a normal and transparent electoral process is held in palestine so that sharon can no longer use the argument of the lack of a legitimate and valid interlocutor on the palestinian side, but also, given the insulting disregard that sharon has shown not only with regard to human rights but also with regard to international legality, instead of continuing to export arms to israel - as many european countries have been doing in recent years, including austria, belgium, france, germany, greece, italy, spain and the united kingdom, among others - i believe that the time has come for the european union to take much more forceful measures to put pressure on the current israeli government, including the cancellation of the association agreement. charles chaplin in the movie monsieur verdoux said it very clearly: if you kill five people you are a murderer, if you kill 5,000 you are a hero. please, let's stop making mr. sharon into a hero.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this reform of the system of generalized preferences completes the picture of human rights as an indivisible reality by directly linking the concepts and policies of trade, development and human rights. the reform of the gsp incorporates the idea that the best trade preferences are conditional on compliance with certain standards of social protection, human rights, good governance and sustainable environmental development. the unification of all these criteria into one gsp plus category, in addition to simplifying the system and making it more generous, as the commissioner says, is on the right track in terms of the coherence of community policies affecting developing countries and corrects the fragmentation that has traditionally been addressed in development policy. as the spokesman for the socialist group in the subcommittee on human rights, i cannot but congratulate the commission on this aspect of its proposal, without prejudice to the fact that other points in the proposal are clearly improving, particularly those which establish rigid mechanisms for the preferences established for the least developed countries. we will closely monitor the reform, its implementation and its effectiveness in terms of good development and, above all, human rights.

the next item is the report (a6-0014/2004) by mr lipietz, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the 2003 annual report of the european central bank (2004/2144 (ini)).
mr president, mr trichet, mr almunia, ladies and gentlemen, i warmly greet everyone in this debate which makes visible the democratic sense of the independence of the european central bank, which means parliamentary responsibility and control. i fully share the aspects of mr lipietz's report concerning the favourable assessment of the reaction of the european central bank during 2003: the low levels of interest rates, the clarification of the concept of stability and the enlargement of the euro area. the concern is that economic activity slowed down in 2003, especially in the euro area, and that risks to growth persist today. the union is designed to bring about the twin of stability and growth; one leg is not enough. that is why commissioner almunia's initiative is very relevant and will need support. the report also stresses the need for the european central bank to be closely associated with investment and growth policy. on the contrary, the need for structural reforms must not be distorted by misleading signals; the link between weak economic activity and low working time should therefore be excluded from the resolution. it does not conform to the criteria of flexibility, which is opposed to rigidity, nor to those of productivity. the essential thing is to create more value per unit of time and not with more units of time. in short, a bottom-up model will be dissolving, and we need an integrated, intelligent and ambitious economic, social and environmental governance.
mr president, in this last speech i would like to stress three points. firstly, it is emphasized that the history of economic and monetary union has been a success story, and it is said that this is due to the work of the bank. i agree with the rapporteur on this point and i would encourage the governor of the bank of spain to continue to set price stability as his main objective and not to listen to the siren song of the left to move towards other objectives. secondly, i would ask the president to tell the commissioner, who is standing by his side, that the flexibility of the pact he is proposing, the establishment of an a la carte pact, is a real time bomb for prices, sterilising the efforts of the central bank, for interest rates and therefore for investment and employment, for the pensions of the future and for the lisbon reforms. because if the pact is broken or relaxed, we'll need tomorrow's taxes to pay today's obligations. why don't we grow up? not because governments have been disciplined in complying with the pact, but because they have done the opposite and, moreover, because they have not fulfilled the obligations we have laid down for them in the lisbon pact and in the broad economic guidelines. i encourage both the president of the central bank and the commissioner to make an action plan, in the same way as we have achieved an integrated financial market with a financial services action plan, setting out the reforms and objectives we must achieve, the barriers which are hampering growth and which we must remove, the actions we must take and the timetable we must respect. mr president, do not listen to governments when they urge you to turn a blind eye, to look the other way, when their tax decisions are not being followed. instead, i suggest that you, like ulysses, when you hear those sirens, tie yourself to the mast and follow the course that such good success gives us and that you convince the commissioner that this is the course to follow.

the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the price of oil has risen considerably this year, reaching all-time highs - in dollars - in nominal terms. its impact on the economy is mainly due to the sharp rise in recent months, since, taking into account the evolution of the euro-dollar exchange rate and inflation, the current real price level in euro is comparable to that of 2000. the very short-term expectations are that the price of oil will remain high, due to higher than expected growth in demand, especially demand from the big asian countries and in particular from china, to the limited additional capacity to increase supply in the short term and to global and regional political uncertainties, in particular the conflict in iraq, of course. the upward trend has also been reinforced by certain speculative movements, attracted by the price volatility caused by the uncertainties just mentioned. this increase clearly has a negative impact on growth in 2004 and on the growth forecast for next year. the dollar price of oil is now 60% higher than it was six months ago when the commission published its spring economic forecasts. the commission will publish tomorrow its autumn economic forecasts, which include an estimate of the price of oil, which is of course higher than it was six months ago. according to the econometric model of simulations that the ecfin directorate-general has, if the price of oil were to remain at $50 a barrel - and today i believe that the brent barrel has traded above $51 - the impact would be an accumulated loss of growth over three years of almost one point of gross domestic product, with the price of oil remaining at $50 a barrel throughout that period. in fact, in the economic forecasts which the commission will present tomorrow, a higher oil price assumption has been taken into account than we took into account in the spring, although it is also true that, in relation to these estimates of the macroeconomic model, our assumptions of oil price developments for 2005 and 2006 are slightly more optimistic. we do not therefore expect it to remain at the level of 50 dollars, but to decline gradually. however, despite this negative impact, european economies are able to withstand this price increase, thanks in particular to two factors. on the one hand, the real price of oil - as i said - is considerably lower than previous highs. not only is it not higher than in 2000, but it is well below the peak reached in real terms in 1981 and is also significantly lower than the peak reached in 1973, more than 30 years ago. in addition, european economies have meanwhile, over that 30-year period, significantly increased their energy efficiency, reducing their dependence on oil from that which existed in the 1980s, making us less vulnerable to rising energy prices. in addition, the major changes in the formation of wages in the european economies, which are now less linked to price developments, should make it possible to reduce the side effects of the increase in energy prices or inflation, to which the president of the european central bank referred this afternoon. unlike in previous crises, so far at least, inflation expectations have not risen, despite the rise in oil prices. that said, it must be acknowledged, mr president, that certain sectors are being particularly affected because of their specific characteristics and circumstances, and i am obviously referring, as the wording of this point in the debate does, to agriculture and fisheries. the commission is well aware of the specific difficulties which arise in these sectors with the increase in fuel prices. in both cases, producers, both in the agricultural and fisheries sectors, can hardly pass on the increase in their costs to prices. the need for specific action is therefore not in doubt and the commission, in accordance with the request made to us last week by the eurogroup, has committed itself to presenting next month to the eurogroup and the ecofin a report on the measures that member states may envisage in accordance with the rules of the treaty, thus not breaking the existing legislation on state aid and preserving a principle which we believe is essential in economic and monetary union, namely the coordination of individual member states' initiatives in order to avoid distortions of competition. the ministers of finance, in ordering the commission to draw up this report, again stressed the need not to adopt unilateral measures and that any possible measures which might affect competition should first be subject to a mechanism of coordination and prior consultation. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. firstly, it is good to note that the appropriate policies to ensure the stability of energy supply are being properly implemented and coordinated at international, community and national level, and, of course, it must be made clear that there is no reason to fear a disruption of energy supply in the industrialized countries, since the current level of strategic oil reserves, whether in the united states, the european union or other oecd countries, allows problems in the supply of crude oil, if they arise, to be dealt with over a long period of time. this is important to remember, because the perceived risk of possible future oil shortages is contributing to the high level of oil prices, which i think is unjustified given the characteristics of the functioning of that market and the level of those strategic reserves. and finally, and looking ahead, it is important that we continue the reforms that we have undertaken in the past at the level of the european union, continued reforms to further improve our energy efficiency, because that will improve the ability of our economies to cope with external economic disruptions, such as this rise in the price of oil, and at the same time, by taking those energy efficiency measures, we will increase the long-term growth potential of the economies of the union.
mr president, let me first of all regret that this house has missed today the opportunity to provide the citizens with a package of real solutions to the crisis caused by the price of oil in certain sectors, as our committee on fisheries had initially proposed. the commissioner has said that the consequences are particularly serious in the fisheries sector, and neither the community institutions nor certain member states, including, unfortunately, my own, are taking any action. our house has decided to join in this inaction, preferring a mere statement by the commission to committing itself by means of a resolution, as our political group proposed. in fisheries, this statement is of little or no use to us today, because we already know the opinion of commissioner fischler, which is to pass on the increases to consumers. the problem is that the commissioner - and i am glad that you, commissioner, are saying the opposite today - was unaware that this is an impossible solution in this sector, since it is governed by a system of auctioning down. the situation is quite different, mr president. the oil price crises of 1993, 1994, 2002 and 2004 already show that this is not a short-term problem but a cyclical one, and cycles are expected to be shorter and shorter, as this is an exhaustible source of energy. we are therefore faced with a structural deficiency which will have to be addressed by structural measures. the european people's party therefore calls for the creation of a community instrument which can be triggered almost automatically in these periods of crisis. but we also need urgent measures to support the sector until such an instrument is part of community legislation, measures which include the granting of low-interest or zero-interest loans and the fixing of a maximum price, the amount of which is compensated up to the real price by means of financial measures and temporary deductions from social security and taxation.
mr president, what strikes me today in this house is above all the absence of the commissioner responsible for two sectors - agriculture and fisheries - from whom the initiative to propose measures to mitigate the negative impact of the rise in oil prices on two sectors that are inescapably dependent on it should start. two strategic sectors for the maintenance of employment and the food supply of the union. both sectors have - as commissioner almunia has acknowledged - difficulties in passing on the price increase, something which mr fischler does not seem to have understood yet. i would say that we have a duty to act with diligence - and the commission too - in crisis situations. in this respect, i would say to commissioner almunia that we do not want to go back to the scenario experienced in the year 2000, when the commission decided to declare illegal and to force the reimbursement of the state aid received by these professionals. a similar situation would be detrimental to the credibility of the institutions, not only community but also national. i agree with the commissioner that it is appropriate to adopt a mechanism capable of responding at community level to this situation, which is endangering two of our most sensitive productive sectors. i do not think it is too much to wait a month if it is to allow the design of an appropriate community framework capable of setting the scope and duration of the measures that can be taken by both the european union and the individual member states, the only way in our view to avoid the problems of distortion of free competition that could be generated by each member state adopting them on its own.
mr president, since the beginning of this year the price of agricultural fuel has risen by 40%. if we talk about a case that i know well - the case of spain - this has caused very heavy losses to producers who have not been accompanied, in any case, by national compensatory measures in a timely manner. spanish farmers are very concerned about the spanish government's inaction in this matter. last week a motion was tabled in this house for this parliament to pass a resolution in favour of long-term measures to reduce farmers' dependence on diesel. this project - the only one i have seen circulating on agriculture - did not go ahead, which, in my view, can be interpreted as a sign of this house's lack of solidarity with farmers, one of the two sectors - along with fisheries - most affected by price increases and because, in neither case, producers can pass on this increase in their prices. to solve this problem, i propose five measures: firstly, that the member states take coordinated action to avoid distortions of competition between neighbouring countries; secondly, that the european commission shows the utmost benevolence in authorising national aid; thirdly, that the european union should once and for all undertake a mature reflection on the means at its disposal to tackle the crises which have been occurring for years - let us recall the 1993/94 campaign, the year 2000 and all these campaigns in which price increases have been totally bloody for producers; fourthly, on that matter which was aborted at the conference of presidents last week, i proposed to ask the european union to bring forward the report it has to draw up on aid for the production of biofuels in order to seek as soon as possible viable solutions to the community regulation, and also to reduce the dependence of farmers on oil, as the european parliament and the commission have proposed in the last report, and fifthly, that the european union should take the long-term approach to reducing dependence on oil.

(applause from the left) in 1950 the founding fathers took the first initiative to create the european communities, the forerunners of our union. the older generation was mainly interested in the idea as a way to eliminate war on our continent. for the younger generation, it was above all an inspiring ideal and a challenge. at the age of 23, i was asked to give a speech on this subject to an international group of young people who felt connected to this european ideal. they then challenged me not to stop at these words but to call on young people in other countries to think together about the future of europe. we have also started with great enthusiasm. europe then offered us a whole new perspective. we saw the opportunity to reach out to peers across borders, to establish contacts and to develop initiatives together. what had begun with such prosaic concrete building blocks as coal and steel grew into a movement that would break down the walls of division in europe, preserve peace and give our continent new resilience and energy - certainly not, as robert schuman said, as a saut dans l'inconnu - a leap into the unknown - but as a leap towards a common future, this time clearly defined and enshrined in treaties. we, the young people of that time, would gladly have participated in it and thus helped to shape our own future. i gave that speech at a rencontre européenne des étudiants, a european student congress, in toulouse. when i reread those words now, i recognize the enthusiasm that gripped us then. we admired the vision and courage of the founders of the european communities, but felt that the older generation was putting too much into words and too little into action to really bring about european unity. 'let us recognize,' i said at the final session of the congress, 'that instead of common ideals we have only problems and that it is these problems which today constitute the only european unity.' fortunately, 43 years later, those words are no longer true. european unity has been firmly established and has become a part of our lives. but little remains of the enthusiasm of those days. many are now critical and are particularly concerned about the obstacles which still have to be overcome. the implementation of agreements is sometimes more difficult than expected, and the consensus on the course to be followed does not always hold. fortunately, we can see that the problems that are looming are often the direct result of the rapid progress made in european integration. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the original idea - the unification of europe - has taken an incredible flight, which would probably have surprised the great founding fathers of the years after the catastrophic second world war, despite their vision and ambitions. the union has abolished war on its territory, subordinated power to the rule of law and brought unprecedented prosperity to the participating countries. the unique european experiment has produced impressive results despite periods of delay and setbacks. the union now unites 25 european nations. as the first head of state to address your assembly since the accession of the new member states, i would like to extend a warm welcome to their representatives in this parliament. (applause) everyone who cares about the european ideal has been looking forward to this moment. your countries have always been part of europe. many have been freed from the years of oppression that divided our continent into two camps. we have the deepest respect for the conviction and the determination with which they have done so. we also admire the enormous efforts made by all the countries to undertake in a short time the many and often far-reaching preparatory measures necessary for their accession to the union. with their arrival the european family has become a - what is called in enthusiasm that they showed when they liberated themselves from soviet domination and in the impressive efforts with which they prepared for membership. it is almost certain that the union as a whole will find strength and inspiration in this enthusiasm and the enthusiasm with which you are beginning this new chapter, often with the involvement of the younger generation. adjustment problems will always be faced by those who join a new family - especially if it is a family outside their own country. we have some experience in my family! the newcomer is usually asked to make the biggest adjustment, although it would be fairer if this task were shared between both parties. this is also true of the enlargement of our community. the new members will make an effort to join what is already in place in the union, but the older members must also show a willingness to adapt. this is not only the collegial attitude to be expected in this circle, it is also the shortest way to good cooperation. the fundamental principle in the european union is that it is based on a community of law. the countries which are part of it - including those which have traditionally been among the most powerful countries in europe - have placed themselves under the rule of law in the interests of their common future. this is a unique step in the history of europe. this also means respecting the rights of every individual citizen. this legal anchoring of the union is well symbolized by the oath taken by its highest officials before the full court of justice. our 25 countries are united - but 'in diversity'. they cherish their own identity, their own language and their own cultural heritage. this is the great distinctive strength of europe and it is in the interest of all of us to carefully preserve and protect it. the constant confrontation with other cultures makes us more aware of both our own culture and our common heritage. it also gives us a stronger defense against the spirit of materialism and mass culture that is unmistakably spreading throughout the world - and in ever more threatening forms. in order to function properly, the union needs to have clear powers in a number of areas. in other areas, where success depends less on the pooling of forces, it may make sense, as a counterbalance, to leave more room for governments, lower levels of government and citizens themselves to find their own solutions - either at national level or in euroregions. a good balance between central and delegated governance can help to avoid the union's appearance as a big bureaucracy that alienates the people. if responsibilities are clear and defined and carried out where they serve the community best, citizens will also better understand and respect the common interest. more than a pursuit of an end, europe is a history of formation. for some, the process is too slow, for others, it is too fast. success often brings about adversity. they need not discourage the rapporteur. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we said in the september plenary session that we had received a draft budget from the council which was to be interpreted more in the accounting sense than in the political sense. on thursday we shall be voting here in parliament on a clearly political reading of the budget. the promotion of measures which i hope will be reflected in this draft budget which i am presenting for approval. it is also political because it follows a usual strategy of the council, which is to finance its priorities rather than those of parliament. in other words, with the vote on thursday we will try to balance the interinstitutional balance, a balance without which the european union cannot function properly. i would like to say a few words, mr president, to the commissioner who is leaving her post as a member of the european commission today. a commissioner for budgets always has away. the commissioner is largely responsible for the budgetary peace of these years and that is why, i should like to say, thanks to the agreements which the commissioner and her team have presented the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission would like to stress that the state aid which is being recovered, because it is considered to be illegal and incompatible, must be returned to the member state concerned and not to the commission. this is a confusion that sometimes occurs: whereas a fine imposed by the commission for a cartel or abuse of a dominant position is charged to the community budget, an order to repay illegal and incompatible state aid results in a transfer of money from the undertaking which unlawfully received it to the member state concerned, and not to the community budget. in accordance with the case law of the court of justice and article 10 of the treaty, where a member state encounters difficulties in implementing a commission decision requiring the recovery of unlawful and incompatible state aid, the member state and the commission must cooperate in order to find a solution to that difficulty. this is not a negotiation and the commission's decisions remain valid in all respects. such cooperation is currently taking place between spain and the commission. the commission does not intend to review the decisions in question as this would create a distortion of competition in the eu shipbuilding market. the commission has received numerous complaints from competitors in the european union in recent years concerning aid granted to spanish shipyards. moreover, it would appear to be legally impossible to authorise the aid in question, given the condition that no further aid be granted to spanish shipyards in the future, which was laid down by the council in 1997 and taken over by article 5 of the shipbuilding regulation applicable at the time the aid was granted.
