commission. mr president, still on behalf of mr prodi's commission, i would like to share with you some views of the commission that simply reflect some of the concerns which you have raised now and which are raised in the resolution about the situation in côte d'ivoire and recent violations of human rights. the european union has consistently expressed its deep concern at the violence by both camps since the start of the crisis in september 2002. while the situation improved slightly last year, it has deteriorated again since the beginning of this year, particularly recently. as mrs kinnock said, côte d'ivoire was known as an economically successful country, but clearly there is no long-term economic prosperity without political stability and respect for human rights. in march, the government security forces and parallel militias indiscriminately killed innocent civilians in abidjan and committed massive human rights violations. we know that at least 120 people were killed. abidjan has changed and mrs kinnock compared it to kinshasa. as mrs aubert and others have stressed, several mass graves containing more than 100 bodies were discovered in june in the northern part of the country now controlled by the ex-rebels of the new forces. freedom of expression and the media have been serially breached. on 1 november the main opposition newspapers were looted and vandalised by the young patriots. pro-gbagbo extremists took control of the public radio and television. they have been inciting violence against foreigners. international radio transmissions have been sabotaged. another issue of concern is the government's decision to cut off electricity supplies. in the northern part of the country water supplies are also cut off. under pressure from the international community, including the commission, electricity supplies were resumed, only to be cut off again. if the government continues to cut electricity this will lead to a humanitarian catastrophe. the commission is considering preparing a new humanitarian aid decision to improve the situation, notably in the north of the country. the international community must react to the situation and to the violation of human rights. the commission therefore welcomes the un sanctions, the arms embargo, the travel ban and the freezing of assets, not only for those who block the full implementation of the marcoussis and accra iii agreements, but also for anyone else found to be responsible for serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law. the commission fully supports the african union and president mbeki's mediation efforts. on 15 november president mbeki met president-designate barroso in brussels. the commission shares the concerns expressed by president mbeki about côte d'ivoire's future. in august this year the commission proposed to the council that consultations be opened under article 96 of the cotonou agreement. at that time the member states did not wish to proceed with the proposal. they did not want to jeopardise the accra iii agreement, which was signed just a few days before. recent developments and the non-implementation of the accra iii agreement demonstrate the importance of opening article 96 consultations to put pressure on the côte d'ivoire authorities to resume talks.

commission. mr president, distinguished members of parliament, i appreciate your contributions, which were completely unequivocal. the commission shares your views and is greatly concerned at the eritrean government's tightening of its grip in the area of human rights. the government is introducing restrictions on freedom of expression and the right to information, association and movement. some of these points have been elaborated by mrs lichtenberger and mr kohlíček. the commission regrets that there are no indications that democratic reforms will be introduced in the foreseeable future. the restriction of religious freedom is part of the overall trend of severely restricting civil and political rights in eritrea. the commission is aware of recent reports from different international partners to the effect that the eritrean government has violated human and religious rights and is restricting freedom of worship for some religious minorities. according to various sources of information, the government has harassed, arrested and detained members of non-approved religious groups, such as jehovah's witnesses, and adherents of the baha'i faith. on 4 november, the commission witnessed events in asmara during which eritrean security forces indiscriminately arrested thousands of youths suspected of evading military conscription. these arrests took place in the streets, shops and offices, at roadblocks and in homes. those arrested are being held in army prisons and are thought to be at serious risk of ill treatment. reports say that some have been shot dead and that many more were wounded following a disturbance at one prison. relatives and lawyers have no access to the prisoners. so what is being done? the commission is endeavouring to address the problem through support for ngo projects in eritrea in the areas of human and civil rights awareness, strengthening of civil society organisations and independent media. eritrea is a focal country under the european initiative for democracy and human rights and is allocated eur 1.6 million per year from this budget line. it has been difficult though to identify civil society and human rights projects because of the weak capacity of local civil society and the fragile political situation. secondly, the commission considers that we are seeing a pattern of human rights violations and, in coordination with member states, is closely following developments. the commission is analysing the situation and will soon present proposals on the basis of cotonou agreement, as was called for by mr kohlíček, mr gahler and mr tannock. however, the commission must emphasise that it has been very difficult to establish dialogue with the government of eritrea. now that it has been established, the commission considers that it should be pursued with a view to seeking improvements in the internal situation and external relations. we wish to avoid threats and feel that confidence-building is more likely to contribute to an improvement of the human rights situation. the commission will continue, as part of this dialogue, to address human rights violations, and in particular the case of the so-called asmara-11 group and the continued detention of independent journalists. in conclusion, on regional relations, the european union is anxious, as a witness to the algiers agreement on the solution of the border dispute between ethiopia and eritrea, to maintain open, balanced and measured dialogue with both parties.

mr president, on world aids day i would first of all like to draw the attention of the institutions, as other members have done, to the most dramatic aspect of this tragedy: its spread among women and young people. in this way, in addition to fulfilling my personal political commitment to women, i am also pointing to the enormity of the problem in terms of humanity, in terms of development and in terms of the global future. half of the 40 million people infected with the virus are women and girls, a proportion that is growing in almost all regions, reaching 57% in sub-saharan africa. for the industrialized world, i'll just give one example: latino and african-american women make up a quarter of the women in the united states and 80 percent of the aids cases. the feminization of aids is another, the latest, form of violence against women, who have not been provided with the means to defend themselves against the disease, with basic means such as sex education, the protection of reproductive health rights, or information on measures to prevent infection. social norms that impose ignorance on girls and young women about sexuality and that do not criminalize sexual violence within and outside marriage multiply the danger of the spread of infection. the socialist group welcomes the commission's decision to make education a priority in its policy framework for combating poverty-related diseases. secondly, mr president, i want to make a complaint. i denounce the responsibility of the catholic hierarchy for its negligence in the fight against aids. today the vatican marks the international aids day by condemning the disease as a pathology of the spirit, which it calls "moral immunodeficiency syndrome", which ethically and technically disqualifies the catholic church. through the secretary of the spanish episcopal conference - spain is precisely the country in europe where the number of infections is increasing the most - the catholic church intends to politically boost the global campaign to fight aids by warning about the insecurity of condoms and proposing chastity and fidelity as a method of prevention. this statement would not be worth further comment if aids were not the death sentence of millions of people, including children; if sexual violence, which leaves no choice for chastity, were not a daily reality in many societies in africa and asia; if there were not 15 million orphaned children; if it were not an attack on men's sexual and reproductive freedom; if it were not, in short, an attack on human rights and a real genocide. we are talking about life or death; we do not know whether the episcopal conference has understood it that way.

the next item is the debate on the annual report of the court of auditors for the financial year 2003. the president of the court of auditors, mr fabra vallés, who we welcome to this house, has the floor to speak first.
president of the court of auditors. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, at the meeting of the committee on budgetary control on 15 november last i presented the annual report of the european court of auditors for the financial year 2003. i had the opportunity to give a detailed account of the observations and conclusions contained in our report. today i would like to focus my presentation on the conclusions in three areas: the declaration of assurance, budgetary management and the commission's reform process. chapter 1 of the court's report contains the das statement of assurance which is published in the official journal together with the consolidated accounts of the community. as in the previous year, the statement of assurance is based on four pillars which are the result of the evolution of the methodology used by the court to provide greater robustness to the outcome of its work. these four pillars are: first, the quality of the control systems of the community institutions and the member states; second, the examination of a sample of commitments and payments in each area of expenditure; third, the analysis of the annual declarations of the directors-general of the commission; and fourth, the examination of the work carried out by other auditors. as a result of this audit work, the court is of the opinion that the consolidated annual accounts for the financial year 2003 presented by the commission have been drawn up in accordance with the financial regulation. the accounts shall give a true and fair view of the revenue and expenditure for the financial year and of the financial position of the community, with the exception of the entry for several debtors. the court notes, as in previous years, that in 2003 the accounting system used by the commission was not prepared to ensure a complete inventory of its assets. the accounting modernisation plan approved by the commission in 2002 should take effect from january 2005. the court considers that the full implementation of the new set of rules and accounting plans will require considerable effort on the part of the institutions whose accounts are to be consolidated. as regards the legality and regularity of the transactions and as regards the revenue, commitments and administrative expenses, the court considers that the underlying transactions are legal and regular. the court's observations on the other chapters of the budget reveal weaknesses in the systems for monitoring and controlling the management of community funds in general. in the agriculture chapter, payments were again affected by material errors. in the field of structural actions, weaknesses persist at member state level in the monitoring and control systems. in the chapters on internal policies, external actions and preaccession aid, errors affecting the legality and regularity of transactions have also been detected. therefore, despite the considerable efforts made by the european institutions in recent years, the european court of auditors recommends that efforts be stepped up in the management and control systems in these areas. the court again emphasises that in the areas of shared, indirect or decentralised management, more errors continue to appear and that these are the areas where more efforts need to be made. in this respect, opinion 2/2004 of the court on the single audit method, to which i shall refer in more detail below, is a concrete proposal for improving control systems which could in turn contribute to better management of community funds in the member states. i shall now turn to the comments on budgetary management. the total payment budget for 2003 was eur 98 billion, with payments of eur 90 500 million, an increase of around 6% on 2002. the budget surplus has been reduced significantly, from eur 15 billion in 2001 to eur 7 billion in 2002 and eur 5 500 billion in 2003. despite this improvement, the court considers that the budget surplus figure is still high and that it indicates the existence of systematic problems which should be corrected by better budget forecasting. the main cause of the surplus remains the difference between planned and actual expenditure. the court noted that it would be unrealistic to expect 100% implementation of the budget, given that 80% of the community budget is shared or decentralised and requires action by the member states for its implementation. however, in 2003, the rate of implementation of the budget, as far as the implementation of payments is concerned, reached a ratio of 92%, which is a considerable improvement on the figure of 86% in the previous year. as regards the budgetary management of the european development funds, we note that the renewed report on financial management is an effort to improve the quality of information on the management of the financial year. the commission has endeavoured to reduce the volume of commitments still to be settled. the implementation of payments was also hampered by a shortage of financial resources: eur 270 million. to complete its report, the commission should include the costs of managing the european development funds. i will end my presentation by referring to the state of play of the administrative reform launched by the commission in 2000. in february 2004, the commission published a report on the degree of implementation of the actions resulting from the white paper on reform. the court of auditors acknowledges the progress made by the commission in the new control framework, but considers that the results of the implementation of the system are not yet satisfactory. in the court's view, for eight of the actions that were theoretically completed at the end of 2003, including those concerning minimum internal control standards or internal audit structures within each directorate-general, the degree of implementation is still not satisfactory. the court therefore considers that, despite the progress made, the implementation of the commission's internal control standards cannot be considered as yet sufficient to give reasonable assurances as to the legality and regularity of transactions. the court encouraged the commission to complete the implementation of the new internal control system, in particular in the areas of shared management, risk analysis and debt recovery. finally, let us remember that the reform of the commission is based on the principle of the responsibility of the manager, accountability and evaluation of results. in this connection, the european commission presented, for the first time in 2003, an analysis of the degree of reliability of its supervisory and control systems in relation to the legality and regularity of the underlying transactions, thus assuming responsibility for the management of the community budget, as provided for in article 274 of the treaty on the european community. the commission has stated that it is not yet in a position to make an unreserved statement on an important area of its management, the structural funds, which has been corroborated by the court of auditors' observations. in other areas of management, the commission refers to the statements of the directors-general, 21 of which contained reservations. these reservations limit the assurance given by directors-general in their statements. the court also considered that, despite the efforts and progress made by the commission, these efforts were not sufficient if they were not accompanied by an improvement in the controls of community funds by the various administrations involved in the management of these funds at national level. this issue was addressed in opinion 2/2004 of the european court of auditors, issued last april, on the feasibility of introducing a single audit model, to which i referred at the beginning of my speech. this opinion was drawn up in the light of the paper produced by the section for industry, commerce, crafts and services, chaired by mr de gucht. the purpose of the single audit model would be to develop an efficient and effective internal control framework in the european union, which ensures the reliability of the results and allows their use by all parties involved in the control. this is an area where the european institutions and the member states, with the collaboration of their national control institutions, can work closely together to develop a legal framework for improving the control of community funds. before i conclude my speech, i will be allowed to take a few words off the agenda. as you know, my term as president of the court ends in january 2005. i have thus completed the three-year cycle which i began with the presentation to cocobu of the court's work programme for 2002. during these three years i have worked to develop and maintain the best working and trusting relations with the european parliament, mainly through collaboration with its committee on budgetary control. better communication, information exchange and closer cooperation between the two institutions have been promoted. i think the balance is positive and that the court is providing parliament with independent and professional assistance of a higher quality every day. that can only be achieved by respecting the independence and mandates of our respective institutions. the court also undertook internal reform of its organisation and structure to make it more effective in carrying out its duties and to give a 25-member college greater flexibility and efficiency. this reform, which is a direct consequence of enlargement and the treaty of nice, was designed to ensure its effectiveness while respecting its legal framework. at the same time, the court has worked with the audit institutions of the new states to prepare them for the important work they will have to do as liaison institutions in the court's audits in their respective states. these, together with other technical and human resources measures, should help us to continue and improve our work in an enlarged europe. today i think we can celebrate the achievement of these goals. i would like to end by thanking you, ladies and gentlemen, for your attention. very painful. mr president, mrs ferrero-waldner, there is no doubt that after forty years of armed conflict, colombia continues to suffer from a significant deficit in peace and social justice. and yet the uribe government continues to insist on a fundamentally military response, while still failing to recognize the existence of an armed conflict with political roots. the european union can do much more to promote peace in colombia. firstly, the european union can demand that the colombian government comply with the recommendations on respect for human rights made annually by the union's office in bogotá, as a precondition for receiving community aid. secondly, the european union's aid must be used to dismantle paramilitarism as a phenomenon, which means going far beyond the simple abandonment of arms and tackling its political and social dimension. thirdly, the european union must make a clear commitment to facilitating processes of exploration, political negotiation and peace agreements with all the actors, including the eln and the farc, which in turn also requires gestures on the part of the latter, such as the release of the thousands of people who have been kidnapped. and fourthly, the european union must also promote humanitarian agreements within the framework of the geneva conventions, as proposed by the permanent assembly of civil society for peace.
mr president, unfortunately the reality in colombia is that of terrorism fuelled by kidnapping and blackmail. many people probably do not know, or do not want to know, that in addition to the former presidential candidate, ingrid betancourt, more than 3 000 colombian citizens are still being held hostage by guerrillas, treated in an inhuman way and in deplorable conditions in the jungle. i wonder if that's the way to fight for social justice. not long ago some members of the former european parliament welcomed president uribe by leaving the chamber in protest at the lack of democracy in colombia. they probably didn't know or didn't want to know that mr. uribe had won the first round of the presidential elections - a fact unprecedented in the history of colombia. perhaps many are also unaware, or do not want to know, that the farc, the eln and the auc are terrorist organizations included in the list of terrorist organizations of the european union. only in this way can the crime of terrorist financing be explained which an ngo from a member country of the european union has just committed by handing over $8 500 to the farc. the uribe government has entered into dialogue with a section of the paramilitaries willing to disarm, with the only requirement that they lay down their arms. and he's been heavily criticized for it. however, the case of the farc is different. the possibility of negotiation is not open as long as they refuse to disarm, as long as they are not also recognized as a clearing zone in which to continue to commit crimes. i remember that it has been five years since president pastrana tried to negotiate; but society will never find support for the farc, a society overwhelmed by the pain and blood of its loved ones. in the meantime, part of the international community, through so-called ngos, is criticizing the legitimate and democratic government of that country, influencing and even manipulating many of us. finally, i would like to recall the experience of spain. we did not begin to defeat the terrorism that was operating in spain until the european union took it on as something that also affected the coexistence of europeans. let colombia follow suit.
i would like to ask the president-in-office to speak on the basis of rule 145 of the rules of procedure on personal grounds. i said in my speech that the farc terrorist guerrillas have kidnapped 6,000 people in recent years, politicians, civilians and military personnel, who are being held hostage in the jungle in inhuman conditions, many of them sick and suffering great suffering and hardship. i have also said that the farc guerrillas have many people kidnapped, and i am well placed to do so because, when the dialogue table with president pastrana was open, i met with mr marulanda and, with other colleagues in the european parliament, i pleaded for the release of several european union hostages. these facts and figures cannot be ignored and i have simply said that only ignorance and bad faith can prevent these facts from being taken into account. mr president, in my speech i asked the government to take up its responsibilities; that it can do more and better, although it has done a lot, and that, of course, the burden of proof should fall on those who extort, kidnap, murder and blackmail colombian society.

the next item is the report by mr eurlings on turkey's progress towards accession (a6-0063/2004). i call mr eurlings.
mr president, i would first like to congratulate mr eurlings on the excellent work he has done on a subject which, as we have seen in this debate, is controversial and difficult. it really does elicit strong support at the start of the negotiations. on the other hand, some members have shown fundamental opposition. i think that this debate must be conducted calmly and on the basis of objective premises. turkey is a candidate country by decision of the european council in helsinki. the prodi commission has given a positive opinion on the opening of negotiations, which, as mr rehn has told us, has been endorsed by the barroso commission. turkey is linked to the european union by an association agreement and is part of the customs union. at the same time - and this is important in the debate - turkey is a loyal partner of the west in the atlantic alliance and, in my view, mr president, the question we have to ask ourselves at this moment, given the strategic situation of turkey, which has an absolutely crucial position in the transit of hydrocarbons from the caspian sea and also has a decisive position in terms of the stability of the middle east and central asia, is whether we want turkey to be linked to the western value system of the european union or whether we want turkey to drift towards islamic fundamentalism or enter the orbit of russia. the response of the eurlings report is a critical but constructive response and i believe, mr president, that there are other questions on the table which are also legitimate and legitimate, such as whether european public opinion is now ready to admit turkey into the union. but time and the citizens of the european union will answer that question in due course.
mr president, this is not a debate for or against turkey: that would be a huge debate and i do not wish to be part of that game. this is a debate about our own future as part of a political project and about the legitimate right of turks to benefit from the kind of growth and stability that can only be brought from europe. it is our duty to find new kinds of relationships with our neighbours and allies, so that both goals can be made equally compatible without endangering the success of our own projects and dreams and making them collapse, which is what could happen if things are not done properly. membership of the european union cannot be the only option we give to our neighbours and friends. that needs to be said very clearly. other very clear options have to be kept in mind. finally, the european leadership has ignored public opinion and the citizens of europe too often. this time that neglect on the part of our political elite – treating our citizens as babies – could have catastrophic effects.
mr president, today's report on turkey is of vital importance, because the decision taken by the european council on 17 december has a historical significance which goes beyond the political frontier indicated by mr eurlings' report. the committee on industry, research and energy is also keen to highlight and welcome the progress made by turkey in the economic field in line with the criteria laid down by the union and, in particular, we want to stress its conformity with the acquis communautaire in areas such as energy policy, industrial policy, research and development and telecommunications. but although the line taken is correct, progress in each of these fields has been uneven, so that in future progress will be necessary in at least four areas which i shall mention by telegraph. first, it must improve administrative capacity to complete and strengthen the implementation of the acquis communautaire. secondly, there is a need for more independence in the monitoring of state aid. thirdly, it must increase the budget devoted to research and development in relation to its gdp. and fourthly, the legal framework in the telecommunications sector should be reviewed. that is the essence of the amendment which the committee on industry, research and energy is proposing to add to mr eurlings' report.

mr president, the socialist group has ambitions in the field of development cooperation and humanitarian action which we shall try to include in parliament's recommendations to the commission and its president. the impetus we want from the union is based on the european constitution and it is very encouraging that here, as in other areas, the constitution is imposing its logic and its budget even before it is ratified. the main contribution of the socialists to the process of european construction was to introduce solidarity as one of the essential pillars of our project, solidarity not only as a great moral and political value but also as a guarantee for peace, stability and prosperity in europe. in an exercise of remarkable consistency, we have succeeded in bringing this principle up to date in the constitution, translating it into the reality of a globalised world. in these new circumstances, intra-european solidarity can no longer suffice, at least for the socialists. we can no longer be satisfied with solidarity confined to the territories and the citizens of the union. on the contrary, this solidarity must also be a sign of the european union's identity on the international scene, solidarity in particular with the peoples who are struggling against underdevelopment, in pursuit of their dignity and prosperity. our solidarity, in the new context of globalisation, must therefore guide the european union's action in the world, but it must also transcend all community policies horizontally. it will be a key priority for the commission to contribute to the achievement of the millennium development goals, with particular emphasis on the eradication of poverty and hunger, by acting both in the least developed countries and in the pockets of the most disadvantaged population that we find in somewhat more advanced countries. the fight against aids and other diseases linked to poverty and underdevelopment, such as malaria and tuberculosis, must also be our priorities, as must the promotion of women in the countries with which we cooperate to achieve their development and the dialogue between civilizations, launched by the president of the spanish government. in all this the commission will have a great responsibility in promoting and coordinating its action with that of the member states of the union, with a view to achieving complementarity and coherence, particularly in our presence and influence in the united nations development agencies. for all this, it will be essential to maintain and even increase the effort to finance our development and humanitarian policies, keeping to the commitments and timetable we made in barcelona and monterrey and not being satisfied with that, but setting ourselves ever more ambitious goals.
president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have listened to each and every one of you with the greatest attention. i am grateful for your contributions which show a wide variety of perspectives in this parliament. i also look forward with great interest to the outcome of your vote next thursday. the resolution that is adopted will certainly be very important for the common strategic vision we want for the european union. i think i could draw three preliminary conclusions at this stage. i note that the vast majority of the speakers first of all agree with the need to set priorities that correspond to the expectations of the citizens and think that it is important for the european union and its institutions to respond to what are the first concerns of the europeans. secondly, the vast majority of speakers identified three key areas for action: the area we can call lisbon, the lisbon strategy (economic reform with a social and environmental dimension), the areas linked to security and justice and europe's role in the world. thirdly, i have seen that there is also a broad consensus on the need for a strong cohesion policy, a genuine policy of solidarity in europe. i hope in particular that this point has been heard well by the governments of the member states. i think we can then conclude that there is a consensus on the need for growth and jobs in europe. without growth, without job creation, without more dynamism in our economy, we will not be able to maintain the high levels of social protection and environmental requirements which we consider to be part of what is commonly called the european model. the point is not, and never has been, the destruction of the european model. what is really at stake is the need to adapt and modernise this european model, to take account of some of the new challenges that are emerging today in europe and in the world. our ageing population, the effects of globalisation, all of this is forcing europe to adapt and move in this more competitive context. so i would like to say to you that it does not seem to me to be impossible to reconcile concerns for economic efficiency with concerns for social justice. these objectives - greater competitiveness with sustainable development and social concern - cannot in any way be incompatible. we have to work on their compatibility. these are goals that define us as a priority. i think, therefore, that we must work towards maximum consensus, but a dynamic consensus, a consensus which does not result from the overriding of opposing views because also, we must admit, there are some priorities here which are contradictory in parliament. we must therefore define the maximum common denominator for a dynamic consensus. i think one consensus that emerged clearly was that we need to strengthen our solidarity at a time when we have an enlarged europe. we have a europe on the road to reunification. this enlargement is an enlargement which has only just begun. we have signed the treaties and we have ten new member states among us, but we must do everything we can to ensure that in due course we no longer talk about old and new member states, but that we are truly one union and that is why we need an active cohesion policy. that is why i insist on this value system, and solidarity is certainly a value that can bring us together. that is why i say to you that today, when i see so many times in europe that the question of european identity is being discussed, i must stress that it is based on respect for different national, regional and local identities. european diversity is what really defines our identity, and if we want to define identity, we must define it in terms of the values enshrined in the european constitution and the charter of fundamental rights, namely respect for the dignity of the human person, human rights, justice, the rule of law and the principles of freedom and equality. these are the values that define our identity. respect for the principle of non-discrimination and tolerance towards all those who enter our borders. it is therefore on the basis of these values that we can promote the idea of europe in the world. i have already said in my opening remarks that it is on the basis of these values that we can best defend our interests. we are defending our interests with a more ambitious neighbourhood policy, a neighbourhood policy towards the east or the mediterranean that promotes stability and peace, as we have been doing, for example, in ukraine. i would like to stress - and this has not always been said - that the signals given by the european union in this crisis in ukraine have been very positive. without any struggle for prominence, we had the presidency of the council, the european council, the european commission and some member states involved in the search for a peaceful and democratic solution for ukraine. that is very positive for our europe. but also with a generous development policy. i have already said that europe cannot be selfish. a policy which is also the translation into the external sphere of what we are doing internally, after we have overcome so many historical differences through cooperation between member states which, in the past, have often been at war with each other. that is why i believe we have a duty to defend effective multilateralism, working on a level playing field and with respect for our key partners, seeking to revitalise the transatlantic alliance, uniting all our partners around values such as freedom, peace and democracy. this is how europe moves forward, enriching its heritage, building and updating dynamic consensus, seeking to value in the world what makes its difference. i would like to conclude, ladies and gentlemen, by assuring you that the commission will seek to take parliament's positions into account in order to integrate them into what we want to be a strategic vision, not of this or that institution, but a strategic vision for all the european institutions and for the european union as a whole over the next five years.
representative of the association of journalists of belarus. the speech was delivered in russian. this is a translation. mr president, members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, this is a very emotional moment for me, because this is an extremely important, significant moment for my colleagues and i. the fact that we are receiving this prize as an organisation is a sign of solidarity and support for the entire belarusian democratic movement and support for the political forces that will finally ensure that in future there will be a link between belarus and the european union. the fact that this prize was initially put forward for two belarusian organisations – the second organisation was the youth organisation zubr – is probably a sign that belarus is the focus of international attention and that my country, which one of my colleagues has described as a chess piece which has fallen off the chess board, will once again become an independent entity in european politics and will one day take a worthy place among the other nations around the european table. the prize is such an important signal for us because we understand our problems, but they are not just a matter of upholding our own professional principles. it is also about defending the rights of all our citizens to receive objective, uncensored information. it is extremely important that our problems are understood by you and by european politicians. unfortunately, the belarusian authorities have managed to create a closed society built on isolation and disdain for democratic values. they protect their stability and survival by means of total control over the flow of information. the electronic media are almost totally monopolised by the authorities. the situation is worse because the work of these monopolised media is directed at discrediting any political adversaries, and the monopolised media try to reinforce stereotypes and myths. one such widespread myth in belarus is that nobody in europe is watching us, nobody expects us to join them and europe is hostile and aggressive towards us, the only guarantee of stability in our country is the head of state, and so on and so forth. despite our constitutional provisions, there is only one obligatory ideology that prevails in belarus now. in belarus a process has now been completed – the creation of a new state structure which is known as the ideological 'vertical'. there is total intolerance of criticism and we are not allowed to object or express our views. my colleagues know that we are subject to use of the criminal code against us if we criticise the president. two years ago, paval mazheika, a young journalist, was given a prison sentence under the criminal code. during political campaigns there is even more pressure on the non-state press; the referendum and the recent parliamentary elections are a case in point. on the eve of the referendum my colleague, elena ravbetskaya, the editor of the newspaper birzha informatsii published an article in which she said that calling the referendum was 'a challenge to society' and that to carry it out required a total lack of conscience and total neglect of public opinion. my colleague was also tried and fined as a result. her newspaper has also been punished and has been closed down for three months as a result of that article. again, two weeks ago, a very well-known person, garry pahaniayla, vice-president of the belarus helsinki committee, was also sentenced for slander against the state. the reason for this was a cassette taped by a swedish television journalist, which was confiscated from him at the border. mr pahaniayla had given an interview and mentioned the names of those suspected of involvement in the disappearance of belarusian opposition politicians. that was sufficient for them to bring him to trial and he may well be imprisoned for five years as a result. we are very concerned that, despite the conclusions reached in the report on the disappearances of belarusian politicians and journalists by christos pourgurides, a council of europe special rapporteur, and despite the international community's close attention to this subject, it seems that the belarusian authorities are still not interested in a full in-depth investigation of these disappearances or in publishing such an investigation. we still do not know what happened to dmitry zavadsky, who disappeared four years ago. he is a journalist and a member of our organisation and the authorities have never told us what happened to him. his wife, svetlana zavadskaya, is on our delegation. the issue of the disappeared is still in the newspapers. three years ago, during the presidential election campaign, we were punished for mentioning this. there was direct censorship. at the beginning of this year, in the last campaign for parliamentary elections and the referendum, we saw for the first time the summary closure of newspapers at the behest of the ministry of information. there were 19 cases of suspension of the activities of independent media outlets. our colleague, andrey shantarovich, actually went on hunger strike as a result of his paper being shut down. after the hunger strike he was charged with carrying out an unauthorised protest. this was absurd. the information about his hunger strike had been published all around the city and, as a result, he was fined for the hunger strike. suspending the activities of newspapers is aimed firstly at hitting the newspapers economically. economic discrimination has become one of the ways of restricting the activities of the independent press. my colleagues in the press are coming up against major obstacles in the distribution of their newspapers. the distribution of alternative, accurate information to citizens is one of the major problems facing our society. if a publication criticises the authorities, this automatically leads to problems with the printing houses. according to the ministry of information, there are hundreds of independent printing presses, but already five independent publications can no longer be printed in our country; they have to be printed in smolensk in russia because they cannot use printing presses on belarusian territory. i can say quite categorically that the journalists – my colleagues from the independent press – remain true to the principles of their profession. the independent press, which still appears in belarus, is virtually the only institution which exercises any scrutiny over the state and it is the only source of free information to citizens. it would not be possible for us to survive without the collective support of international and european organisations. i would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to article 19; to the international federation of journalists; reporters without borders; the international league for human rights; the danish organisations; the helsinki committee from sweden and norway; the centre of extreme journalism, as it is called – a russian organisation; and the glasnost defence foundation. all these are partner organisations that are helping us, and our strength lies in this partnership and cooperation. it is very important for us that european society and the european institutions should not weaken their position with regard to the principles of freedom of speech and human rights. if there were to be any weakening of those positions, then the repressive machine within belarus would start to go into overdrive and we would feel even more pressure against us. recently, at international level, many politicians from eastern european countries have expressed their concerns about the situation in belarus and are prepared to work towards formulating a strategy towards belarus at european level. i would like to express our support for that and the certainty that a common european strategy towards belarus will emerge and will very much help our situation. we can only combat a totalitarian regime by creating an open information society; a society that would encourage debate; a forum – which is a place for people to receive accurate information. we have a comprehensive programme which we feel will help to unlock the situation in our country. we are prepared to discuss that with you. i will just mention a few of the priorities. we need support for what is legal and what is still working in belarus. basically, what i am referring to is the independent press and the non-governmental organisations that are still operating in our country. what is also very important for us is the effect of the strengthened presence of the european union in belarus – something that we would encourage. perhaps there is some way of establishing a european union special representative for belarus. we feel it is very important that our people should receive a message from the european union. its value would be that our return to europe depends on us, the belarusian people. we understand that today, belarus's visiting card unfortunately implies the lukashenko regime. in fact there are ten million people in our country and at least half of those associate the future of our country with a return to europe. i should like to take this opportunity to urge the members of the european parliament – especially the members of the delegation to belarus – to support our proposals with regard to staging hearings on the media situation in belarus. such hearings might lead to recommendations on bringing our legislation into line with european standards and would help us to demonopolise the mass media. once again, i thank you for this award. 'on the application of this provision in this case, after having heard those who have spoken on points of order and after, of course, having sought the opinion and advice of the legal services of the house and the general secretariat, which is my duty, i can say the following: firstly, that the competent services confirm to me that these petitions are endorsed by a sufficient number of members and that they have indeed been submitted in good time. secondly, as some of you have said, there is a question of interpretation as to whether we are obliged to vote by secret ballot, since article 162 (2), which has been invoked so many times here this morning, says that 'the vote may be secret' and does not say 'it shall be secret'. there is therefore a margin of interpretation as to what the regulation says. the presidency, knowing that this would be a subject for debate, has analysed the precedents and the case law of the court of justice before coming to this part-session and, irrespective of my personal opinion that i deserve to do so in one way or another, it is my duty to try to interpret the rules of procedure in the most lawful way and, in this connection, i must remind the house that there is a precedent according to which president cox understood already, at the meeting of 12 june 2002, that the term 'may be secret' implied the automaticity of the proposal and that if there were a sufficient number of members who requested it, his request should be granted. moreover, the court of first instance of the european communities has issued a judgment in october 2001 where it also interpreted the term 'may' as a mandatory condition in reference to an article of the regulation similar to the one we are now dealing with. in accordance with these precedents and regardless - i repeat - of the views that anyone may have on the opportunity to do so in one way or another, the presidency considers that, having submitted a request in due time and form, we should proceed to a secret vote ... (applause)... without prejudice to submitting this matter, for future occasions, to the consideration of parliament's committee responsible for regulatory matters. we will probably have to clarify in the future whether the interpretation that the presidency is making is the correct one or not, but at this stage of the procedure the presidency has to take the responsibility of deciding, without being able to refer to the advice that the relevant committees might give it, and i believe in good conscience, after having listened to all the members and the legal services, that the correct interpretation of the rules is to proceed with the secret ballot that we have been asked to hold and that is what we are going to do. as regards the manner in which the vote will be taken, i would inform the honourable members that i have decided to use the electronic procedure in accordance with rule 161 (1) and that there will therefore be no need to appoint a college of voters. it'll be secret, but electronic. that said, we'll start the voting. on amendment no 71: the commission has

council. madam president, it is a great pleasure to be able to inform you formally that on 13 december 2004 the general affairs council closed the negotiations with bulgaria. we will now start the last, very important phase before entering the eu. the remaining two years should be used to prepare thoroughly for membership. the eu congratulates bulgaria on this positive result, which has taken much effort and energy. it is a new step towards a truly reunited europe, based on mutually accepted principles of democracy and the rule of law. the negotiations with bulgaria closed at the technical level in june 2004. this reflects the progress that the bulgarian government has made in recent years, which resulted in strong confidence on the part of all those involved and the ability to assume all membership obligations by january 2007. still, as the committee on foreign affairs also states clearly in its motion for an ep resolution on bulgaria's progress towards accession, we should closely monitor the progress which still has to be made by bulgaria. the commitments made in the justice and home affairs chapter might need an amendment of the constitution, which is a long and difficult process. other important areas, as the committee on foreign affairs states, are the quality of border management, the fight against corruption, and the prevention of abuse of powers by state authorities against persons entering or transiting bulgaria. the new penal code still has to be approved. administrative capacity in a number of areas, including the agencies involved with the use of pre-accession funds, should improve. both in bulgaria and in romania, improvements in the standard of living should be a priority. the economic growth that bulgaria and romania have seen in recent years has had a positive effect on purchasing power, but the effects at grass-roots level, especially for the elderly, have remained limited. there are at least two more years to go before accession. an historic step will be made on 17 december when the negotiations regarding the fifth enlargement have come to an end. monitoring of the last part of the fifth enlargement will continue until 2007, in order to welcome the two new, long-awaited members then ready to join the european union. as mrs kuneva said in october, she would like to publish the monitoring report on a big wall in sofia in order to keep the process going. i think bulgaria has made good progress, which gives us confidence for the numerous tasks still remaining. the council looks forward to the finalisation of the accession treaty with a view to its signature in spring 2005, after the treaty has been submitted to the european parliament.
commission. madam president, we have come a long way since bulgaria applied for eu membership in 1995 and opened its negotiations in 2000. yesterday the eu finalised the accession negotiations with bulgaria in the accession conference, with a view to accession on 1 january 2007 and with the signature of the accession treaty in sight in the spring of next year. i would like to thank the european parliament for its constant and balanced support for bulgaria's ambition to accede to the european union and i would also like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr van orden, for the sound and even-handed report he has produced. in the past few years bulgaria has made steady progress in all areas in its preparation for accession and for meeting the copenhagen criteria. important and necessary decisions have been taken in this respect. four units of the kozloduy nuclear power plant are being closed on agreed dates for final decommissioning, showing bulgaria's determination to respect commitments. substantial support from the union is being provided as assistance to these efforts. overall, bulgaria has consolidated and deepened the stability of its institutions. continuation on its current reform path should enable the country to cope with competitive pressures and market forces within the european union. we will, however, need to keep a close watch on some areas. our intention now is to intensify our monitoring of the commitments that have been made and of continuing preparations in general, in order to ensure that progress continues after the closure of negotiations and that bulgaria will be effectively ready for membership in 2007. in this regard, solid efforts remain necessary concerning the reform of the judiciary, the fight against organised crime and the fight against corruption. bulgaria has made progress in gradually building up its administrative capacity but further efforts remain necessary in this regard in a number of areas. as from november 2005 the commission will issue yearly comprehensive monitoring reports for the council and parliament following the same methodology as was applied to the new member states that joined the union in may 2004. these reports will focus particularly on public administration, the judiciary and the fight against corruption, as well as the track record in economic reforms. it is also necessary to take account of a longer period between completion of the negotiations and the effective date of accession than in previous waves of accession. a specific safeguard was agreed, which allows the commission to recommend to the council to decide by unanimity, at any time, to postpone the date of accession by one year to january 2008 if there is clear evidence that bulgaria is manifestly unprepared. let me conclude by saying that i share the conclusions of the report of your rapporteur, mr van orden, which are, by and large, in line with the 2004 regular report. the commission will continue to keep the european parliament informed of bulgaria’s progress towards accession. bulgaria is on track for accession on 1 january 2007. with the accession of bulgaria and romania, the fifth round of eu enlargement will be concluded. thus the black sea will become a new coastline for an enlarged and unified europe.
as rapporteur for the committee on budgets, i would first like to point out that the pre-accession financial aid granted to bulgaria in the period 2000-2004 amounted to approximately eur 178 million per year from the phare, sapard and ispa programmes. the committee on budgets also supports additional funding from the phare programme of eur 200 million for the period 2000-06 to close the kozloduy nuclear power station. it also welcomes the establishment of a new financing framework for bulgaria in spring 2004 and welcomes the commission's approach of limiting the aid package to a three-year period from bulgaria's accession in 2007 in order to adapt it to future policy reforms that may be needed as a result of the new financial perspective. the committee on budgets stresses once again that financial assistance will depend on the new financial perspective, but also on the adjustment of the annual budget, depending on the financial perspective.
madam president, it is true that bulgaria's capacity to comply with the acquis communautaire has increased considerably and is increasing. however, the committee on industry, research and energy would like to stress that in the areas of research and development, energy, industrial policy and telecommunications policy, additional efforts are needed if we want bulgaria's accession to be a historic success, as the date of accession is already very close. in addition, in order to properly assess the progress achieved and, consequently, to propose the changes that still need to be made, it would be necessary to take into account not only the report of the european commission but also the assessments of various international bodies and other independent research centres, whose opinion can be of great help in analysing and assessing bulgaria's capacity in these areas, with a view to its integration into the european union. in any event, our thoughts at this stage, in relation to each of the sectors within the competence of our committee, are as follows: as regards energy policy, bulgaria - intensifying, the reforms needed. on competition policy, this chapter is at the core of the internal market and european economic integration. the proper enforcement of eu competition rules is a precondition for creating a reliable business environment and requires appropriate administrative capacity. this is a long-term process. it is for those reasons that competition discipline is also a key aspect of the europe agreement. other key aspects are legislative alignment and the institutional and administrative structures in romania. what needs to be done to bring all legislation, including secondary legislation, into line with the requirements in the areas of antitrust and state aid, in particular in relation to fiscal aid? the romanian competition council should be given the powers, resources and the well-trained staff it needs to fulfil its role. this council should prohibit any measures which would be in contradiction with the state aid acquis and the europe agreement. let me turn to the steel sector, which is a sensitive sector across the eu. romania has asked for a prolongation of the so-called 'grace period' under the europe agreement for restructuring the steel industry. again, we only agreed to this now it is clear that romania will abide by all the commitments and all the conditions set out in the eu's position. these commitments include drawing up a national restructuring programme as well as an individual business plan, capacity reduction and dismantling of the installations. the european union expects romania to respect all its commitments and take all the necessary measures within the deadlines laid down in the eu's position. in this context, i should recall the safeguards we have at our disposal. in october 2005 the commission will present to the council a written report assessing romania's progress in the area of competition policy. any serious shortcomings observed in this report regarding romania's obligations under the europe agreement and/or the fulfilment of the commitments can form the basis for a recommendation by the commission to invoke safeguards, in particular the one postponing romania's accession by one year. here the council can decide by a qualified majority. on this understanding, i have come to the conclusion that this chapter does not require further negotiations. let me say that it is now in romania's hands to ensure that it meets all its commitments in this chapter, allowing romania's smooth integration into the european union. turning to justice and home affairs, this is a chapter which is both extensive and complex. it is at the heart of our objective of maintaining and developing the european union as an area of freedom, security and justice. it has a direct bearing on the lives of every eu citizen, and is therefore a key part of the acquis which must be respected. negotiations on this chapter have been long and detailed. romania has made a considerable number of firm commitments on all areas of the justice and home affairs acquis. there are several areas to which particular attention should be paid, such as implementation of the schengen action plan; ensuring a high level of control and surveillance at the external borders of the union; implementing the reform of the judiciary; stepping up the fight against corruption to ensure that corruption cases are dealt with in a swift and transparent manner; making considerable progress in filling the large number of vacancies in the police forces; as well as developing and implementing a coherent multiannual anti-crime strategy. these issues have also been addressed in mr moscovici's report on romania. the union will closely monitor romania's implementation of all its commitments related to justice and home affairs, right up to the moment of accession in order to meet eu standards. this includes adhering to the planned legislative schedule and taking further measures to develop the institutional and administrative capacity of all romanian law enforcement authorities and of the judiciary. we believe that this should be possible if the necessary political effort, as well as the required financial and human resources, are deployed to this end. if, however, any serious shortcomings are observed in the fulfilment by romania of its commitments and in particular any of the specific commitments listed in the eu position, this can form the basis for invoking the safeguard clause postponing romania's accession by one year. here again, the council can decide by qualified majority. the european union will continue to monitor closely romania's preparations and achievements, including the effective implementation of the commitments undertaken in all areas of the acquis and in particular the areas of justice and home affairs, competition and the environment. to this end, the commission will continue to submit annual reports on romania's progress towards accession, together with recommendations if appropriate. i welcome the statement in the report by mr moscovici that the european parliament will monitor the developments in romania as well and encourage the new romanian government to fulfil all the commitments made during the negotiations. it is quite clear that the report adopted by the european parliament in march 2004 has fulfilled its purpose as a wake-up call to the romanian government. that is how the romanian government has perceived it; and it has convinced it to intensify the accession strategy and policies. i was delighted to learn that parliament, in its latest report about romania, could subscribe to the recommendations of the regular report of the commission. since then - and i paraphrase the wording of the commission - we all have made every effort to meet the european council objectives to bring the negotiations with bulgaria and romania to a successful conclusion in 2004, on the basis of its own merits, with a view to signing the accession treaty as early as possible in 2005, and we all expect bulgaria and romania to fulfil the economic and acquis criteria and to be ready for membership on 1 january 2007.

mr president, the welfare of animals during transport has been a recurring theme in this parliament for some years now, even more so than the situation of millions of children who are starving in our europe or who live in poor conditions, also in our europe. if the humanitarian organizations defending these people had shown the same strength as the organizations defending animals, something could probably have been done for these european children who die every day. parliament - i am concentrating more on the subject - has delivered two opinions in three years on the welfare of livestock during transport. in my view, we should not insist any further on this matter, which was fortunately settled last november following the agreement reached by the council of ministers of the european union. although the compromise proposal put forward by the irish presidency was - to my mind - more satisfactory because it limited the duration of transport to a reasonable period, both from the point of view of the welfare of livestock and from the point of view of the free movement of goods within the european union - we remember that it is 9 hours of travel plus 12 hours of rest and another 9 hours of travel - the agreement which has now been reached, under the dutch presidency, does not change the existing rules as regards the duration of journeys at all, leaving a decision on this crucial point of the debate for some six years. the postponement, which - let us remember - is the result of the differences which still exist between the member states, has been put on the table. however, i would like to clarify something here that i am sure many people listening to these debates do not take into account and that i think should be made very clear to the public: the current regulations already limit to a maximum of 8 hours the transport of animals carried out in vehicles which do not comply with the standards of livestock welfare required by the regulations, standards which have also been reinforced by the recent agreement reached by the council of ministers.
mr president, i too would like to welcome very positively the political agreement which will be formally approved next week by the agriculture council, because i think it has one great virtue: it leaves aside - until 2011 - the most controversial issues, which were precisely the ones that caused the negotiations to fail last april - the maximum length of journeys and the loading density of vehicles. in the debate we had with mr maat last term, and which some of us here remember, it became clear that the proposals - as mrs mcguinness has just said - on these two issues, distance and density, lacked a sound scientific basis and, moreover, seriously penalized the large and peripheral states. this whole economic background was disguised as animal welfare, as if we members from the big countries and the peripheral countries were not concerned about animal welfare. in my view, commissioner, the political agreement substantially improves the shortcomings identified in the current legislation. that is the most positive aspect: it improves the control systems, introduces technological elements that facilitate control, establishes a clear and transparent registration system and improves the systems of cooperation between member states and, in addition, establishes the obligation to implement training systems which will also improve the transport of animals. i particularly welcome the wording of article 32, because it clearly states what elements future revisions of this regulation should be based on. for these reasons, i can only congratulate the council on unblocking this issue and hope for a successful implementation of the new text.
mr president, first of all i should like to express my surprise that a rapporteur, mr ribeiro, has devoted himself to defending amendments which have been rejected by the majority of the committee on fisheries. that said, i have to say that our group will support the commission's proposal, the ribeiro report, as adopted in the committee on fisheries, and will vote against the amendments tabled. and i want to explain why. we do not want to include bottom-set gillnets because, as everyone knows, these are static nets which, by their very configuration, do not erode the seabed. the biological disaster which this amendment is intended to evoke could in any case be linked to the loss of these gears and their subsequent ghost fishing activity. as the commissioner has said, this effect has not been scientifically quantified, either by zone or by species. that is why it seems to me frivolous and a bad precedent to ban or attempt to ban these arts in these areas, because, on the same grounds, we would have to ban them in all community waters and then we would see whether all those who defend it in this case would also defend it in the rest. as regards the second amendment, which, based on criteria of marine biology and geology, seeks to replace the protected areas proposed by the commission with the political criterion of 200 miles - a criterion which, in the field of fisheries management, no longer exists in community legislation, whether we like it or not - i would like to stress once again that corals are not distributed over a radius coinciding with the 200 miles of the canary islands, madeira and the azores. it is scientifically assumed that corals are normally distributed around a thousand-meter diameter line. the commission has therefore, in accordance with the precautionary principle, extended the bathing water line to 1 500 metres, lines which obviously do not follow political and administrative divisions. but, moreover, in this case, the zones which the european commission has marked go beyond, in some cases, 200 miles, even reaching international waters. for all these reasons, mr president, our group will not support the amendments tabled.
mr president, i - who welcomed the ribeiro report and the rapporteur's work at the time because, like all of us, i think it is important to protect deep-sea coral reefs - have to say - in the same vein as my colleague mrs fraga has just done - that i hope that i will not see some day on mr ribeiro's table flags - like the ones i see over there - because, to some extent, some of the statements i have heard from the rapporteur's mouth have really surprised me. i would like to say, of course, that we do not agree with amendment no 7 - neither the first part nor the second part. we agree with the commission's proposal, but we cannot agree to the addition of ' gillnets' without further scientific criteria to the commission's proposal, which talks about 'bottom trawls' or 'similar trawls'. we believe that adding ' gillnets' without further details can cause serious damage to certain fleets and, moreover, set a dangerous precedent. we also disagree with the second part, because it seeks to replace the maritime coordinates established by the commission, based on scientific criteria, by the terms 'waters under the jurisdiction' of the member states.
commission. mr president, i welcome the generally positive comments on the proposal, and will respond very briefly to some of the criticisms made. on the possible damage by fishing other than trawls: according to the ices 2003 report, trawls are the main cause of damage to deep-water coral reefs. there is little evidence of passive gear damaging coral reefs, although ices mentions some of these effects. the commission is ready to amend its proposal if there is new scientific evidence or if the member states agree on such an amendment. with regard to the point concerning the extension of the protective zone to the whole eez, i would underline that the proposal delimited an area that includes most of the submarine mountains that have been kept in good condition. extending the zone of prohibition would add insignificant protection and would therefore run c ounter to the principle of proportionality. having said that, i would also refer to the question of the exclusive competence of the commission with regard to marine resources, which is found in the constitution and to which reference has been made. this is a principle which was already established by european court of justice case law, and all the constitution does is to codify it. however, the commission does not deny the rights of spain and portugal over their european economic zone. it is just that there is no need to mention these rights of jurisdiction since the area of prohibition is delimited by topography and by geographical features. on the point made by mrs attwooll concerning the role of the regional advisory councils, there would be a legal problem and in order to accept that amendment the regulation on racs would itself have to be amended. on another point made by mrs attwooll, the commission has recently tabled a proposal on conditions for deep-water fishing, which will lend protection to these important resources.

thank you, chief. the vote will take place at the end of the debate. the debate is closed. bhopal the president. - the next item is the debate on six motions for resolutions on bhopal.
mr president, twenty years after the toxic gas leak at a union carbide corporation fertilizer plant in bhopal, the harmful effects and environmental pollution continue to affect the lives of thousands of people today. on the night of 2 to 3 december 1984, more than 7 000 people died as a result of this gas leak, but the effects of the accident have since caused the death of another 15 000 people and continue to cause chronic illnesses to more than 100 000 people. neither the indian government, nor union carbide or dow chemical, the company that currently owns the fertilizer plant, have taken responsibility for the impact of the accident on the lives of thousands of people and the environment. as the resolution we are voting on today states, there is a need for an independent inquiry into the current situation in bhopal, which could be carried out under the auspices of the united nations commission on human rights, with the involvement of experts, to examine, during visits to india, the consequences of the activities of union carbide and the bhopal disaster for the pollution of groundwater and the environment, and therefore for the human rights of the affected areas and communities. but the sad case of bhopal also shows how, in a context of economic globalisation, it is urgent to demand that companies meet the same responsibilities as states, that they be subject to international treaties and conventions and that their impact be assessed, both in respect for human rights and in situations of armed conflict and tension. the amendments tabled by the green group are in this direction. i would ask you to read them carefully so that you can assess whether you voted yes or no. in addition to echoing the proposal of the school of culture of peace at the autonomous university of barcelona, i would like to urge the house - and also the european union - to promote 3 december as an international day of corporate responsibility and human rights so that companies can commit themselves to the promotion and protection of human rights throughout the world. this commemorative date should serve as an opportunity for all international actors - states, international organisations and civil society, but especially businesses - to reflect on their shared responsibility for building a fairer and more sustainable world.
commission. mr president, the commission welcomes parliament's initiative to launch an urgent debate on this issue. it is an important opportunity for us to reflect on the way in which we can offer help to the victims and how to prevent that set of disasters from occurring in future. let me assure parliament that the commission has been ready to support india in dealing with this tragedy and will do so in the future. through our decentralised cooperation budget line, we have supported local non-governmental organisations in bhopal with rehabilitation and skills training for victims of the disaster, as well as giving support to women’s self-help groups. through our health and family welfare programme, we have supported the bhopal district hospital, as well as patient welfare societies of district hospitals and community centres in the region. special assistance was given to the municipal corporation of bhopal for the preparation of an urban reproductive and child health plan. in addition, the commission has provided a grant of eur 10 million for the funding of the government of india's national disaster risk management programme. at the recent eu-india summit held in the hague, india reconfirmed its interest in pursuing an environment dialogue with the european union and proposed the organisation of an eu-india environment forum. this forum will be a first step in tackling the enormous environmental problems that threaten both india and the european union. let me finish by expressing our deepest sympathy for all the victims and our firm hope that such a catastrophe will never occur again.
thank you, chief. we shall now vote on these motions for resolutions. the debate is closed.
mr president, i would just like to point out that there is an error in the voting list which has been distributed to the socialist group and that, as regards the bhopal amendments, we vote against the first and in favour of the other three.
we've noted your circumstances. (parliament adopted the joint resolution)
